SQL Problem Patterns: A Practice Guide

224 problems classified into 12 SELECT recipe categories by input and output shape, plus a Procedures tab for procedural shapes (DO blocks, sequential UPDATE, RETURNS TABLE), with a diagnostic process, decision tree, step-by-step templates, full solutions, and technique reference.

Last updated: April 2026

Six-Step Diagnostic Process

A systematic process for solving SQL problems. Use the reference cards below to work through the six-step diagnostic, then copy the template into your IDE.

Process The Six Steps (expand for details on each)

▼

Before writing any SQL, work through these six steps. They take 2-3 minutes and prevent the most common mistakes: wrong JOIN type, missing GROUP BY column, or picking the wrong window function.

Step 1: Map Inputs and Output

▼

Read the problem statement and write down what you start with and what you need to produce.

What to write down:

  • Input table(s): Name each table and its columns. Note primary keys and foreign keys.
  • Output columns: List exactly what the result set should contain.
  • Output grain: What does one row in the output represent? (one user? one month? one department?)
  • Row count direction: Will the output have fewer rows, the same rows, or more rows than the input?

Step 2: Classify Inputs

▼

Pick one of three source types: Single table, Join 2+ tables, or Union queries.

Decision checklist:

  • How many tables? Count the FROM/JOIN tables you will need.
  • Joining or stacking? If 2+ tables, do they share a key (JOIN) or do you need to stack independent results (UNION)?
  • Self-join or scalar subquery? Self-joins and subqueries against the same table involve a virtual second copy — treat as Join 2+. Common self-join shapes: employee/manager (managerId → id), category/parent (parent_id → id), user/referrer (referee_id → id). The recipe for these is enrich-join, not row-compare (row-compare is reserved for sequential LAG/LEAD comparisons, not foreign-key lookups).
  • Post-join is single-table: After a JOIN the result is one set of rows, so any single-table shape recipe (filter, aggregate, scalar, rank, transform, compare, window) applies to the joined result.

Step 3: Name the Shape

▼

Use the signal words reference to identify which recipe category this problem matches.

Scan the problem statement for signal words and match them to a recipe shape. Use the reference table below this section for the full mapping. Common shapes:

  • Fewer rows, filtered: row-filter (WHERE conditions)
  • Fewer rows, grouped: group-aggregate (GROUP BY + SUM/COUNT/AVG)
  • Same rows, new column: row-transform (CASE WHEN) or row-compare (LAG/LEAD)
  • Single scalar value: scalar-extract (MAX, Nth value, overall percentage)
  • Multi-table enrichment: enrich-join or enrich-aggregate
  • Ranked per group: rank-partition (DENSE_RANK PARTITION BY)

Composite problems: Some problems chain two recipe moves in sequence (e.g., enrich-join then group-aggregate). If you see two shapes, plan for a CTE or subquery to handle the first shape, then apply the second.

Step 4: Walk the Decision Tree by Elimination

▼

Open the Decision Tree tab and follow the branches. Eliminate categories that do not match.

Open the Decision Tree tab and answer two questions:

  1. How does my data arrive? Single table, Join 2+ tables, or Union queries — tap the matching source card.
  2. What does the output look like? Filter, Aggregate, Scalar, Rank, Transform, Compare, Window, Pair, or Dedup — tap the matching shape leaf inside that source.

Two taps land you on the recipe. Inside the Join 2+ panel, the same nine shape leaves appear under "any single-table shape applied to the joined result," so post-join problems route through the same recipes.

If your Step 3 answer and Step 4 answer disagree, re-read the problem. One of your assumptions is wrong.

Step 5: Grab the Recipe Template

▼

Go to the recipe card and use its technique as your SQL skeleton.

Each recipe card lists:

  • Signal words — confirm this is the right recipe
  • Technique — the SQL pattern to use (GROUP BY, LAG, JOIN, etc.)
  • Example problems — expand any problem to see full ranked solutions

Write your SQL skeleton based on the technique, filling in your specific table and column names.

Step 6: Sanity Check

▼

Before submitting, verify your query against common SQL traps.

Checklist:

  • Row count: Does SELECT COUNT(*) match your expectation from Step 1?
  • NULL handling: Did you account for NULLs in JOIN keys, WHERE filters, and aggregates?
  • Integer division: Did you cast to NUMERIC before dividing? (PostgreSQL: col::numeric)
  • GROUP BY completeness: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY.
  • ORDER BY + LIMIT: If using LIMIT, is ORDER BY deterministic? (add a tiebreaker column)
  • Edge cases: Empty tables, single-row tables, all NULLs, ties in ranking.

Reference Single Table Shape Comparison: Why This Recipe and Not That One

▼

Use this table to confirm your shape choice in Step 3 and rule out alternatives in Step 4. Each row explains what makes a single table recipe different from the others.

Recipe When to Use How to Confirm Not This If...
Output: fewer rows than input
Filter Rows The output is a subset of original rows that pass a condition. This includes deduplication via SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY (the table itself is not modified) Output columns match the input. Rows are removed, not combined. The original table is unchanged after the query runs The output has "for each" or "per" grouping, adds new computed columns, or the problem asks you to physically delete rows from the table
Aggregate Per Group The output has one summary row per group with a count, sum, or average The output has fewer rows than the input, and every value is either a group key or an aggregate Every input row appears in the output, or the answer is a single number
Extract Single Value The entire answer is one number or one row: any aggregate (SUM, COUNT, AVG, MAX, MIN, etc.), an Nth value, or a percentage across the whole table with no grouping The output is exactly one row with one or two columns The output has multiple rows, or you need a value "for each" group
Rank Within Groups You need the top, bottom, or Nth row within each group from a single table using a window function to rank and then filter The output keeps only some rows per group based on position (top 1, top 3, most recent). A window function assigns the rank, then you filter on it You need all rows per group with a summary value (that is Aggregate Per Group), or the ranking requires data from multiple tables (that is Multi Table > Rank Within Groups)
Output: same row count, new or rewritten column
Add or Rewrite Columns Every row stays but gets a new label, category, or reformatted value Output row count equals input row count. The new column depends only on values in that same row The new column needs to reference the previous or next row, or requires a window function
Compare Row to Neighbor Each row needs to see the previous or next row to detect changes, streaks, or gaps Output row count equals input row count. The new column compares a value to the row before or after it The comparison is against a rolling window or running total, not just the immediate neighbor
Output: time-based aggregate over ordered rows
Rolling or Cumulative Window Each row needs an aggregate computed over a date range or a running total up to that point The problem mentions "rolling," "cumulative," "last N days," or "running total" You only need to compare to the immediate previous row (that is Compare Row to Neighbor)
Special: pair flattening or physical deletion
Normalize Bidirectional Rows like (Alice, Bob) and (Bob, Alice) represent the same relationship and need to be merged before counting The table has two ID columns where the roles are interchangeable (sender/receiver, requester/accepter) The two columns have distinct roles (manager/employee, buyer/seller) where direction matters
Remove Duplicate Rows The problem asks you to physically DELETE rows from the table, not just query it. After the query runs, the table itself has changed The expected output is a modified table, not a SELECT result. The word "delete" or "remove" appears in the prompt. If you ran the query twice, the second run would find nothing to delete You just need unique rows in your output but the table should stay unchanged (that is Filter Rows with SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY)

Reference Multi Table Shape Comparison: Why This Recipe and Not That One

▼

Use this table to confirm your recipe choice when the problem gives you two or more tables. Each row explains what makes a multi table recipe different from the others.

Post-join reminder: after a JOIN the result is effectively one table. If your shape is not enrich-join or enrich-aggregate, use any single-table shape recipe (Filter, Scalar, Rank, Transform, Compare, Window, Pair, Dedup) on the joined output. The Decision Tree's Join 2+ panel lists those cross-references explicitly.

Recipe When to Use How to Confirm Not This If...
Look Up Columns You need to attach descriptive columns from a reference table (names, labels) to fact rows. Includes self-joins where one table plays two roles (employee/manager, parent/child, referrer/referee) After joining (or self-joining), the row count stays roughly the same and no aggregation is needed After joining, you still need to GROUP BY and SUM/COUNT (that is Join Then Aggregate)
Join Then Aggregate You need to combine tables and then produce summary statistics from the joined result The output has fewer rows than either input table, and values are aggregates (totals, counts, rates) The output keeps every row from one table and just adds columns from another (that is Look Up Columns)
Rank Within Groups You need the top N rows within each group after joining tables The output asks for "top," "highest," or "first" per group, and the ranking requires data from multiple tables You need all rows per group, not just the top N (that is Join Then Aggregate or Look Up Columns)
Reshape (Pivot / Unpivot / Combine) The output reshapes rows to columns, columns to rows, or stacks independent queries that share the same column structure The result pivots long to wide, unpivots wide to long, or has sections that could each be written as standalone queries with no JOIN between them The rows need to be merged on a shared key (that is a JOIN, not a reshape)

▼

Scan the problem statement for these phrases, match them to a shape, and go straight to the recipe.

Signal Words in the Problem Shape (Output Pattern) Recipe
Core Shape Recipes (single table or post-join)
find where, exclude, valid, not null, matching, whose, not boring Fewer rows → filtered subset Filter Rows
for each, per, how many, total, average, count of, at least N Fewer rows → one row per group Aggregate Per Group
the single, second highest, the one, overall percentage Single scalar value Extract Single Value
top N per department, highest in each, first per group, most recent per Ranked → top-N per partition Rank Partition
fix, convert, classify, label each, if...then, concatenate, swap Same rows → new/rewritten column Row Transform
rising, consecutive, previous day, day over day, increasing, streak, gap Same rows → neighbor comparison Row Compare
rolling, running total, cumulative, last N days, moving average, most recent before Time → windowed aggregate Time Window
friends, connections, either side, requester/accepter, both directions Bidirectional → flatten then count Normalize Bidirectional
delete, remove duplicates, keep only, deduplicate In-place deletion Delete Duplicates
Join-Specific Recipes (when the join itself is the core move)
replace ID with, look up, show name, regardless of, include from, manager/employee, parent/child, referrer/referee Enrichment or self-join → fact + dimension lookup Enrich Join
for each... from another table, rate, percentage, weighted, all products Enrichment → join then aggregate Enrich Aggregate
Reshape Recipe (pivot, unpivot, combine)
report X and also Y, fixed buckets, combine, categorize into, pivot, unpivot, long to wide, wide to long Rows reshaped to columns, columns to rows, or queries stacked Reshape

Reference Step-by-Step Reference: How to Use the Diagnostic Template

▼

Expand each step to see what it means, how to fill it out, and a worked example using #1193 Monthly Transactions I.

PROBLEM — Rewrite the Prompt

▼

Force yourself to actually read the problem by restating it in your own words.

What to do: Rewrite the prompt in plain language. If you can’t restate it simply, you don’t understand it yet. This single step catches most misreads before you write any SQL.

Worked example (#1193):

For each month and country, count total transactions and
sum amount, plus count and sum of approved transactions only.

Step 1: Map the Inputs and the Output

▼

Identify input tables, output columns, and the grain (what makes each row unique).

What to do: List every input table and its columns. Then list the output columns the problem asks for. Determine the grain — what combination of columns gives you exactly one row. Finally, note the row count direction:

  • Fewer rows → filter or aggregate
  • Same rows → transform or compare
  • Single value → scalar extract

This immediately narrows the decision tree before you even think about SQL.

Worked example (#1193):

Input: Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date)
  where state is 'approved' or 'declined'
Output: month, country, trans_count, trans_total_amount,
  approved_count, approved_total_amount
Grain: one row per (month, country)
Row count direction: fewer rows (grouped)

Step 2: Classify the Inputs

▼

Pick one of three source types: Single table, Join 2+ tables, or Reshape.

What to do: Decide how the data arrives. Watch for disguised multi-table problems: scalar subquery denominators and self-joins involve a virtual second table. Remember: after a join, the result is effectively one table, so any single-table shape recipe (filter, aggregate, scalar, rank, transform, compare, window, pair, dedup) still applies to the joined result.

Worked example (#1193):

[x] Single table  [ ] Join 2+ tables  [ ] Reshape

The "approved only" counts might tempt you to think you
need a second table, but everything lives in one
Transactions table.

Step 3: Name the Shape

▼

Match signal words from the prompt to a recipe category and state the shape in one sentence.

What to do: Scan the prompt for verbs and phrases that map to a recipe. Use the Signal Words Reference table to match them. Then say the shape in one sentence: “This is a __________ because __________.”

The 14 recipe category IDs:

CORE SHAPE RECIPES:
  row-filter               Keep/exclude rows by WHERE condition
  group-aggregate          One summary row per group
  scalar-extract           Reduce table to single value
  rank-partition           Top-N per group via window ranking
  row-transform            Add/rewrite columns, keep row count
  row-compare              Compare each row to neighbor (LAG/LEAD)
  time-window              Rolling/cumulative aggregate
  normalize-bidirectional  Flatten symmetric pairs
  delete-duplicates        Remove duplicate rows in place

JOIN-SPECIFIC RECIPES:
  enrich-join              Look up columns from reference table
  enrich-aggregate         Join tables then aggregate

RESHAPE RECIPE:
  reshape                  Pivot, unpivot, or UNION independent queries

PROCEDURAL RECIPES:
  function-wrapped         SELECT inside CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS TABLE
  do-block-sequential      DO $$ ... END $$; with FOR loop + UPDATE

Composite problems: A problem is composite when your sentence has two or more verbs (“join tables THEN aggregate THEN rank”) or two branches survive Step 4 elimination. Intermediate prep steps (assigning row numbers, building a calendar) count as their own move.

Worked example (#1193):

Signal words: "for each month and country" -> GROUP BY
  "count... and sum" -> aggregate
  "approved transactions only" -> conditional aggregation

Named shape: "This is a group-aggregate because I need
  one summary row per (month, country) with conditional splits."

Recipe category: group-aggregate
Composite: No (single recipe)

Step 4: Walk the Decision Tree by Elimination

▼

Rule out every wrong branch with a reason. The last one standing is your answer.

What to do: Go through every recipe on your decision tree side and say why each one is wrong. The last one standing is your answer. If two survive, it is a composite problem. This feels slow at first but it catches mistakes.

Copy-paste elimination sentences:

SOURCE (pick one, rule out the other two):
  Not Single table because I need to match rows across two tables
  Not Join 2+ tables because all the data lives in one table
  Not Reshape because the tables share a key and need to be joined

SHAPE (rule out shapes you do not need):
  Not Filter because I need to group or transform, not just keep/exclude rows
  Not Aggregate because the output is not one summary row per group
  Not Scalar because the output has multiple rows, not a single number
  Not Rank because I need all rows, not just top or bottom N per group
  Not Transform because the output has fewer rows, not the same count
  Not Compare because I do not need to compare each row to its neighbor
  Not Window because I am not computing a running total or moving average
  Not Pair because the columns have distinct roles, not interchangeable
  Not Dedup because this is a SELECT, not a physical DELETE

Worked example (#1193):

Ruled out:
  Not Filter — I need to group, not just keep/exclude rows
  Not Scalar — output has multiple rows, not a single number
  Not Rank — I need all rows, not top-N per group
  Not Transform — output has fewer rows than input
  Not Compare — no row-to-row comparison needed
  Not Window — not a running total or moving average
  Not Pair — columns have distinct roles
  Not Dedup — this is a SELECT, not a DELETE

Remaining: Aggregate Per Group

Step 5: Grab the Recipe, Adapt from a Linked Problem

▼

Pull the template from the recipe card and adapt column names, conditions, and edge cases.

What to do: Open the recipe card for your surviving branch. Copy its SQL template. Find the most similar linked problem inside that recipe card and adapt: join keys, column names, filter conditions, output columns, and edge cases (nulls, duplicates, empty groups).

Worked example (#1193):

Recipe template:
  SELECT group_cols, AGG(value_cols)
  FROM table
  GROUP BY group_cols
  HAVING condition (optional)

Adaptations:
  Group columns: TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), country
  Aggregates: COUNT(*), SUM(amount) for totals
  Conditional splits: SUM(CASE WHEN state='approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
  Date formatting: TO_CHAR for month extraction

Step 6: Sanity Check

▼

Run verification checks against common failure modes before submitting.

What to do: Look up the failure mode for your recipe branch (listed on each recipe card). Then run through the checklist:

  • Row count matches Step 1 expectation
  • NULL handling covered (JOIN keys, WHERE, aggregates)
  • Integer division cast to NUMERIC
  • GROUP BY includes all non-aggregated SELECT columns
  • ORDER BY is deterministic (tiebreaker if using LIMIT)
  • Edge cases: empty table, single row, all NULLs, ties

Red flags (if any appear, go back to Step 4): row count wrong, output grain wrong, missing expected groups.

Common failure modes by recipe:

row-filter:             Off-by-one, unintended NULL exclusion
group-aggregate:        Wrong grain, missing GROUP BY column
scalar-extract:         NULL when no rows qualify
row-transform:          CASE WHEN missing ELSE clause
row-compare:            Wrong ORDER BY in LAG/LEAD
time-window:            Wrong frame spec (ROWS vs RANGE)
normalize-bidirectional: Double-counting after UNION ALL
delete-duplicates:      Deleting wrong row (keep MIN id)
enrich-join:            Wrong join type, NULL join keys
enrich-aggregate:       Row explosion from many-to-many
rank-partition:         RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER
reshape:                Column count/type mismatch in UNION

Worked example (#1193):

Failure mode: group-aggregate — wrong grain or missing GROUP BY column

Checks:
  [x] Row count: one row per (month, country) combo
  [x] NULL handling: country could be NULL (GROUP BY treats as one group)
  [x] Integer division: not applicable (counts and sums, not ratios)
  [x] GROUP BY: TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), country matches SELECT
  [x] CASE WHEN ELSE 0: prevents NULL in approved sums
  [ ] Edge case: month with zero approved transactions still appears

Reference SQL Execution Order (How the Engine Processes Your Query)

▼

Understanding this order helps you predict which clauses can reference which aliases and columns.

  1. FROM / JOIN — Tables are loaded and joined first
  2. WHERE — Row-level filtering (no aggregates allowed here)
  3. GROUP BY — Rows are grouped
  4. HAVING — Group-level filtering (aggregates allowed here)
  5. SELECT — Columns are computed (window functions run here)
  6. DISTINCT — Deduplication
  7. ORDER BY — Sorting (can reference SELECT aliases)
  8. LIMIT / OFFSET — Final row restriction

see problems ▾
Two approaches — choose by data shape:
Window function (ROW_NUMBER) — one pass, no self-join, generally more efficient. Best when you only need the latest row per entity.
GROUP BY + self-join — find max date per group, then join back to get the full row. Necessary when you also need a default value for entities with no history (use LEFT JOIN + COALESCE).
ROW_NUMBER() = 1
latest per entity, one pass
FIRST_VALUE()
grab value from first/last row in window
GROUP BY + MAX(date)
find latest date, then self-join
LEFT JOIN + COALESCE
default value when no history exists
WHERE date <= cutoff
filter to events before target date
Efficiency comparison:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY date DESC) = 1 — single table scan, no self-join. Preferred when no default value is needed.
GROUP BY id + MAX(date) + self-join — requires a second pass (the self-join). Use when you need COALESCE for a default value or when you need multiple columns from the matching row.
Pair
bidirectional symmetric — friends, both directions, either side, sender/receiver, A-to-B same as B-to-A

JOIN Checklist

  1. Identify the join key(s) — columns that connect the tables
  2. Choose join type: INNER (default), LEFT (keep all from first table), CROSS (all combinations)
  3. Check for duplicates in keys — many-to-many creates row explosion
  4. Handle NULL join keys — NULLs never match in a standard JOIN
  5. After joining: verify row count to ensure no unexpected multiplication
Single-Table Recipes

9 recipe categories covering 121 problems. These are the core shape recipes — they apply when your input is a single table and they also apply to the result of a JOIN. The Decision Tree's Join 2+ panel cross-links to every recipe here, so post-join problems land on the same page. Rank Within Groups physically lives under Multi-Table Recipes since most ranking problems involve joins.

Reference Technique Quick Reference: When and Why Each Method Works

▼

A quick lookup for the SQL techniques used across all 9 single table recipe categories, with explanations of when each method applies.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
Filtering Techniques
WHERE Keeps or removes rows based on a condition before any grouping happens The condition can be evaluated row by row without needing an aggregate 
SELECT name
FROM Users
WHERE age > 18;
HAVING Filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregate results The condition depends on a count, sum, or other aggregate (e.g., "groups with more than 1 row") 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*)
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
IN / NOT IN Checks whether a value appears in a list or subquery result You need to filter rows based on whether a value exists in another set of values 
SELECT *
FROM Orders
WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped');
DISTINCT Removes duplicate rows from the output You want unique values but do not need a count or other aggregate 
SELECT DISTINCT country
FROM Customers;
String Techniques (for filtering and transforming text)
LIKE / NOT LIKE Pattern matches using % (any characters) and _ (one character) You need to filter rows where a text column starts with, ends with, or contains a substring 
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
REGEXP / RLIKE / ~ Matches rows using a regular expression. MySQL uses REGEXP or RLIKE, PostgreSQL uses ~ (case sensitive) or ~* (case insensitive) LIKE is not powerful enough: you need anchoring, alternation, character classes, or other regex features 
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE phone REGEXP '^[0-9]{10}$';
POSITION / STRPOS / INSTR Returns the position of a substring inside a string (0 or NULL if not found). PostgreSQL: POSITION(sub IN col) or STRPOS(col, sub). MySQL: INSTR(col, sub) You need to check whether a substring exists and LIKE's wildcards aren't precise enough, or you need the position for slicing 
SELECT POSITION('@' IN email) AS at_pos
FROM Users;
CONCAT Joins strings together. The space trick CONCAT(' ', col) adds a leading space so every value starts at a word boundary You need to combine columns into one string, or prepend a space so LIKE '% prefix%' won't false match mid-word 
SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name
FROM Users;
SUBSTRING / LEFT / RIGHT Extracts part of a string by position. LEFT(col, 4) grabs the first 4 characters You need to pull a fixed length prefix, suffix, or slice from a text value 
SELECT LEFT(name, 4)         AS first_four,
       SUBSTRING(name, 2, 3)  AS slice
FROM Users;
UPPER / LOWER Converts text to all uppercase or all lowercase You need case insensitive matching or the output requires a specific casing 
SELECT UPPER(name) AS upper_name,
       LOWER(email) AS lower_email
FROM Users;
REPLACE / TRIM Swaps or removes characters. TRIM strips leading/trailing whitespace You need to clean up messy text data or swap out specific characters in a column 
SELECT REPLACE(phone, '-', '') AS digits,
       TRIM(name)              AS clean_name
FROM Users;
STRING_AGG / GROUP_CONCAT Concatenates values from multiple rows into one comma separated string. Use ORDER BY inside to control sort order The output needs a list of values collapsed into a single cell per group (PostgreSQL: STRING_AGG, MySQL: GROUP_CONCAT) 
SELECT dept,
       STRING_AGG(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS members
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept;
Aggregation Techniques
GROUP BY Collapses rows into one row per group so aggregates can be computed The output needs one summary row per group (per department, per month, per user) 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept;
SUM / COUNT / AVG / MAX / MIN Computes a single summary value from multiple rows With GROUP BY: one value per group. Without GROUP BY: one value for the whole table (scalar extract) 
SELECT MAX(salary) AS top_pay,
       AVG(salary) AS mean_pay,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount
FROM Emp;
LIMIT / OFFSET Restricts how many rows are returned or skips a number of rows from the top You need the top 1, the Nth value, or need to skip incomplete window rows 
SELECT name
FROM Emp
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;  -- 2nd highest
Row Transform Techniques
CASE WHEN Returns different values based on conditional logic, like an if/else per row You need to classify, label, or remap values based on conditions 
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN age >= 18 THEN 'Adult'
            ELSE 'Minor' END AS group
FROM Users;
UPDATE Modifies existing column values in place The problem asks you to change a column's value for rows that meet a condition 
UPDATE Emp
SET salary = salary * 1.10
WHERE dept = 'Engineering';
COALESCE Returns the first non NULL value from a list of columns or expressions You need a fallback value when a column might be NULL 
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Unknown') AS display_name
FROM Users;
Window Function Techniques
LAG / LEAD Accesses the value from the previous (LAG) or next (LEAD) row in order Each row needs to compare itself to its immediate neighbor to detect changes, streaks, or gaps 
SELECT day, sales,
       LAG(sales)  OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day,
       LEAD(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS next_day
FROM Daily;
ROWS BETWEEN Defines a sliding window frame (e.g., 6 preceding and current row) for a window aggregate You need a rolling average, running total, or cumulative sum over a fixed number of rows 
SELECT day,
       AVG(sales) OVER (
         ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS rolling_7d
FROM Daily;
SUM() OVER / AVG() OVER Computes an aggregate across a window without collapsing rows You need a running or rolling aggregate while keeping every row in the output 
SELECT day, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day
       ) AS running_total
FROM Trans;
ROW_NUMBER() Assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition You need to identify duplicates for deletion or pick one row per group 
SELECT *,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
         PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
       ) AS rn
FROM Emp;
Structural Techniques
UNION ALL Stacks rows from two queries vertically into one result set Two column roles are interchangeable (sender/receiver) and both directions need to appear as one column 
SELECT name FROM Customers
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM Vendors;
LEAST / GREATEST Returns the smaller or larger of two values, normalizing pair order You need to treat (A, B) and (B, A) as the same pair by sorting them into a consistent order 
SELECT LEAST(user1, user2)    AS person1,
       GREATEST(user1, user2) AS person2,
       COUNT(*)               AS calls
FROM Calls
GROUP BY person1, person2;
DELETE + CTE Removes rows from the table using a CTE to identify which rows to keep or remove The problem asks you to physically modify the table, not just query it 
WITH dups AS (
  SELECT id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id
         ) AS rn
  FROM Users
)
DELETE FROM Users
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM dups WHERE rn > 1);

Filter Rows by Column Conditions 27 problems

▼

A single table with all rows visible → a subset of rows matching WHERE conditions.

Signal words: "find all where," "which rows," "valid," "not null," "matching," "whose," "exclude," "not boring"

Technique: WHERE, IS NULL/IS NOT NULL, LIKE, REGEXP, MOD, DISTINCT, NOT IN subquery

Reference Techniques used in Filter Rows

▼

5 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
WHERE Keeps or removes rows based on a condition before any grouping happens The condition can be evaluated row by row without needing an aggregate 
SELECT name
FROM Users
WHERE age > 18;
IN / NOT IN Checks whether a value appears in a list or subquery result You need to filter rows based on whether a value exists in another set of values 
SELECT *
FROM Orders
WHERE status IN ('paid','shipped');
DISTINCT Removes duplicate rows from the output You want unique values but do not need a count or other aggregate 
SELECT DISTINCT country
FROM Customers;
LIKE / NOT LIKE Pattern matches using % (any characters) and _ (one character) You need to filter rows where a text column starts with, ends with, or contains a substring 
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
REGEXP / RLIKE / ~ Matches rows using a regular expression (MySQL: REGEXP; PostgreSQL: ~) LIKE is not powerful enough: you need anchoring, alternation, character classes, or other regex features 
SELECT *
FROM Users
WHERE phone REGEXP '^[0-9]{10}$';

Deduplication belongs here, not in Row Cleanup: If the problem says "find" or "show" unique values, use SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY here. The table stays unchanged. Row Cleanup > Remove Duplicate Rows is only for when the problem says "delete" or "remove" and the table itself must be physically modified.

Easy #1757 Recyclable and Low Fat Products

▼

Find product IDs that are both low fat AND recyclable.

Tables: Products (product_id, low_fats, recyclable)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

An e-commerce company maintains a product database and needs to create a "sustainable choices" catalog highlighting products that are both environmentally friendly (recyclable) and healthy (low fat). This query extracts the product IDs for marketing campaigns.

▶ 1 Simple AND Condition
-- Most efficient: direct AND condition SELECT product_id FROM Products WHERE low_fats = 'Y' AND recyclable = 'Y';

Why this is best: Direct WHERE condition on two columns. Single table scan, no joins or subqueries needed.

Performance: O(n) single table scan. If low_fats and recyclable are indexed, the database engine can use indexes to short-circuit evaluation.

▶ 2 Boolean Expression (Alternative Style)
-- Alternative: using boolean expressions SELECT product_id FROM Products WHERE (low_fats, recyclable) = ('Y', 'Y');

Why this works: Row value comparison compares tuples directly. Some databases support this; PostgreSQL does.

Performance: Same as AND, but slightly less portable across database systems.

Easy #584 Find Customer Referee

▼

Find customer names who are either not referred (NULL) or referred by someone other than customer ID 2.

Tables: Customer (id, name, referee_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering (Note: NULL handling)

Real-World Example

A CRM system tracks customer referrals. To identify customers for a retention campaign, you exclude referrals from a competitor (customer ID 2) but include both organic sign-ups (NULL referee_id) and referrals from other sources.

▶ 1 OR with IS NULL (Correct NULL Handling)
-- Most efficient: OR condition with IS NULL SELECT name FROM Customer WHERE referee_id != 2 OR referee_id IS NULL;

Why this is best: Correctly handles NULL values. In SQL, NULL != 2 evaluates to NULL (unknown), not TRUE, so you must explicitly check for NULL.

Performance: Single table scan. Both conditions are fast; OR allows short-circuit evaluation.

▶ 2 COALESCE to Default Value
-- Using COALESCE to replace NULL with a safe value SELECT name FROM Customer WHERE COALESCE(referee_id, 0) != 2;

Why this works: COALESCE converts NULL to 0, which is always != 2. Simpler than OR but assumes no one is referred by ID 0.

Performance: Single table scan. Slightly slower than OR if many rows are non-NULL (function call on every row).

▶ 2 NOT with Negation
-- Using NOT to exclude referee_id = 2 SELECT name FROM Customer WHERE NOT (referee_id = 2);

Why this works: NOT (referee_id = 2) correctly treats NULL rows as included because NOT(NULL) = NULL, which is falsy.

Performance: Equivalent to the first solution, but less readable for this scenario.

Easy #595 Big Countries

▼

Find countries with either area >= 3 million km² OR population >= 25 million.

Tables: World (name, continent, area, population, gdp)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A geographic analysis tool filters a world dataset to identify "major" countries by economic or demographic significance. Threshold-based filtering on numeric columns is a common pattern in data warehousing and business intelligence.

▶ 1 Simple OR on Two Conditions
-- Most efficient: direct OR on numeric thresholds SELECT name, population, area FROM World WHERE area >= 3000000 OR population >= 25000000;

Why this is best: Single pass through table. Both conditions are simple numeric comparisons. OR allows early exit (if area is large, skip population check).

Performance: O(n) single scan. Indexes on area and population enable fast filtering.

▶ 2 UNION of Two Queries
-- Alternative: UNION of two separate queries SELECT name, population, area FROM World WHERE area >= 3000000 UNION SELECT name, population, area FROM World WHERE population >= 25000000;

Why this works: Each query uses a single index independently. UNION removes duplicates (e.g., countries meeting both criteria).

Performance: Slower: scans table twice plus UNION overhead. Use only if index selectivity heavily favors one condition over OR.

Easy #1148 Article Views I

▼

Find all authors who viewed at least one of their own articles (author_id = viewer_id). Return distinct author IDs sorted by ID.

Tables: Views (article_id, author_id, viewer_id, view_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering + DISTINCT

Real-World Example

A content platform detects "self-view" behavior to identify authors who are artificially inflating view counts on their own content. This metric is used for fraud detection or engagement analysis.

▶ 1 WHERE + DISTINCT + ORDER BY
-- Most efficient: filter, deduplicate, sort SELECT DISTINCT author_id AS id FROM Views WHERE author_id = viewer_id ORDER BY id;

Why this is best: Single pass filtering, then DISTINCT removes duplicates (same author viewed multiple articles). ORDER BY on a small result set is cheap.

Performance: O(n) filter + O(k log k) sort (where k = distinct authors). DISTINCT uses a hash set or sort underneath.

▶ 2 GROUP BY with MIN/MAX
-- Alternative: GROUP BY to get unique authors SELECT author_id AS id FROM Views WHERE author_id = viewer_id GROUP BY author_id ORDER BY id;

Why this works: GROUP BY guarantees one row per author. No aggregate function needed; just grouping handles deduplication.

Performance: Similar to DISTINCT. GROUP BY may be slower if the database uses a sort-based grouping algorithm instead of a hash.

Easy #1683 Invalid Tweets

▼

Find tweet IDs where the content length is strictly greater than 15 characters.

Tables: Tweets (tweet_id, content)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering + Pattern L: String/Text Operations

Real-World Example

A social media platform enforces content moderation rules: tweets with certain properties (e.g., length) violate policy and are flagged for review. String length validation is a foundational content moderation check.

▶ 1 LENGTH() Function
-- Most efficient: use built-in LENGTH function SELECT tweet_id FROM Tweets WHERE LENGTH(content) > 15;

Why this is best: LENGTH() is optimized for string operations and counts characters (not bytes). Most databases support this function.

Performance: O(n) single pass. LENGTH is a fast function call. If you add an index on tweet_id, retrieval is instant.

▶ 2 CHAR_LENGTH() (PostgreSQL Alternative)
-- Alternative for some databases: CHAR_LENGTH SELECT tweet_id FROM Tweets WHERE CHAR_LENGTH(content) > 15;

Why this works: PostgreSQL uses CHAR_LENGTH as an alias for LENGTH. Same performance, different naming convention.

Performance: Identical to LENGTH(). Use based on your database's documentation.

Medium #620 Not Boring Movies

▼

Find movies with odd-numbered IDs and descriptions that are not "boring". Return sorted by rating descending.

Tables: Cinema (id, movie, description, rating)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering + Modulo arithmetic

Real-World Example

A movie recommendation engine filters out low-quality or "boring" content while also applying a weighting bias (odd IDs get higher priority). This combines business rules (genre exclusion) with technical filters (ID-based sampling).

▶ 1 Modulo (%) for Odd ID + NOT EQUAL String
-- Most efficient: modulo for odd check, NOT EQUAL for string SELECT id, movie, description, rating FROM Cinema WHERE id % 2 = 1 AND description != 'boring' ORDER BY rating DESC;

Why this is best: Modulo (id % 2 = 1) checks for odd IDs efficiently. String inequality is a fast comparison. Both conditions can use indexes if available.

Performance: O(n) filter + O(k log k) sort (k = result rows). Short-circuit evaluation: if id is even, skip string check.

▶ 2 MOD() Function (Alternative)
-- Alternative: using MOD() function SELECT id, movie, description, rating FROM Cinema WHERE MOD(id, 2) = 1 AND description != 'boring' ORDER BY rating DESC;

Why this works: MOD() is a standard SQL function equivalent to %. Slightly more portable across databases than %.

Performance: Identical to %. Some databases optimize % better than MOD() or vice versa; benchmark if critical.

▶ 3 CAST and Bitwise AND (Advanced)
-- Advanced: bitwise AND to check last bit SELECT id, movie, description, rating FROM Cinema WHERE (id & 1) = 1 AND description != 'boring' ORDER BY rating DESC;

Why this works: Bitwise AND (id & 1) checks if the least significant bit is set (odd). Fastest on many CPUs but less readable.

Performance: Microscopically faster than %, but negligible in practice. Use only for extreme optimization or in low-level code.

Easy #1527 Patients With a Condition

▼

Find patients who have Type I Diabetes (conditions containing DIAB1 prefix). DIAB1 can appear at the start or after a space.

Tables: Patients (patient_id, patient_name, conditions)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering + Pattern L: String/Text Operations

Real-World Example

Clinical data systems store diagnoses as space-separated ICD codes. To extract patients with Type I Diabetes for a clinical trial, you filter the conditions column by the DIAB1 prefix, which may appear at the start or after other codes.

▶ 1 LIKE with % Wildcards
-- Most efficient for this data: LIKE pattern matching SELECT patient_id, patient_name, conditions FROM Patients WHERE conditions LIKE 'DIAB1%' OR conditions LIKE '% DIAB1%';

Why this is best: LIKE is fast for pattern matching and handles both cases: DIAB1 at the start or after a space. Easy to understand and maintain.

Performance: O(n) scan. LIKE with leading '%' is slower than without, but checking 'DIAB1%' first (no leading %) can short-circuit many rows. Indexes on conditions help if supported.

▶ 2 CONCAT Space Trick (single LIKE, works in PostgreSQL and MySQL)
-- Prepend a space so every code has a space before it SELECT patient_id, patient_name, conditions FROM Patients WHERE CONCAT(' ', conditions) LIKE '% DIAB1%';

Why this works: Adding a space to the front means even the first condition code now has a space before it. One LIKE pattern catches all positions without needing an OR. Also prevents false matches like "SADIAB100" because the space must appear before "DIAB1".

Performance: Same O(n) scan as the two-LIKE approach but simpler logic. Works in both PostgreSQL and MySQL since CONCAT and LIKE are standard SQL.

▶ 3 Regular Expression (PostgreSQL only)
-- Alternative (PostgreSQL): regex for precise matching SELECT patient_id, patient_name, conditions FROM Patients WHERE conditions ~ '(^| )DIAB1';

Why this works: Regex (^| ) means "start of string OR space". Matches DIAB1 at start or after a space. More precise than multiple LIKE clauses.

Performance: Regex can be slower than LIKE for simple patterns, but on this query is comparable. Regex indexes (GIN/GIST) in PostgreSQL accelerate this further.

▶ 3 String Position Check (INSTR/POSITION)
-- Alternative: check position of DIAB1 SELECT patient_id, patient_name, conditions FROM Patients WHERE conditions LIKE 'DIAB1%' OR POSITION(' DIAB1' IN conditions) > 0;

Why this works: POSITION returns 0 if not found, > 0 if found. Handles both start and middle cases.

Performance: Slightly slower than LIKE due to function calls, but clearer intent. Use if code readability is a priority.

Easy #1517 Find Users With Valid E-Mails

▼

Find users with valid emails where the email is at domain @example.com and the prefix starts with a letter and contains only alphanumeric, underscore, period, or dash characters.

Tables: Users (user_id, name, mail)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering + Pattern L: String/Text Operations

Real-World Example

An email marketing system validates user emails before sending campaigns. Data quality checks filter out invalid formats and domains not matching the organization. This prevents bounces and ensures message delivery to the right audience.

▶ 1 Regular Expression (PostgreSQL)
-- Most precise: PostgreSQL regex validation SELECT user_id, name, mail FROM Users WHERE mail ~ '^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9._-]*@example\\.com$';

Why this is best: Regex precisely validates the format: must start with letter, contain allowed chars only, end with @example.com. Single condition, clear intent.

Performance: O(n) scan. Regex matching is efficient in PostgreSQL. More precise than LIKE, avoiding false positives.

▶ 2 LIKE with Domain Check
-- Alternative (less precise): LIKE pattern SELECT user_id, name, mail FROM Users WHERE mail LIKE '[A-Za-z]%@example.com';

Why this works: LIKE pattern checks domain and that the prefix starts with a letter. However, LIKE allows invalid characters (!, #, etc.) between the letter and @.

Performance: Slightly faster than regex but much less accurate. Only use if the data is pre-validated.

▶ 3 String Function Composition
-- Advanced: using string functions for validation SELECT user_id, name, mail FROM Users WHERE mail LIKE '%@example.com' AND SUBSTRING(mail, 1, 1) ~ '[A-Za-z]' AND mail !~ '[^A-Za-z0-9._\-@]';

Why this works: Breaks validation into steps: domain check, first-char check, and no-invalid-chars check. Verbose but readable for teams unfamiliar with complex regex.

Performance: Slower: multiple function calls and regex checks. Use only if maintainability trumps performance.

#1978 Employees Whose Manager Left the Company (Easy)

▼

After layoffs or departures, HR audits the employee table for orphaned manager references (records pointing to deleted managers), often filtering by salary band to prioritize severance or reassignment.

Schema: Employees(employee_id, name, manager_id, salary)

Find employee_ids where: salary < 30000 AND manager_id IS NOT NULL AND manager_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Employees). These employees have a manager who left (deleted from table).

Business Context: HR Data Quality Audit

After layoffs or departures, HR audits the employee table for orphaned manager references (records pointing to deleted managers), often filtering by salary band to prioritize severance or reassignment.

▶ Rank 1: NOT IN with Subquery Straightforward and explicit
SELECT employee_id FROM Employees WHERE salary < 30000 AND manager_id IS NOT NULL AND manager_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Employees) ORDER BY employee_id;

Why this ranks first: Logic is clear: filter for salary, exclude NULLs, then find managers not in the employee list. Subquery is uncorrelated (runs once). Simple to understand and maintain.

▶ Rank 2: LEFT JOIN with IS NULL Avoids NOT IN (NULL safety)
SELECT e.employee_id FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id WHERE e.salary < 30000 AND e.manager_id IS NOT NULL AND m.employee_id IS NULL ORDER BY e.employee_id;

Tradeoff: LEFT JOIN self on manager_id. If JOIN finds a match, m.employee_id is NOT NULL. If no match (manager left), m.employee_id IS NULL. Safer with NULL values than NOT IN in some SQL dialects.

▶ Rank 3: NOT EXISTS with Correlated Semantic alternative
SELECT e.employee_id FROM Employees e WHERE e.salary < 30000 AND e.manager_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Employees m WHERE m.employee_id = e.manager_id ) ORDER BY e.employee_id;

Tradeoff: Correlated subquery runs for each employee. O(n) + O(n) lookup overhead. Semantically clear ("does manager exist?"). Slower than Rank 1 on large tables but acceptable for <10k employees.

NOT IN vs. LEFT JOIN vs. NOT EXISTS

NOT IN (Rank 1) subquery runs once; if the subquery has NULLs, NOT IN returns unknown (slow). LEFT JOIN (Rank 2) is SQL-standard and NULL-safe. NOT EXISTS (Rank 3) is correlated and slower for large tables. For employee tables, any method is fast, but Rank 2 is most robust.

Easy #183 Customers Who Never Order

▼

Find customers whose id does not appear in the Orders table.

Tables: Customers (id, name), Orders (id, customerId)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A retention team wants to target customers who created accounts but never placed an order so they can send a first-purchase promo. This query returns the list of dormant accounts.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN with NULL Check
-- Anti-join pattern using LEFT JOIN SELECT c.name AS Customers FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customerId = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and attaches any matching order rows. Customers without a match show NULL on the Orders side, which the WHERE clause filters to only those dormant customers.

Performance: O(n + m) with indexes on customerId. Usually faster than NOT IN on large tables because it avoids building an in-memory list and is NULL-safe.

▶ 2 NOT IN Subquery
-- Alternative using NOT IN SELECT name AS Customers FROM Customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customerId FROM Orders);

Why this works: Reads naturally and is portable. Works well when the Orders.customerId column is guaranteed NOT NULL.

Performance: If customerId has any NULL values, NOT IN returns no rows (SQL three-valued logic pitfall). LEFT JOIN avoids that risk.

Easy #607 Sales Person

▼

List salespeople who did not make any order to a specific company (RED).

Tables: SalesPerson (sales_id, name), Orders (order_id, sales_id, com_id), Company (com_id, name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A sales manager wants to know which reps have never worked with a key competitor account so she can assign them to prospect it without channel conflict.

▶ 1 NOT IN with Subquery
-- Exclude salespeople linked to RED via Orders + Company join SELECT s.name FROM SalesPerson s WHERE s.sales_id NOT IN ( SELECT o.sales_id FROM Orders o JOIN Company c ON c.com_id = o.com_id WHERE c.name = 'RED' );

Why this is best: The inner query returns every sales_id that has ever sold to RED. NOT IN returns everyone else, which is the answer.

Performance: Subquery evaluates once. Index Company.name for the filter and Orders.com_id for the join.

Easy #1084 Sales Analysis III

▼

Find products sold only within Q1 2019 (Jan 1 through Mar 31), never outside.

Tables: Product (product_id, product_name), Sales (product_id, sale_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

Merchandising wants to identify seasonal Q1-only products so they can plan end-of-season clearance before those SKUs are restocked.

▶ 1 GROUP BY with MIN/MAX Bounds
-- All sale dates fall inside Q1 2019 SELECT s.product_id, p.product_name FROM Sales s JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id GROUP BY s.product_id, p.product_name HAVING MIN(s.sale_date) >= '2019-01-01' AND MAX(s.sale_date) <= '2019-03-31';

Why this is best: If the earliest and latest sale both fall inside Q1, every sale in between does too. This is the cleanest range-containment test.

Performance: Single group-by pass over Sales, then join to Product. Fast with an index on sale_date.

Medium #1270 All People Report to the Given Manager

▼

Find all employees who report (directly or indirectly) to manager with id 1.

Tables: Employees (employee_id, employee_name, manager_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

HR needs the full org subtree under the CEO to send a company-wide compliance training and confirm everyone in the hierarchy has been notified.

▶ 1 Recursive CTE
-- Walk down the reporting tree from manager 1 WITH RECURSIVE Subordinates AS ( SELECT employee_id, manager_id FROM Employees WHERE manager_id = 1 AND employee_id <> 1 UNION ALL SELECT e.employee_id, e.manager_id FROM Employees e JOIN Subordinates s ON e.manager_id = s.employee_id ) SELECT employee_id FROM Subordinates;

Why this is best: Recursive CTE is the canonical pattern for hierarchy traversal. It starts with direct reports and repeatedly adds their reports until no new rows appear.

Performance: O(n) where n is subtree size. Unbounded trees should also have a depth guard in production, but the prompt guarantees depth 3.

▶ 2 Three Self-Joins (Fixed Depth)
-- Works when depth is known to be at most 3 SELECT e1.employee_id FROM Employees e1 JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.manager_id = e2.employee_id JOIN Employees e3 ON e2.manager_id = e3.employee_id WHERE e3.manager_id = 1 AND e1.employee_id <> 1;

Why this works: The prompt constrains the tree to 3 levels, so three self-joins capture every subordinate. Simpler than recursion.

Performance: Joins are fast with an index on manager_id. Fragile if depth ever grows beyond 3.

Easy #1350 Students With Invalid Departments

▼

List students whose department_id does not exist in the Departments table.

Tables: Students (id, name, department_id), Departments (id, name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A registrar cleans up enrollment records each semester. Students pointing to nonexistent department IDs signal data-entry errors that must be corrected before transcripts are generated.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN Anti-Pattern
-- Students whose department join fails SELECT s.id, s.name FROM Students s LEFT JOIN Departments d ON d.id = s.department_id WHERE d.id IS NULL;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN brings NULL for orphaned department references. Filtering to NULL returns exactly the invalid rows.

Performance: O(n + m) with indexes. Preferred over NOT IN when the referenced column may be NULL.

Medium #1398 Customers Who Bought Products A and B but Not C

▼

Identify customers who purchased both A and B but never C.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, customer_name), Orders (order_id, customer_id, product_name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

Product marketing wants to cross-sell product C to customers who already use the related products A and B. The list drives a targeted email campaign.

▶ 1 GROUP BY with Conditional SUM
-- Per-customer flags summed into HAVING SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name HAVING SUM(product_name = 'A') > 0 AND SUM(product_name = 'B') > 0 AND SUM(product_name = 'C') = 0 ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Why this is best: Conditional SUM counts rows matching each product. HAVING encodes the three conditions at once in a single group-by pass.

Performance: One scan of Orders, one group-by. No subqueries.

Hard #1412 Find the Quiet Students in All Exams

▼

Return students who took at least one exam and never scored the min or max on any exam.

Tables: Student (student_id, student_name), Exam (exam_id, student_id, score)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

An academic advisor wants to spot consistently middle-of-the-pack students who never stood out. These students are candidates for a mentoring program.

▶ 1 Window Functions with MIN/MAX per Exam
-- Flag each row with per-exam extremes, then exclude any student ever matching WITH ranked AS ( SELECT student_id, score, MIN(score) OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id) AS min_score, MAX(score) OVER (PARTITION BY exam_id) AS max_score FROM Exam ) SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name FROM Student s WHERE s.student_id IN (SELECT student_id FROM Exam) AND s.student_id NOT IN ( SELECT student_id FROM ranked WHERE score = min_score OR score = max_score ) ORDER BY s.student_id;

Why this is best: Per-exam MIN/MAX identifies who is loud on any exam. Anti-join removes those students; the remaining ones are quiet across every exam they took.

Performance: One window pass, one anti-join. Linear in the number of exam rows.

Easy #1495 Friendly Movies Streamed Last Month

▼

Return distinct movie titles streamed in June 2020 that are rated family-friendly.

Tables: TVProgram (program_date, content_id, channel), Content (content_id, title, Kids_content, content_type)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A streaming service plans a summer kids-friendly landing page and needs the distinct titles that played last month to prioritize editorial copy.

▶ 1 Join with DISTINCT and Date Range
-- Join streaming log to content metadata SELECT DISTINCT c.title FROM TVProgram t JOIN Content c ON c.content_id = t.content_id WHERE c.Kids_content = 'Y' AND c.content_type = 'Movies' AND t.program_date BETWEEN '2020-06-01' AND '2020-06-30';

Why this is best: Straight inner join with range filter. DISTINCT removes duplicates from rebroadcasts.

Performance: Index on program_date and content_id. Fast even on multi-million row logs.

Easy #1511 Customer Order Frequency

▼

Find customers who spent at least $100 in both June and July 2020.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, name, country), Product (product_id, description, price), Orders (order_id, customer_id, product_id, order_date, quantity)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A loyalty program wants to reward repeat summer buyers. Customers spending $100+ in both months earn an exclusive VIP tier upgrade.

▶ 1 GROUP BY with Conditional SUM
-- Separate sums for each month using CASE SELECT c.customer_id, c.name FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = o.product_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.order_date) = 6 AND YEAR(o.order_date) = 2020 THEN o.quantity * p.price ELSE 0 END) >= 100 AND SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(o.order_date) = 7 AND YEAR(o.order_date) = 2020 THEN o.quantity * p.price ELSE 0 END) >= 100;

Why this is best: Conditional SUMs compute each month's spend per customer in one pass. HAVING enforces both thresholds at once.

Performance: Single join + group-by. Indexes on order_date and customer_id help.

Easy #1607 Sellers With No Sales

▼

List sellers who made no orders in 2020, ordered by name.

Tables: Customer (customer_id, customer_name), Orders (order_id, sale_date, order_cost, customer_id, seller_id), Seller (seller_id, seller_name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

Sales leadership needs to review reps who had zero sales last fiscal year as part of a performance plan review.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN Filtered to 2020
-- Sellers whose 2020 orders are all absent SELECT s.seller_name FROM Seller s LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.seller_id = s.seller_id AND YEAR(o.sale_date) = 2020 WHERE o.order_id IS NULL ORDER BY s.seller_name;

Why this is best: Filter the join on 2020 so the anti-match detects sellers with zero 2020 orders even if they had sales in other years.

Performance: Linear in orders + sellers. Index on sale_date and seller_id.

Hard #1767 Find the Subtasks That Did Not Execute

▼

For each task, list its subtask ids that are missing from the Executed log.

Tables: Tasks (task_id, subtasks_count), Executed (task_id, subtask_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

An orchestration platform stores a task with N subtasks. If any subtask never executed, the job is incomplete; this query surfaces exactly which ones failed to run.

▶ 1 Recursive Generator + Anti-Join
-- Generate 1..subtasks_count per task, then LEFT JOIN executed WITH RECURSIVE AllSubtasks AS ( SELECT task_id, 1 AS subtask_id, subtasks_count FROM Tasks UNION ALL SELECT task_id, subtask_id + 1, subtasks_count FROM AllSubtasks WHERE subtask_id < subtasks_count ) SELECT a.task_id, a.subtask_id FROM AllSubtasks a LEFT JOIN Executed e ON e.task_id = a.task_id AND e.subtask_id = a.subtask_id WHERE e.subtask_id IS NULL;

Why this is best: You need every id 1..N per task even if missing from Executed. A recursive CTE manufactures the full expected set; the anti-join returns the gaps.

Performance: Recursion depth = max subtasks_count. Linear overall.

Easy #1809 Ad-Free Sessions

▼

Count playback sessions that had no ad impression during the session window.

Tables: Playback (session_id, customer_id, start_time, end_time), Ads (ad_id, customer_id, timestamp)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A content PM measures how many sessions were ad-free to understand ad-load impact on viewer retention and premium tier value.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN on Time-Range Overlap
-- Anti-join on any ad that fell in the session window SELECT p.session_id FROM Playback p LEFT JOIN Ads a ON a.customer_id = p.customer_id AND a.timestamp BETWEEN p.start_time AND p.end_time WHERE a.ad_id IS NULL;

Why this is best: Join on overlap condition, then return rows that failed to match. Cleaner than a correlated NOT EXISTS for readability.

Performance: Index on Ads.customer_id and timestamp. Range join is the bottleneck at scale.

Medium #2020 Number of Accounts That Did Not Stream

▼

Count accounts that subscribed in 2021 but did not stream anything in 2021.

Tables: Subscriptions (account_id, start_date, end_date), Streams (session_id, account_id, stream_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A subscription service identifies "zombie" accounts that paid but never engaged in 2021. These accounts are a churn risk and candidates for re-engagement offers.

▶ 1 Subscribers Active in 2021 Minus Streamers in 2021
-- Accounts subscribed in 2021 but absent from 2021 stream log SELECT COUNT(*) AS accounts_count FROM Subscriptions s WHERE s.start_date <= '2021-12-31' AND s.end_date >= '2021-01-01' AND s.account_id NOT IN ( SELECT account_id FROM Streams WHERE YEAR(stream_date) = 2021 );

Why this is best: First condition finds accounts with any active day in 2021. The NOT IN clause drops anyone who streamed. COUNT returns the scalar.

Performance: Subquery runs once. Index stream_date and account_id.

Easy #2026 Low-Quality Problems

▼

List problem ids where likes are strictly less than dislikes, sorted descending.

Tables: Problems (problem_id, likes, dislikes)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

Content QA reviews community feedback weekly. Items with more dislikes than likes go on the review queue for editorial cleanup or removal.

▶ 1 Direct WHERE Comparison
-- Two-column comparison SELECT problem_id FROM Problems WHERE likes < dislikes ORDER BY problem_id DESC;

Why this is best: Simplest possible filter. No subqueries needed.

Performance: Single scan.

Medium #2084 Drop Type 1 Orders for Customers With Type 0 Orders

▼

If a customer has any Type 0 order, keep only their Type 0 rows; otherwise keep their Type 1 rows.

Tables: Orders (order_id, customer_id, order_type)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A billing pipeline deduplicates parallel order records: if a customer has a "primary" order type, drop their fallback one. This cleans up the ledger before charge runs.

▶ 1 Per-Customer Has-Zero Flag
-- Use MAX(order_type = 0) per customer as a flag WITH flags AS ( SELECT customer_id, MAX(CASE WHEN order_type = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_zero FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT o.* FROM Orders o JOIN flags f ON f.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE (f.has_zero = 1 AND o.order_type = 0) OR (f.has_zero = 0 AND o.order_type = 1);

Why this is best: Flag each customer once. The WHERE clause applies different rules depending on the flag, keeping the correct rows in one pass.

Performance: One aggregate + one join. Linear.

Medium #2738 Count Occurrences in Text

▼

Count rows where a text column contains both "bull" and "bear" as whole words.

Tables: Files (file_name, content)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A financial news content ops team categorizes articles that mention both bullish and bearish sentiment for editorial balance review.

▶ 1 UNION ALL with Whole-Word Regex
-- Word-boundary match for each term, then union and count SELECT 'bull' AS word, SUM(content REGEXP '[[:<:]]bull[[:>:]]') AS count FROM Files UNION ALL SELECT 'bear', SUM(content REGEXP '[[:<:]]bear[[:>:]]') FROM Files;

Why this is best: Regex with word boundaries avoids false positives like "bullet" or "bearing". Summing the boolean counts matching rows.

Performance: Two table scans. Full-text index would speed this up dramatically on a large corpus.

Easy #2987 Find Expensive Cities

▼

Return cities whose average listed price is strictly above the national average.

Tables: Listings (listing_id, city, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A real-estate search portal ranks cities by pricing power. Cities averaging above the national mean are highlighted as premium markets.

▶ 1 GROUP BY with Global-Average Subquery
-- Compare each city average to the global average SELECT city FROM Listings GROUP BY city HAVING AVG(price) > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM Listings) ORDER BY city;

Why this is best: Subquery returns a single scalar; HAVING compares each city group against it.

Performance: Global AVG evaluated once. Group-by scans Listings once.

Easy #2990 Loan Types

▼

Find user_ids that have both a Refinance and a Mortgage loan.

Tables: Loans (loan_id, user_id, loan_type)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering

Real-World Example

A lender cross-sells personal loans to customers who already hold two product types with them, since two-product holders show higher retention.

▶ 1 GROUP BY with HAVING DISTINCT Count
-- Users with both specific types SELECT user_id FROM Loans WHERE loan_type IN ('Refinance', 'Mortgage') GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT loan_type) = 2 ORDER BY user_id;

Why this is best: Filter to the two types of interest, then require both appear per user via DISTINCT count.
