Collapse Rows Into One Per Group 35 problems

▼

A single table of granular records → one summary row per group with aggregated values.

Signal words: "for each," "per," "how many," "total," "average," "count of," "at least N"

Technique: GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT DISTINCT, CASE WHEN inside aggregates, self-join + GROUP BY

Reference Techniques used in Aggregate Per Group

▼

5 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
GROUP BY Collapses rows into one row per group so aggregates can be computed The output needs one summary row per group (per department, per month, per user) 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept;
HAVING Filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregate results The condition depends on a count, sum, or other aggregate (e.g., "groups with more than 1 row") 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*)
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
SUM / COUNT / AVG / MAX / MIN Computes a single summary value from multiple rows With GROUP BY: one value per group. Without GROUP BY: one value for the whole table 
SELECT MAX(salary) AS top_pay,
       AVG(salary) AS mean_pay,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount
FROM Emp;
CASE WHEN Returns different values based on conditional logic, like an if/else per row You need to classify, label, or remap values based on conditions 
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN age >= 18 THEN 'Adult'
            ELSE 'Minor' END AS group
FROM Users;
DISTINCT Removes duplicate rows from the output You want unique values but do not need a count or other aggregate 
SELECT DISTINCT country
FROM Customers;

#2356 Number of Unique Subjects Taught by Each Teacher (Easy)

▼

For each teacher, count distinct subjects taught (across all departments).

Schema: Teacher(teacher_id, subject_id, dept_id)

Goal: For each teacher, count distinct subjects taught (across all departments).

Why this matters
Universities need to understand teacher versatility and curriculum coverage.
▶ Rank 1: Simple GROUP BY + COUNT(DISTINCT)
SELECT teacher_id, COUNT(DISTINCT subject_id) AS cnt FROM Teacher GROUP BY teacher_id ORDER BY teacher_id;

Why rank 1: Straightforward, efficient. COUNT(DISTINCT col) handles duplicates automatically. Single scan of the table with in-database deduplication.

Performance: O(n) with early aggregation. No subqueries or joins.

#1729 Find Followers Count (Easy)

▼

For each user, count how many followers they have. Ordered by user_id ascending.

Schema: Followers(user_id, follower_id)

Goal: For each user, count how many followers they have. Ordered by user_id ascending.

Why this matters
Social media platforms need to track influence and user engagement metrics at scale.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY user_id + COUNT + ORDER BY
SELECT user_id, COUNT(follower_id) AS followers_count FROM Followers GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id ASC;

Why rank 1: Direct aggregation with sorting. Each user_id groups all their followers; COUNT(follower_id) tallies each group.

Performance: Single pass with sort at the end (linear for small result sets). No risk of NULL issues since we count a NOT-NULL column.

#596 Classes With at Least 5 Students (Easy)

▼

Find all classes with 5 or more students (filter after grouping).

Schema: Courses(student, class)

Goal: Find all classes with 5 or more students (filter after grouping).

Why this matters
Schools use enrollment thresholds to determine whether classes run or merge; HR departments filter teams by minimum size for resource allocation.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY class + HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
SELECT class FROM Courses GROUP BY class HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

Why rank 1: HAVING is the correct clause for filtering groups after aggregation. WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so it can't see aggregate results.

Performance: O(n log n) due to grouping, but scales well. HAVING condition is evaluated after aggregation, avoiding unnecessary work.

⚠️
Common Trap
Using WHERE instead of HAVING: WHERE COUNT(*) >= 5 will error because WHERE runs before GROUP BY. Always use HAVING for aggregate conditions.

#1211 Queries Quality and Percentage (Medium)

▼

For each query_name, calculate quality (avg of rating/position) and poor_query_percentage (% with rating < 3), both rounded to 2 decimals.

Schema: Queries(query_name, result, position, rating)

Goal: For each query_name, calculate quality (avg of rating/position) and poor_query_percentage (% with rating < 3), both rounded to 2 decimals.

Why this matters
Search engine and database optimization: ranking quality by position and user satisfaction (rating), identifying low-quality queries for improvement.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY + AVG(rating/position) + Conditional Aggregation
SELECT query_name, ROUND(AVG(rating::numeric / position), 2) AS quality, ROUND(100 * SUM(CASE WHEN rating < 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS poor_query_percentage FROM Queries GROUP BY query_name ORDER BY quality DESC, query_name;

Why rank 1: Demonstrates conditional aggregation with CASE WHEN inside SUM/COUNT. The casting to numeric avoids integer division. Single pass through data.

Performance: O(n) scan with in-database aggregation. CASE WHEN is evaluated row-by-row within each group.

⚠️
Integer Division Trap
In PostgreSQL, integer / integer = integer (truncates). Cast to numeric: rating::numeric / position, or use CAST. Otherwise 1 / 200 = 0 instead of 0.005.

Easy #1141 User Activity for the Past 30 Days I

▼

Count daily active users (DAU) for a 30-day period ending 2019-07-27. A user is active if they had ≥1 activity on that day.

Tables: Activity (user_id, session_id, activity_date, activity_type)

View on LeetCode →

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering + Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

Product analytics generates Daily Active Users (DAU) metrics for management dashboards. A 30-day rolling metric shows user engagement trends; users with multiple activities in one day count as 1 DAU.

▶ 1 WHERE with Date Range + GROUP BY + COUNT DISTINCT
SELECT activity_date AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users FROM Activity WHERE activity_date BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY activity_date ORDER BY activity_date;

Why this is best: BETWEEN filters to exact 30-day window (inclusive both ends). COUNT DISTINCT user_id deduplicates multiple activities per user per day. Simple and efficient.

Performance: O(n) for WHERE, then aggregation. Index on activity_date helps filter. COUNT DISTINCT adds minimal cost (hash or sort).

▶ 2 WHERE with Date Arithmetic
SELECT activity_date AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users FROM Activity WHERE activity_date >= '2019-07-27' - INTERVAL '29 days' AND activity_date <= '2019-07-27' GROUP BY activity_date ORDER BY activity_date;

Why this works: Dynamically calculates date range from end date. "29 days" (not 30) because we include both endpoints. Useful for parameterized queries (pass @end_date dynamically).

Performance: Identical to approach #1. INTERVAL syntax varies (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLServer differ). Slightly more flexible.

▶ 3 Subquery with DISTINCT (Less Efficient)
SELECT activity_date AS day, COUNT(*) AS active_users FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id, activity_date FROM Activity WHERE activity_date BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' ) unique_activities GROUP BY activity_date ORDER BY activity_date;

Why this works: Subquery deduplicates (user_id, activity_date) pairs first, then GROUP BY counts. COUNT(*) instead of COUNT DISTINCT on pre-deduplicated data.

Performance: Subquery adds overhead: extra scan for DISTINCT, then outer GROUP BY. Slower than approach #1 (two aggregation passes). Use only if readability strongly preferred.

#1193 Monthly Transactions I (Medium)

▼

For each month and country, count total transactions and sum amount, plus count and sum of approved transactions only.

Schema: Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date) where state is 'approved' or 'declined'

Goal: For each month and country, count total transactions and sum amount, plus count and sum of approved transactions only.

Why this matters
Financial reporting and compliance: tracking transaction volumes and values by geography and time, separately for approved vs. all transactions to measure approval rates and fraud risk.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY month + country + Conditional SUM for approved
SELECT TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, country, COUNT(*) AS trans_count, SUM(amount) AS trans_total_amount, SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved_count, SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_total_amount FROM Transactions GROUP BY TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), country ORDER BY month, country;

Why rank 1: Single pass with all metrics calculated in one GROUP BY. CASE WHEN inside SUM filters by state for conditional aggregation. TO_CHAR formats dates to YYYY-MM.

Performance: O(n) scan. All aggregations happen in one group-by phase—very efficient.

💡
Date Formatting
PostgreSQL uses TO_CHAR for date formatting. MySQL uses DATE_FORMAT. Always adjust for your database system. Some systems also support DATE_TRUNC for month boundaries.

#1612 Monthly Transactions II (Medium)

▼

Extend #1193 with chargebacks: for each month and country, report approved count/amount and chargeback count/amount, excluding all zero rows.

Schema: Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date), Chargebacks(trans_id, trans_date)

Goal: For each month and country, report approved_count, approved_amount, chargeback_count, chargeback_amount. Chargebacks use the chargeback date (not the original transaction date). Exclude rows where all four values are zero.

View on LeetCode →

Why this matters
Chargeback monitoring is critical for payment fraud detection and merchant risk scoring. Combining approved transactions with chargebacks by month and country reveals dispute hotspots and helps compliance teams flag anomalies.

Composite (3 moves): Move 1: pre-filter (WHERE state = 'approved' so declined rows never enter the pipeline). Move 2: enrich + union-stack (JOIN chargebacks to transactions for country/amount, then UNION ALL both streams with a type label). Move 3: pivot-aggregate (conditional SUM/COUNT by type).

▶ Rank 1: Pre-filter + UNION ALL + Conditional Aggregation
WITH approved AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', trans_date)::date AS month, country, amount FROM Transactions WHERE state = 'approved' ), chargebacks AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', c.trans_date)::date AS month, t.country, t.amount FROM Chargebacks AS c JOIN Transactions AS t ON c.trans_id = t.id ), stacked AS ( SELECT month, country, amount, 'approved' AS type FROM approved UNION ALL SELECT month, country, amount, 'chargeback' AS type FROM chargebacks ) SELECT TO_CHAR(month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, country, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved_count, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_amount, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'chargeback' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_count, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'chargeback' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_amount FROM stacked GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1;

Why this works: Three CTEs, each with one job. approved pre-filters to only approved transactions, so declined rows never enter the pipeline. chargebacks joins to the original transaction for country and amount, using the chargeback date for the month. stacked combines both streams with a clean type label. The final SELECT pivots with conditional aggregation.

Performance: Two scans (Transactions + Chargebacks), one join, one UNION ALL, one GROUP BY pass.

Key details:

  • Pre-filter eliminates HAVING: by excluding declined transactions upfront, every row in stacked contributes to at least one output column, so no all zero rows can form
  • Chargeback date vs transaction date: the problem counts chargebacks by when they were filed (c.trans_date), not when the original transaction occurred
  • Type label instead of flag: a readable 'approved' / 'chargeback' string makes the CASE WHEN expressions self documenting
  • No DISTINCT needed: source tables have unique rows, so DISTINCT adds overhead without changing results
💡
Builds on #1193
#1193 Monthly Transactions I uses the same conditional aggregation pattern but on a single table. This sequel adds a second table (Chargebacks) requiring a UNION ALL stack. The key insight: pre-filtering to approved transactions avoids the all zero row problem entirely, eliminating the need for a HAVING clause.

#1731 The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee (Easy)

▼

For each manager (employee with at least 1 direct report), show their id, name, count of direct reports, and average age of reports (rounded).

Schema: Employees(employee_id, name, reports_to, age)

Goal: For each manager (employee with at least 1 direct report), show their id, name, count of direct reports, and average age of reports (rounded).

Why this matters
Organizational hierarchies and team management: understanding span of control and team composition (age diversity, team size).
▶ Rank 1: Self-JOIN + GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT >= 1
SELECT e1.employee_id, e1.name, COUNT(e2.employee_id) AS reports_count, ROUND(AVG(e2.age)) AS average_age FROM Employees e1 JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.employee_id = e2.reports_to GROUP BY e1.employee_id, e1.name HAVING COUNT(e2.employee_id) >= 1 ORDER BY e1.employee_id;

Why rank 1: Self-join connects each employee to their direct reports. GROUP BY manager, aggregate report counts and ages. HAVING filters to managers only.

Performance: O(n log n). The inner join naturally excludes employees with no reports (no matching rows), so HAVING >= 1 is implicit and safe.

Note on ROUND
PostgreSQL's ROUND(numeric) rounds to nearest integer. For 38.5, it rounds to 39 (banker's rounding in some versions, but standard rounding in others—test with your database).

Medium #570 Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports

▼

Find managers (employees who have ≥5 direct reports). Return manager names.

Tables: Employee (id, name, department, managerId)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

Organizational analysis identifies managers with large span of control. HR uses this to assess management workload and plan succession for high-span-of-control roles.

▶ 1 Self-Join with GROUP BY and HAVING
SELECT m.name FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id GROUP BY m.id, m.name HAVING COUNT(e.id) >= 5;

Why this is best: Self-join pairs each employee (e) with their manager (m). GROUP BY m aggregates reports per manager. HAVING filters to ≥5. Clear intent.

Performance: O(n log n) for self-join. Hash join optimal. Index on (managerId) speeds up join. One pass for GROUP BY/HAVING.

▶ 2 Subquery with IN
SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE id IN ( SELECT managerId FROM Employee WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL GROUP BY managerId HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 );

Why this works: Subquery finds manager IDs with ≥5 reports, then outer query retrieves their names. Two-stage: aggregate first, then fetch.

Performance: Two scans. IN with subquery has been optimized in modern DBs to equivalent of join. Slightly slower if subquery returns many managers, but often comparable to approach #1.

▶ 3 Window Function (PostgreSQL)
WITH report_counts AS ( SELECT managerId, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY managerId) AS report_count FROM Employee WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL ) SELECT DISTINCT m.name FROM report_counts rc JOIN Employee m ON rc.managerId = m.id WHERE rc.report_count >= 5;

Why this works: Window COUNT tallies reports per managerId in one scan. Then JOIN to get names, filter to ≥5.

Performance: One pass for window function, one join. Comparable to approach #1, but more complex code. Use if reporting on multiple aggregates per manager.

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Medium #1098 Unpopular Books

▼

Return books available before last month that sold fewer than 10 copies in the past year.

Tables: Books (book_id, name, available_from), Orders (order_id, book_id, quantity, dispatch_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

A bookseller trims catalog bloat. Older titles that sold fewer than 10 copies in the last year are flagged for delisting.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN with Date Filter + HAVING
-- Keep books old enough to have had a fair shot, then sum trailing-year sales SELECT b.book_id, b.name FROM Books b LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.book_id = b.book_id AND o.dispatch_date BETWEEN '2018-06-23' AND '2019-06-23' WHERE b.available_from < '2019-05-23' GROUP BY b.book_id, b.name HAVING COALESCE(SUM(o.quantity), 0) < 10;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN preserves books with no sales. COALESCE treats missing sums as zero so never-sold books are correctly flagged.

Why this is best: First-per-user-then-group-by-day is the standard new-user-by-day pattern.

Medium #1205 Monthly Transactions II

▼

For each (month, country), report approved and chargeback counts and amounts.

Tables: Transactions (id, country, state, amount, trans_date), Chargebacks (trans_id, trans_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

A payments team reviews approved vs chargeback volume by country each month to track fraud exposure and cost of risk.

▶ 1 UNION ALL Then Group
-- Combine approved and chargeback rows, then aggregate per month/country SELECT month, country, SUM(approved_count) AS approved_count, SUM(approved_amount) AS approved_amount, SUM(chargeback_count) AS chargeback_count, SUM(chargeback_amount) AS chargeback_amount FROM ( SELECT DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m') AS month, country, CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS approved_count, CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END AS approved_amount, 0 AS chargeback_count, 0 AS chargeback_amount FROM Transactions UNION ALL SELECT DATE_FORMAT(c.trans_date, '%Y-%m'), t.country, 0, 0, 1, t.amount FROM Chargebacks c JOIN Transactions t ON t.id = c.trans_id ) u GROUP BY month, country HAVING approved_count + chargeback_count > 0;

Why this is best: Stacking two queries into a common schema, then grouping once, is clean for mixed-source metrics.

Performance: Two linear passes and a group-by. Index trans_date.

Why this is best: NULLIF guards against divide-by-zero when an ad has no eligible rows. IFNULL returns 0 CTR in that case.

Performance: One aggregate pass.

A league feed computes a running standings table updated after every match. Points = 3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss.

▶ 1 UNION ALL Home/Away + GROUP BY
-- Normalize home and away into a per-team row, then aggregate WITH perteam AS ( SELECT home_team_id AS team_id, home_team_goals AS gf, away_team_goals AS ga FROM Matches UNION ALL SELECT away_team_id, away_team_goals, home_team_goals FROM Matches ) SELECT t.team_name, COUNT(*) AS matches_played, SUM(CASE WHEN gf > ga THEN 3 WHEN gf = ga THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS points, SUM(gf) AS goal_for, SUM(ga) AS goal_against, SUM(gf) - SUM(ga) AS goal_diff FROM Teams t LEFT JOIN perteam p ON p.team_id = t.team_id GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name ORDER BY points DESC, goal_diff DESC, t.team_name;

Reduce a Table to a Single Value 12 problems

▼

A single table (possibly grouped first) → one row, one column: a scalar result.

Signal words: "the single," "the highest," "second highest," "the one," "overall percentage"

Technique: MAX of filtered set, OFFSET for Nth value, MIN subquery + percentage

Reference Techniques used in Extract Single Value

▼

3 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
SUM / COUNT / AVG / MAX / MIN Computes a single summary value from multiple rows With GROUP BY: one value per group. Without GROUP BY: one value for the whole table 
SELECT MAX(salary) AS top_pay,
       AVG(salary) AS mean_pay,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount
FROM Emp;
LIMIT / OFFSET Restricts how many rows are returned or skips a number of rows from the top You need the top 1, the Nth value, or need to skip incomplete window rows 
SELECT name
FROM Emp
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;  -- 2nd highest
CASE WHEN Returns different values based on conditional logic, like an if/else per row You need to classify, label, or remap values based on conditions 
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN age >= 18 THEN 'Adult'
            ELSE 'Minor' END AS group
FROM Users;

Common Trap: WHERE Returns 0 Rows Instead of NULL

Many scalar-extract problems expect NULL when nothing qualifies (e.g., "second highest salary" when there is only one salary, or the table is empty). If you use WHERE rank = 2 and no row has rank 2, your query returns 0 rows — not a row containing NULL. That fails the test case.

Why it breaks: WHERE can only remove rows. If every row gets removed, the result set is empty. There is no row left to hold a NULL value.

The fix: Move the filter into a subquery inside SELECT. The outer SELECT has no FROM clause, so it always produces exactly 1 row. The subquery fills in the value — if nothing matches, it returns NULL.

-- BREAKS: returns 0 rows when nothing qualifies
SELECT salary FROM rankings WHERE rank = 2;

-- WORKS: always returns 1 row, NULL if nothing qualifies
SELECT (SELECT salary FROM rankings WHERE rank = 2) AS result;

How to spot this: If the problem says "return NULL if no result exists" or the expected output includes a NULL row, you need the subquery-in-SELECT pattern. Look for phrases like "if there is no second highest," "if no such value exists," or an empty table test case.

#619 Biggest Single Number (Easy)

▼

Find the largest number that appears exactly once. Return NULL if no such number exists.

Schema: MyNumbers(num)

Goal: Find the largest number that appears exactly once. Return NULL if no such number exists.

Why this matters
Data quality and outlier detection: finding records that occur exactly once (duplicates removed) vs. those appearing multiple times.
▶ Rank 1: Subquery with GROUP BY + HAVING + MAX
SELECT MAX(num) AS num FROM ( SELECT num FROM MyNumbers GROUP BY num HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 ) AS singles;

Why rank 1: Clear intent: first isolate single numbers with HAVING, then find the max. Handles NULL correctly (no single numbers → NULL result).

Performance: Two passes (subquery aggregation + outer MAX), but still O(n). Simpler to read than CTE version.

#176 Second Highest Salary (Medium)

▼

HR teams use second-highest salary to find runner-up compensation levels for benchmarking and market analysis.

Schema: Employee(id, salary)

Find the second highest distinct salary. Return NULL if fewer than 2 distinct values exist.

Business Context: Compensation Benchmarking

HR teams use second-highest salary to find runner-up compensation levels for benchmarking and market analysis.

▶ Rank 1: Subquery in LIMIT OFFSET Uncorrelated, NULL-safe with IFNULL
SELECT IFNULL( (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1), NULL ) AS SecondHighestSalary;

Why this ranks first: Uses OFFSET to skip the highest and grab the next. Wrapping in IFNULL handles empty result sets (returns NULL when only 1 distinct salary exists). Uncorrelated subquery executes once.

▶ Rank 2: DENSE_RANK Window Function Window function alternative (PostgreSQL 12+)
SELECT COALESCE( (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM ( SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee ) ranked WHERE rnk = 2), NULL ) AS SecondHighestSalary;

Tradeoff: More explicit (DENSE_RANK = 2 clearly means "second value"), but requires wrapping in subquery to extract the single result. Works in modern PostgreSQL.

▶ Rank 3: MAX WHERE salary < MAX Nested aggregates (avoid—often slower)
SELECT IFNULL( MAX(salary), NULL ) AS SecondHighestSalary FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);

Tradeoff: Reads Employee twice (once for MAX, once for WHERE filter). Clear intent but less efficient than LIMIT OFFSET on larger datasets.

Performance Note: LIMIT vs. Window vs. Nested

LIMIT OFFSET is typically fastest on indexed salary (single scan with sort). Window functions (DENSE_RANK) require a scan and rank computation. Nested MAX requires two full table scans. For small Employee tables, differences are negligible; for 1M+ rows, LIMIT OFFSET wins.

#1174 Immediate Food Delivery II (Medium)

▼

Food delivery platforms track the percentage of customers whose first order was fulfilled immediately (same day) to measure onboarding success.

Schema: Delivery(delivery_id, customer_id, order_date, customer_pref_delivery_date)

For each customer's first order (MIN order_date), count how many have order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date (immediate). Return as a percentage, rounded to 2 decimals.

Business Context: First-Order Experience Quality

Food delivery platforms track the percentage of customers whose first order was fulfilled immediately (same day) to measure onboarding success.

▶ Rank 1: CTE with Conditional Aggregation Readability + performance
WITH FirstOrders AS ( SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date FROM Delivery GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT ROUND( 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2 ) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery d INNER JOIN FirstOrders f ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id WHERE d.order_date = f.first_order_date;

Why this ranks first: CTE makes the "first order per customer" logic explicit. CASE WHEN counts immediate orders (order_date = pref_date). JOIN isolates first orders only. Single pass through Delivery.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery in WHERE (Uncorrelated) Inline, no CTE
SELECT ROUND( 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2 ) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery WHERE (customer_id, order_date) IN ( SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) FROM Delivery GROUP BY customer_id );

Tradeoff: Subquery in WHERE finds (customer_id, first_order_date) pairs. Avoids CTE syntax but slightly less readable. Same efficiency.

▶ Rank 3: Correlated Subquery (Slow) For small datasets only
SELECT ROUND( 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2 ) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery d WHERE d.order_date = ( SELECT MIN(order_date) FROM Delivery WHERE customer_id = d.customer_id );

Tradeoff: Correlated subquery runs for each row in Delivery. O(n²) complexity. Avoid for 100k+ rows. Readable but inefficient.

Uncorrelated vs. Correlated Trade-off

The CTE (Rank 1) and IN subquery (Rank 2) compute "first order per customer" once. The correlated subquery (Rank 3) computes it per row. For 10k customers, correlated runs the MIN() 10k times. Use uncorrelated unless table is under 1k rows.

Medium #177 Nth Highest Salary

▼

Return the N-th highest distinct salary, or NULL if there are fewer than N.

Tables: Employee (id, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

HR asks analytics for the "rank N" compensation benchmark to align new hire offers to the distribution.

▶ 1 DENSE_RANK on Distinct Salaries
SELECT ( SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM ( SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee ) t WHERE rnk = N ) AS getNthHighestSalary;

Why this is best: DENSE_RANK handles ties correctly. Returning one row (or NULL) is the scalar output.

Performance: One window scan.

▶ 2 LIMIT/OFFSET with DISTINCT
SELECT IFNULL( (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1), NULL ) AS getNthHighestSalary;

Why this works: OFFSET skips N-1 salaries; LIMIT 1 returns the N-th. Simpler but less expressive on ties.

Performance: One sort. Equivalent cost.

Add or Rewrite Columns, Keep Row Count 19 problems

▼

A single table with N rows → the same N rows with columns added, reformatted, or rewritten.

Signal words: "fix," "convert," "classify," "label each," "if...then," "concatenate," "swap"

Technique: CASE WHEN, CONCAT, UPPER/LOWER, STRING_AGG, conditional column creation

Reference Techniques used in Row Transform

▼

7 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
CASE WHEN Returns different values based on conditional logic, like an if/else per row You need to classify, label, or remap values based on conditions 
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN age >= 18 THEN 'Adult'
            ELSE 'Minor' END AS group
FROM Users;
COALESCE Returns the first non-NULL value from a list of columns or expressions You need a fallback value when a column might be NULL 
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Unknown') AS display_name
FROM Users;
CONCAT Joins strings together You need to combine columns into one string 
SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name
FROM Users;
UPDATE Modifies existing column values in place The problem asks you to change a column's value for rows that meet a condition 
UPDATE Emp
SET salary = salary * 1.10
WHERE dept = 'Engineering';
SUBSTRING / LEFT / RIGHT Extracts part of a string by position You need to pull a fixed-length prefix, suffix, or slice from a text value 
SELECT LEFT(name, 4)         AS first_four,
       SUBSTRING(name, 2, 3)  AS slice
FROM Users;
UPPER / LOWER Converts text to all uppercase or all lowercase You need case-insensitive matching or specific casing 
SELECT UPPER(name) AS upper_name,
       LOWER(email) AS lower_email
FROM Users;
REPLACE / TRIM Swaps or removes characters; TRIM strips leading/trailing whitespace You need to clean up messy text data or swap out specific characters 
SELECT REPLACE(phone, '-', '') AS digits,
       TRIM(name)              AS clean_name
FROM Users;

Easy #1667 Fix Names in a Table

▼

Standardize customer names by capitalizing the first character and lowercasing the rest.

Tables: Users (user_id, name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern L: String/Text Operations

Real-World Example

After a CRM migration, customer names are inconsistently formatted. Data cleaning requires standardizing all names to Title Case (first letter uppercase, rest lowercase) before importing into a production system.

▶ 1 CONCAT + UPPER + LOWER + LEFT + SUBSTRING
SELECT user_id, CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT(name, 1)), LOWER(SUBSTRING(name, 2))) AS name FROM Users ORDER BY user_id;

Why this is best: Straightforward and portable across most SQL dialects. CONCAT is cleaner than || in PostgreSQL. Handles single-character names edge case (SUBSTRING returns empty string if position > length).

Performance: O(n) scan with string operations. Each row processes once. No indexes help, but string operations are fast on modern systems.

▶ 2 || Operator (PostgreSQL)
SELECT user_id, UPPER(LEFT(name, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTRING(name, 2)) AS name FROM Users ORDER BY user_id;

Why this works: String concatenation operator || is native to PostgreSQL and often preferred. Slightly more readable than CONCAT.

Performance: Identical to CONCAT approach. Both compile to the same plan.

▶ 3 INITCAP Function (PostgreSQL)
SELECT user_id, INITCAP(name) AS name FROM Users ORDER BY user_id;

Why this works: INITCAP capitalizes the first character of each word. For single-word names, identical to the required output. Not portable to MySQL.

Performance: Fastest on PostgreSQL; leverages built-in optimizations. However, INITCAP capitalizes every word boundary, so "john-paul" becomes "John-Paul" (may not match requirements for hyphenated names).

Easy #610 Triangle Judgement

▼

For each row with three lengths (x, y, z), determine if they form a valid triangle using the triangle inequality theorem.

Tables: Triangle (x, y, z)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

Engineering validation checks dimensional constraints for manufactured parts. Three measurements are validated against triangle inequality (x+y>z, x+z>y, y+z>x) to ensure geometric feasibility before production sign-off.

▶ 1 CASE with Triangle Inequality All Conditions
SELECT x, y, z, CASE WHEN x + y > z AND x + z > y AND y + z > x THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS triangle FROM Triangle;

Why this is best: Triangle inequality theorem: all three conditions must hold (x+y>z, x+z>y, y+z>x). Single CASE with AND logic is clear and efficient.

Gotcha: Must include ELSE clause. Without it, NULL is returned for false cases, not 'No'. This is a common mistake.

Performance: O(n) row-by-row evaluation. Short-circuit AND: if x+y≤z fails, remaining conditions skip (in most optimizers).

▶ 2 CASE with Negation (Simpler Logic)
SELECT x, y, z, CASE WHEN x + y <= z OR x + z <= y OR y + z <= x THEN 'No' ELSE 'Yes' END AS triangle FROM Triangle;

Why this works: Inverts logic: if ANY condition fails (≤ instead of >), return 'No', else 'Yes'. Equivalent to approach #1, sometimes easier to reason about.

Performance: Identical to approach #1. Choice is stylistic.

▶ 3 CASE with GREATEST (Less Common)
SELECT x, y, z, CASE WHEN GREATEST(x, y, z) < LEAST(x, y, z) + MEDIAN(x, y, z) THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS triangle FROM Triangle;

Why this works: Triangle inequality reduces to: largest side < sum of two smaller sides. GREATEST finds the longest; LEAST and MEDIAN find the two shorter. One comparison only.

Caveat: MEDIAN is not standard SQL. PostgreSQL has percentile_cont; MySQL lacks it. Portable version uses manual sorting with multiple conditions—not simpler.

Performance: If MEDIAN exists, marginally faster (fewer comparisons). Otherwise, less portable and not worth it.

Easy #1789 Primary Department for Each Employee

▼

For multi-department employees, report the primary department (primary_flag='Y'). For single-department employees, report that department (even though primary_flag is 'N').

Tables: Employee (employee_id, department_id, primary_flag)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

HR org charts need to resolve primary assignments for employees spanning multiple departments. When an employee joins another department, they designate a primary; single-department employees implicitly have one primary assignment, even if the flag is 'N' in the schema.

▶ 1 CASE with COUNT Window Function
SELECT employee_id, department_id FROM Employee WHERE CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id) = 1 THEN 1 WHEN primary_flag = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END = 1;

Why this is best: Window function COUNT per employee identifies single-dept employees in one scan. CASE logic: keep if single-dept OR primary_flag='Y'. Clean and efficient.

Performance: Single table scan with window aggregation. O(n) with no subquery overhead.

▶ 2 UNION ALL (Explicit Logic)
SELECT employee_id, department_id FROM Employee WHERE employee_id IN ( SELECT employee_id FROM Employee GROUP BY employee_id HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 ) UNION ALL SELECT employee_id, department_id FROM Employee WHERE primary_flag = 'Y';

Why this works: Two separate queries: one for single-dept employees, one for flagged primary departments. UNION ALL combines. Verbose but semantically clear.

Performance: Two table scans + subquery. Slower than window function approach. Use if clarity is paramount (e.g., code reviews, junior teams).

▶ 3 ROW_NUMBER with Subquery
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT employee_id, department_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY primary_flag DESC, department_id) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id) AS dept_count FROM Employee ) SELECT employee_id, department_id FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

Why this works: ROW_NUMBER ranks by primary_flag DESC (Y first), then breaks ties. Picks the top row for each employee.

Performance: Window operations add overhead. Slower than approach #1. Use only if you need deterministic tie-breaking.

Easy #1484 Group Sold Products By The Date

▼

For each date, count distinct products sold and list them sorted lexicographically.

Tables: Activities (sell_date, product)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

Warehouse management needs to generate daily shipping manifests. For each day, count distinct products sold and list them for packing. STRING_AGG with ORDER BY ensures consistent, sorted output for manifest generation.

▶ 1 STRING_AGG with DISTINCT and ORDER BY
SELECT sell_date, COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS num_sold, STRING_AGG(DISTINCT product, ',' ORDER BY product) AS products FROM Activities GROUP BY sell_date ORDER BY sell_date;

Why this is best: PostgreSQL's STRING_AGG with ORDER BY internally sorts products before concatenation. DISTINCT eliminates duplicates within the aggregation. Clean, readable, one pass.

Gotcha (Critical): ORDER BY inside STRING_AGG uses positional references only in some PostgreSQL versions. Always test. In MySQL/SQLServer, STRING_AGG equivalent (GROUP_CONCAT or STRING_AGG) may not support ORDER BY in the aggregate; use a subquery or window function instead.

Performance: O(n log n) due to internal sort within aggregation. Indexes on (sell_date, product) help GROUP BY. Overall fast for typical daily summaries.

▶ 2 Subquery with DISTINCT and ORDER BY
SELECT sell_date, COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS num_sold, STRING_AGG(product, ',') AS products FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT sell_date, product FROM Activities ) AS unique_products GROUP BY sell_date ORDER BY sell_date;

Why this works: Reduces duplicates early (inner DISTINCT), then STRING_AGG concatenates without ORDER BY. If needed, use LISTAGG or ORDER subquery after.

Note: Products will NOT be sorted in output unless you use a second subquery or window function. Less elegant than approach #1 for PostgreSQL.

Performance: Extra subquery scan adds cost, but deduplication reduces rows for aggregation. Trade-off: slower than direct STRING_AGG but works across more SQL dialects.

▶ 3 Window Function with Sorted Aggregation (MySQL/SQLServer)
WITH ranked_products AS ( SELECT DISTINCT sell_date, product, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY sell_date ORDER BY product) AS rn FROM Activities ) SELECT sell_date, COUNT(*) AS num_sold, STRING_AGG(product, ',') AS products FROM ranked_products GROUP BY sell_date ORDER BY sell_date;

Why this works: ROW_NUMBER enforces sort order before aggregation. Works in MySQL 8.0+ and SQLServer where STRING_AGG ORDER BY is unsupported or limited.

Performance: Window function adds complexity. Three scans: distinct, window, then aggregate. Slower than approach #1, use only if dialect forces it.

#626 Exchange Seats (Medium)

▼

Event organizers swap paired seating: (1,2) -> (2,1), (3,4) -> (4,3). This can balance gender, seniority, or partner groups. Window functions calculate new positions without loops.

📌
Pattern: Conditional LEAD/LAG + CASE

Use LEAD() for even seats, LAG() for odd seats to swap pairs. CASE statement to determine which neighbor to swap with. Business: Seating rearrangement algorithms.

Business Context
Event organizers swap paired seating: (1,2) -> (2,1), (3,4) -> (4,3). This can balance gender, seniority, or partner groups. Window functions calculate new positions without loops.
▶ Rank 1: LEAD/LAG with MOD Logic Most elegant window approach
SELECT id, CASE WHEN MOD(id, 2) = 1 THEN COALESCE(LEAD(student) OVER (ORDER BY id), student) ELSE LAG(student) OVER (ORDER BY id) END AS student FROM Seat ORDER BY id;

Performance Analysis: Single scan of Seat: O(n). ORDER BY id: O(n log n) but id likely already sorted (primary key). LEAD/LAG: O(1) per row once sorted. CASE evaluation: O(1). COALESCE: O(1) - returns LEAD if exists, else student (for last odd-id). Memory: O(n) for sort, O(1) for window frame (only look at current and next). Total: O(n log n) but often O(n) if id already sorted.

Why Rank 1: Perfect use of window functions. Clean logic: odd seats swap with next, even swap with previous.

▶ Rank 2: CASE with Arithmetic Self-join alternative
SELECT s1.id, COALESCE(s2.student, s1.student) AS student FROM Seat s1 LEFT JOIN Seat s2 ON s1.id = ( CASE WHEN MOD(s2.id, 2) = 1 THEN s2.id + 1 ELSE s2.id - 1 END ) ORDER BY s1.id;

Performance Analysis: LEFT JOIN requires join condition evaluation for each s1 row. Condition involves MOD arithmetic and conditional logic. No index can help evaluate MOD(s2.id). Must scan Seat twice, match logic is complex. Hash join: O(n) to build hash, O(n) to probe. But complex join condition means slower hash building. Total: O(n) but higher constant factor than window function.

Why Rank 2: Self-join works but window function is more natural for "move data within same table" problems.

Medium #178 Rank Scores

Return each score with a dense rank so ties share ranks and no holes form.

Why this is best: DENSE_RANK is purpose-built: ties share the rank and the next rank is consecutive.

Hard #1384 Total Sales Amount by Year

▼

For each contract row, expand into yearly segments and report per-year sales.

Tables: Product (product_id, product_name), Sales (product_id, period_start, period_end, average_daily_sales)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

Finance splits multi-year contracts into calendar-year buckets so revenue flows to the correct fiscal period in GAAP reports.

▶ 1 Year Calendar Join with Bounds
WITH years AS ( SELECT 2018 AS yr UNION ALL SELECT 2019 UNION ALL SELECT 2020 ) SELECT s.product_id, p.product_name, y.yr AS report_year, (DATEDIFF( LEAST(s.period_end, MAKEDATE(y.yr, 1) + INTERVAL 1 YEAR - INTERVAL 1 DAY), GREATEST(s.period_start, MAKEDATE(y.yr, 1)) ) + 1) * s.average_daily_sales AS total_amount FROM Sales s JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id JOIN years y ON y.yr BETWEEN YEAR(s.period_start) AND YEAR(s.period_end) ORDER BY s.product_id, y.yr;

Why this is best: Clipping each contract's overlap with each calendar year produces the right per-year days, which times daily rate gives per-year revenue.

Performance: Linear in Sales * overlapping years (3 here).

Medium #1468 Calculate Salaries

▼

Apply a tax rate per company (0/24/49%) and return each employee's post-tax salary.

Tables: Salaries (company_id, employee_id, employee_name, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

A payroll processor applies graduated corporate tax brackets by company size to compute net salary.

▶ 1 Per-Company MAX + CASE Bracket
WITH brackets AS ( SELECT company_id, CASE WHEN MAX(salary) < 1000 THEN 0.00 WHEN MAX(salary) <= 10000 THEN 0.24 ELSE 0.49 END AS tax FROM Salaries GROUP BY company_id ) SELECT s.company_id, s.employee_id, s.employee_name, ROUND(s.salary * (1 - b.tax)) AS salary FROM Salaries s JOIN brackets b ON b.company_id = s.company_id;

Why this is best: Compute the bracket once per company, then apply it per row. Avoids re-evaluating the threshold per employee.

Performance: One aggregate + one join.

SELECT DATE_FORMAT(day, '%W, %M %e, %Y') AS day FROM Days;

Easy #1875 Group Employees of the Same Salary

▼

Return rows whose salary is shared, with a dense team_id shared by equal salaries.

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

A compensation dashboard groups employees by band to show pay parity across a salary cohort.

▶ 1 Filter + DENSE_RANK
SELECT employee_id, name, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS team_id FROM Employees WHERE salary IN ( SELECT salary FROM Employees GROUP BY salary HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ) ORDER BY team_id, employee_id;

Hard #2004 The Number of Seniors and Juniors to Join the Company

▼

Hire as many seniors as fit in the budget, then as many juniors as fit in the remainder.

Tables: Candidates (employee_id, experience, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

A hiring plan operates under a $70k monthly budget. Fill senior slots first, then use the residual to fill juniors.

▶ 1 Running-Total Threshold per Experience
WITH running AS ( SELECT employee_id, experience, salary, SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY experience ORDER BY salary) AS run_total FROM Candidates ), -- Budget left after hiring seniors seniors AS ( SELECT * FROM running WHERE experience = 'Senior' AND run_total <= 70000 ), senior_cost AS (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(salary), 0) AS cost FROM seniors) SELECT experience, COUNT(*) AS accepted_candidates FROM ( SELECT 'Senior' AS experience, employee_id FROM seniors UNION ALL SELECT 'Junior', r.employee_id FROM running r CROSS JOIN senior_cost sc WHERE r.experience = 'Junior' AND r.run_total <= 70000 - sc.cost ) t RIGHT JOIN (SELECT 'Senior' AS experience UNION ALL SELECT 'Junior') base USING (experience) GROUP BY experience;

Why this is best: Running-total window computes per-row cumulative cost; filtering by budget bound gives the greedy hire count within a single aggregate pass.

Performance: Two window passes. Linear in candidates.

Hard #2010 The Number of Seniors and Juniors to Join the Company II

▼

List which specific candidates are hired given the greedy budget policy.

Tables: Candidates (employee_id, experience, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

Like 2004 but returns the actual offer list so recruiters can reach out.

▶ 1 Running Sums + Union of Qualifiers
WITH running AS ( SELECT employee_id, experience, salary, SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY experience ORDER BY salary) AS run_total FROM Candidates ), seniors AS (SELECT * FROM running WHERE experience = 'Senior' AND run_total <= 70000), senior_cost AS (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(salary),0) AS cost FROM seniors) SELECT employee_id FROM seniors UNION ALL SELECT r.employee_id FROM running r CROSS JOIN senior_cost sc WHERE r.experience = 'Junior' AND r.run_total <= 70000 - sc.cost;

Why this is best: Same two-step greedy as 2004; this returns ids instead of counts.

Performance: Same as 2004.

Medium #2051 The Category of Each Member in the Store

▼

Categorize each member as Diamond / Gold / Silver / Bronze by purchase ratio.

Tables: Members (member_id, name), Visits (visit_id, member_id, visit_date), Purchases (visit_id, charged_amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

A loyalty program places every member in a tier based on how often visits turn into purchases. Zero-visit members are Bronze.

▶ 1 Purchase Ratio + CASE
WITH base AS ( SELECT m.member_id, m.name, COUNT(v.visit_id) AS visits, COUNT(p.visit_id) AS purchases FROM Members m LEFT JOIN Visits v ON v.member_id = m.member_id LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON p.visit_id = v.visit_id GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name ) SELECT member_id, name, CASE WHEN visits = 0 THEN 'Bronze' WHEN purchases * 100 >= visits * 80 THEN 'Diamond' WHEN purchases * 100 >= visits * 50 THEN 'Gold' ELSE 'Silver' END AS category FROM base;

Why this is best: Compute visit/purchase counts per member, then encode the tier rules as CASE.

Performance: Two joins + one aggregate.

Medium #2346 Compute the Rank as a Percentage

▼

Return each student with their percentile rank within their department.

Tables: Students (student_id, department_id, mark)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

An education dashboard shows each student their department percentile to motivate study plan choices.

▶ 1 PERCENT_RANK per Partition
SELECT student_id, department_id, ROUND( CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) = 1 THEN 0 ELSE (RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY mark DESC) - 1) * 100.0 / (COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) - 1) END, 2) AS percentage FROM Students;

Why this is best: PERCENT_RANK formula built from RANK + COUNT handles single-student departments correctly.

Performance: Single partitioned window pass.

Medium Top 10% Trial Sites by Enrollment Rate (PERCENT_RANK + ratio output)

▼

Two pieces in one query: PERCENT_RANK over a computed ratio drives the top 10% filter; the ratio itself appears in the output column. Demonstrates the DESC + pr <= 0.10 direction trick that catches ties at the boundary.

Tables: trial_sites (site_id, site_name, trial_phase, enrolled_participants, target_enrollment, principal_investigator)

Real-World Example

A clinical operations team flags the top 10% performing sites for a recruitment award and must include all sites tied at the cutoff so no high performer is missed.

Prompt: Identify the top 10% of trial sites by enrollment rate (enrolled_participants / target_enrollment). Include all sites tied at the 10% boundary. Output columns: site_id, site_name, enrolled_participants, target_enrollment, enrollment_rate (rounded to 4 decimal places). Order by enrollment_rate DESC, then site_id ASC.

▶ 1 Two-CTE staircase: ratio → PERCENT_RANK DESC → filter
WITH base AS ( SELECT site_id, site_name, enrolled_participants, target_enrollment, enrolled_participants::NUMERIC / NULLIF(target_enrollment, 0) AS enrollment_rate FROM trial_sites ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY enrollment_rate DESC) AS pr FROM base ) SELECT site_id, site_name, enrolled_participants, target_enrollment, ROUND(enrollment_rate, 4) AS enrollment_rate FROM ranked WHERE pr <= 0.10 ORDER BY enrollment_rate DESC, site_id;

Why this is best: Two CTEs each with one job — base computes the ratio, ranked attaches the percent rank. The output rounds the ratio for display, but the WHERE filter uses the unrounded percent rank so boundary cases aren't lost to rounding.

The DESC direction trick (key insight):

  • PERCENT_RANK gives tied rows the SMALLER of their tied positions, so flipping ASC/DESC shifts ties asymmetrically.
  • For "top X% HIGHEST", order DESC so the best rows sit at pr = 0, and filter pr <= X/100.
  • For "top X% LOWEST" (e.g., fastest agents), order ASC and use the same pr <= X/100.
  • Same rule both directions: order so the rows you want sit at pr = 0.

Why DESC + pr <= 0.10 instead of ASC + pr >= 0.90:

Scenario DESC + pr <= 0.10 ASC + pr >= 0.90
Single best site at toppr = 0 → qualifiespr = 1.0 → qualifies
Two sites tied at topBoth at pr = 0 → both qualifyBoth share lower rank → pr ~ 0.857 → MISS the threshold

Trace through the example data:

site_id enrolled / target ratio DESC rank pr In top 10%?
10238 / 400.950010.000Yes
101, 103, 10545/50, 72/80, 54/600.9000 (3-way tie)20.143No (0.143 > 0.10)
10642 / 500.840050.571No
10825 / 300.833360.714No
10733 / 400.825070.857No
10428 / 350.800081.000No

Only site 102 sits at pr <= 0.10. If site 102 had been tied with another site at 0.95, both would have shared rank 1 and pr 0, and both would qualify — that's the prompt's "include all tied at boundary" behavior, free from the DESC trick.

Watch out:

  • Integer division flattens the ratio. enrolled_participants / target_enrollment with both INT returns 0 for any sub-100% case. Cast one side to NUMERIC to preserve decimals: enrolled_participants::NUMERIC / target_enrollment.
  • NULLIF(target_enrollment, 0) guards against division by zero. If a denominator could be 0, NULLIF turns it into NULL and the division returns NULL instead of erroring out.
  • Output is the ratio, not the percent rank. The WHERE uses pr, but the SELECT projects enrollment_rate rounded to 4 decimals. Mixing them up leads to a column of mostly 1.0 values (the percent rank) instead of the actual rate.
  • Round only in the final SELECT, not in the CTE. Rounding in the CTE then rounding again in the outer doesn't recover precision. Filter on the unrounded value, round only for display.
  • Cast PERCENT_RANK to NUMERIC if you need ROUND on it. PERCENT_RANK returns DOUBLE PRECISION; ROUND(double, n) isn't supported in PostgreSQL. Either cast first or skip rounding the percent rank entirely (it's only used in the WHERE, so rounding doesn't help here).

Percentile & Distribution Metrics: Pick the Right Method

Four methods cover most percentile and distribution prompts. The choice depends on whether you want a single value, a per-row bucket label, or a per-row rank.

Method comparison

Method What it returns Use when Sort direction trick
PERCENTILE_CONT(p) A single interpolated value at percentile p (continuous) "Find the median latency" or "P90 of session length per region" — you need ONE value per group Aggregate function. WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY metric) — ASC for low percentile, doesn't matter for symmetric percentiles
PERCENTILE_DISC(p) An actual data value at percentile p (discrete, no interpolation) "Find the actual revenue at the 90th percentile" — need a real row's value, not an interpolated number Aggregate function. Same WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY metric) shape as CONT
NTILE(n) A bucket number 1 to n per row "Split into quartiles", "decile every customer", "group rows into N equal buckets" OVER (ORDER BY metric DESC) for "highest in bucket 1"; ASC for "lowest in bucket 1"
PERCENT_RANK() A decimal between 0 and 1 per row, ranking it within the set "Top 10% by metric", "bottom 5%", any prompt with a percentage cutoff and tie handling at the boundary Order so the BEST rows sit at pr = 0: DESC for "top X% highest", ASC for "top X% lowest". Filter pr <= X/100

Quick decision

Prompt asks for... Use
"the median X" / "P90 of X" / single percentile value per group PERCENTILE_CONT(p) or PERCENTILE_DISC(p)
Each row labeled with a quartile / decile / N-tile bucket NTILE(n)
Top X% (or bottom X%) of rows, with ties at the cutoff included PERCENT_RANK() with the direction trick
"Top N rows" with no percentage involved ROW_NUMBER() + WHERE rn <= N — not a percentile shape at all

Easy Quartile Bucketing of Monthly Box Revenue (NTILE direction)

▼

One window function, one ORDER BY direction. Demonstrates the NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY metric DESC) form for "highest in bucket 1" and how NTILE distributes evenly when row count divides cleanly.

Tables: box_assembly_months (month_id, assembly_date, total_revenue)

Real-World Example

A subscription retailer's ops team groups monthly performance into quartiles for a board deck so the highest-revenue months are highlighted in quartile 1.

Prompt: Split months into 4 quartiles by total revenue, with the highest-revenue months in quartile 1. Output month_id, total_revenue, revenue_quartile. Order by revenue_quartile ASC, then total_revenue DESC within each quartile.

▶ 1 NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY metric DESC)
SELECT month_id, total_revenue, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS revenue_quartile FROM box_assembly_months ORDER BY revenue_quartile ASC, total_revenue DESC;

Why this is best: NTILE(4) splits the rows into 4 equal-sized buckets numbered 1 through 4. ORDER BY DESC inside the OVER clause means highest values sit in bucket 1 — that's the prompt's "highest-revenue months in quartile 1" requirement, expressed in one line.

Direction trick:

If the prompt says... Use
"highest in bucket 1" / "best at top"OVER (ORDER BY metric DESC)
"lowest in bucket 1" / "smallest at top"OVER (ORDER BY metric ASC)

Trace through the example data (8 rows ÷ 4 quartiles = 2 per bucket):

month_id total_revenue DESC rank NTILE(4)
2024-025200011
2024-054900021
2024-074700032
2024-014500042
2024-084400053
2024-044100063
2024-033800074
2024-063500084

Watch out:

  • Uneven splits go to LOWER buckets. NTILE distributes leftover rows to bucket 1, then 2, etc. With 11 rows split into 4 quartiles you get bucket sizes 3, 3, 3, 2 — bucket 4 is the smallest. This is consistent and predictable; no ROUND needed.
  • Ties don't get the same bucket. NTILE assigns by row position, not value. Two rows with identical revenue can end up in adjacent buckets if they straddle the boundary. If ties must share a bucket, use NTILE inside a CTE that pre-aggregates, or use PERCENT_RANK with a threshold.
  • The outer ORDER BY is separate from the OVER ORDER BY. The window's ORDER BY drives the bucketing; the outer ORDER BY drives the output sort. The prompt may request a different sort than the bucketing direction.
  • No PARTITION BY = single global bucketing. Add PARTITION BY region (or similar) for "quartiles within each region" instead of one global quartile.
  • NTILE only takes a literal integer. NTILE(4) works, NTILE(some_column) doesn't.

Easy #2377 Sort the Olympic Table

▼

Sort Olympic table by gold, then silver, then bronze, then country.

Tables: Olympic (country, gold_medals, silver_medals, bronze_medals)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

A sports newsroom renders the medal table with the standard tie-break hierarchy.

▶ 1 Compound ORDER BY
SELECT country, gold_medals, silver_medals, bronze_medals FROM Olympic ORDER BY gold_medals DESC, silver_medals DESC, bronze_medals DESC, country;

Why this is best: Pure sort with tie-break keys.

Performance: One sort.

Medium #2394 Employees With Deductions

▼

Employees whose accumulated work time does not meet the monthly requirement lose pay.

Tables: Employees (employee_id, needed_hours), Logs (employee_id, in_time, out_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

A payroll pipeline computes timesheet shortfalls and deducts accordingly, rounded up to whole hours.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN + Conditional Compare
SELECT e.employee_id FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Logs l ON l.employee_id = e.employee_id GROUP BY e.employee_id, e.needed_hours HAVING CEIL(COALESCE(SUM(TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, l.in_time, l.out_time)), 0) / 60.0) < e.needed_hours;

Why this is best: Aggregate actual hours, round up, then compare to the requirement in HAVING.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Medium #608 Tree Node

▼

Label each node as Root, Inner, or Leaf based on whether it has a parent and whether it appears as anyone’s parent.

Tables: Tree (id, p_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern I: Conditional Logic (CASE)

Real-World Example

An ops team categorizes accounts in a referral graph: top-level accounts (no referrer), pass-through accounts (have a referrer AND referred others), and end accounts (have a referrer but referred no one). Same shape as Root / Inner / Leaf and same SQL pattern: a CASE WHEN that asks “does this id appear in some other row’s reference column?”

▶ 1 Ordered CASE with IN-Subquery
SELECT id, CASE WHEN p_id IS NULL THEN 'Root' WHEN id IN (SELECT p_id FROM Tree) THEN 'Inner' ELSE 'Leaf' END AS type FROM Tree;

Why this is best: CASE evaluates top to bottom, so each WHEN can assume the previous ones already failed. Once Root is ruled out, “has a parent” is implicit, so the Inner check only needs to verify “has children” (i.e., this id appears as some row’s p_id). Anything that fails both is by definition a Leaf.

Performance: One scan of Tree plus one subquery. The subquery executes once and is cached for the IN check. O(n) overall.

▶ 2 LEFT JOIN to Self for Children Check
SELECT t.id, CASE WHEN t.p_id IS NULL THEN 'Root' WHEN c.id IS NULL THEN 'Leaf' ELSE 'Inner' END AS type FROM Tree t LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT p_id FROM Tree) c ON c.p_id = t.id;

Why this works: The LEFT JOIN brings in a NULL when this id is not anyone’s parent (= leaf), and a non-NULL when it is (= inner). Equivalent semantics to Rank 1, just expressed as a join instead of an IN subquery.

Performance: Comparable to Rank 1. The IN subquery in Rank 1 is usually optimized into a similar plan.

Compare Each Row to a Neighboring Row 16 problems

▼

A single table with an ordering column → rows satisfying a comparison to the prior or next row in that order.

Signal words: "compared to previous," "rising," "consecutive," "increasing," "day over day," "streak," "gap"

Technique: LAG(), LEAD(), self-join on id+1 / date+1, date arithmetic

Reference Techniques used in Row Compare

▼

3 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
LAG / LEAD Accesses the value from the previous (LAG) or next (LEAD) row in order Each row needs to compare itself to its immediate neighbor 
SELECT day, sales,
       LAG(sales)  OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day,
       LEAD(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS next_day
FROM Daily;
Self-join Aliases the same table twice to compare or look up rows within one table The row needs to look up another row in the same table (employee/manager, parent/child, referrer/referee) 
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON m.id = e.managerId;
Gaps-and-islands Subtracts a row number from a monotonic column (id or date) so consecutive rows share the same "island id" — then GROUP BY that island id to collapse runs You need to find streaks of consecutive ids/dates, runs that stay above a threshold, or gaps in a sequence. Classic signal words: "consecutive," "streak," "3+ in a row," "gap" 
WITH hi AS (
  SELECT id, visit_date, people,
         id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp
  FROM Stadium
  WHERE people >= 100
)
SELECT *
FROM hi
WHERE grp IN (
  SELECT grp FROM hi
  GROUP BY grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
);

Not the same as a self-join lookup. If the row needs to find another row by foreign key (employee → manager via managerId, child → parent via parent_id), that is enrich-join, not row-compare. Row-compare is reserved for sequential neighbor comparisons where ORDER BY defines who counts as "previous" or "next."

#197 Rising Temperature (Easy)

▼

Temperature monitoring systems need to detect anomalies like sudden spikes. A rise of 15 degrees in one day might trigger an alert, while gradual increases don't.

📌
Pattern: Compare Rows with LAG()

Use LAG() to access the previous day's temperature, then compare. Business: IoT sensor monitoring detecting temperature increases day-over-day.

Business Context
Temperature monitoring systems need to detect anomalies like sudden spikes. A rise of 15 degrees in one day might trigger an alert, while gradual increases don't.
▶ Rank 1: Window Function (LAG) Most elegant and standard
SELECT id FROM ( SELECT id, recordDate, temperature, LAG(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_temp FROM Weather ) t WHERE temperature > prev_temp;

Performance Analysis: Single scan of Weather table with window frame computation. PostgreSQL can optimize this with an index on recordDate. Memory usage O(n) for sort. Execution: O(n log n) due to ORDER BY.

Why Rank 1: Clean, expressive, and handles date ordering automatically. No self-joins needed. Best for most databases.

▶ Rank 2: Self-Join with DATEDIFF Works without window functions
SELECT w1.id FROM Weather w1 JOIN Weather w2 ON w1.recordDate = w2.recordDate + INTERVAL '1 day' WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;

Performance Analysis: Requires CROSS JOIN + filter. Without an index on recordDate, this becomes a full table scan. Join condition is selective but requires date arithmetic. Memory: O(n) for sorting both tables. CPU intensive for large tables (50k+ rows).

Why Rank 2: Pre-window-function approach, less maintainable. More rows processed before filtering.

#180 Consecutive Numbers (Medium)

▼

Fraud systems flag patterns like three identical charges in a row (e.g., $99.99, $99.99, $99.99). These often indicate cloning or test transactions.

📌
Pattern: LAG/LEAD + Grouping

Use LAG() and LEAD() to check if three consecutive rows have the same value. Business: Fraud detection finding repeated identical transactions.

Business Context
Fraud systems flag patterns like three identical charges in a row (e.g., $99.99, $99.99, $99.99). These often indicate cloning or test transactions.
▶ Rank 1: LAG + LEAD (Window Functions) Most elegant and efficient
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums FROM ( SELECT num, LAG(num) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num, LEAD(num) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num FROM Logs ) t WHERE num = prev_num AND num = next_num;

Performance Analysis: Single table scan with window frame computation O(n log n). No joins. Memory: O(n) for window frame buffer. Can use index on id for sort. DISTINCT requires hash table O(k) where k = unique consecutive numbers.

Why Rank 1: Clean, efficient, scales well. Window functions avoid quadratic self-join complexity.

▶ Rank 2: Triple Self-Join Pre-window approach
SELECT DISTINCT l1.num AS ConsecutiveNums FROM Logs l1 JOIN Logs l2 ON l1.id + 1 = l2.id AND l1.num = l2.num JOIN Logs l3 ON l2.id + 1 = l3.id AND l2.num = l3.num ORDER BY ConsecutiveNums;

Performance Analysis: Three joins = O(n³) in worst case. With id index, becomes O(n) due to selective seek. Memory: Three hash tables during join. CPU heavy: 2 million rows = 8 trillion comparisons without index. With index on id: O(3n) effective.

Why Rank 2: Much slower than window function. Shows value of window functions: compare 3 rows in O(n) instead of O(n²).

#1661 Average Time of Process per Machine (Medium)

▼

Factory managers need average cycle times per machine to optimize production and identify bottlenecks. If Machine A averages 2 minutes per process and Machine B averages 5 minutes, production can be rebalanced.

📌
Pattern: Self-Join + Aggregation

Join start and end activity records for each (machine, process) pair, then aggregate. Business: Manufacturing tracking average process cycle times.

Business Context
Factory managers need average cycle times per machine to optimize production and identify bottlenecks. If Machine A averages 2 minutes per process and Machine B averages 5 minutes, production can be rebalanced.
▶ Rank 1: Self-Join + Conditional Aggregation Cleanest and most portable
SELECT machine_id, ROUND(AVG(CAST(end_time - start_time AS NUMERIC)), 3) AS processing_time FROM ( SELECT machine_id, process_id, MAX(CASE WHEN activity_type = 'end' THEN timestamp END) AS end_time, MAX(CASE WHEN activity_type = 'start' THEN timestamp END) AS start_time FROM Activity GROUP BY machine_id, process_id ) t GROUP BY machine_id ORDER BY machine_id;

Performance Analysis: Two GROUP BY operations: first to extract start/end per (machine, process), second to average. First GROUP BY scans full table once (O(n)). Memory: O(n) for grouping hash table. Second GROUP BY: O(m) where m = distinct machines. No index required but helps on (machine_id, process_id).

Why Rank 1: Single pass subquery pattern, readable, avoids explicit JOINs. Works across all SQL dialects.

▶ Rank 2: Explicit Self-Join on (machine, process) More readable for some
SELECT a1.machine_id, ROUND(AVG(a2.timestamp - a1.timestamp), 3) AS processing_time FROM Activity a1 JOIN Activity a2 ON a1.machine_id = a2.machine_id AND a1.process_id = a2.process_id AND a1.activity_type = 'start' AND a2.activity_type = 'end' GROUP BY a1.machine_id ORDER BY a1.machine_id;

Performance Analysis: JOIN requires both tables be sorted on join keys. Hash join preferred but requires three conditions (machine, process, activity_type). Matches: O(n/2) * O(n/2) = O(n²/4). With indexes on (machine_id, process_id, activity_type), becomes O(n). Memory usage higher due to hash table for join.

Why Rank 2: More explicit, easier to understand the logic, but slightly less efficient than subquery approach.

Gaps-and-Islands: Pick the Right Form by Data Shape

Four canonical shapes. The formula and the GROUP BY columns change with the data shape; pick once, then the rest of the query (MIN/MAX, ORDER BY) is the same.

Table 1 — Pick the approach by data shape

Data shape Signs in the prompt Formula
Integer ids (with optional status) "consecutive ids", "integer ranges", "differ by 1" 
id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY status
    ORDER BY id
) AS grp
Dates, every day covered "every day in the range", "no missing days", calendar consecutive 
date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY status
    ORDER BY date
))::INT AS grp
Dates, possible missing days "consecutive in the data", missing days allowed, two source tables UNION'd 
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY date)
- ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY status
    ORDER BY date
) AS grp
Per-entity timelines Entity column (order_id, user_id, ticket_id), one timeline per entity 
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY entity
    ORDER BY date
)
- ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY entity, status
    ORDER BY date
) AS grp

Table 2 — Output GROUP BY and key pitfall per approach

Approach GROUP BY in final SELECT Key pitfall
Integer ids status, grp (drop status if no status column) Reaching for the rn-rn formula instead of id-rn; both work but id-rn is one less window function
Dates, every day covered status, grp Breaks on a missing day (e.g., Feb 29 absent). Switch to the rn-rn form if data could have gaps.
Dates, possible missing days status, grp Both windows must ORDER BY date or the math is undefined
Per-entity timelines entity, status, grp Both windows must PARTITION BY entity or other entities' rows split the runs. Never substitute the status column for the entity — that collapses every same-status row into one giant island.

Table 3 — Trace examples (3 sample rows per approach)

Integer ids: seats 101, 102, 103, 105 all active

seat_id rn (per status) grp = id − rn Island
1011100A
1022100A
1033100A
1054101B (gap at 104)

Dates, every day covered: Jan 1 failed, Jan 2 failed, Jan 3 succeeded

date status rn (per status) grp = date − rn Island
2019-01-01failed12018-12-31A
2019-01-02failed22018-12-31A
2019-01-03succeeded12019-01-02B

Dates, possible missing days: Feb 28 active, Feb 29 missing from data, Mar 1 active, Mar 2 active

date status rn_overall rn_per_status grp = overall − per Island
2024-02-28active110A
2024-03-01active220A (Feb 29 ignored)
2024-03-02active330A

Per-entity timelines: order 101 has processing then shipped, order 103 has processing in between

order_id status date rn (per entity) rn (per entity, status) grp Island
101processing2024-01-01110A (101 processing)
101processing2024-01-02220A
101shipped2024-01-04312B (101 shipped)
103processing2024-01-05110C (103 processing, separate from order 101's runs)

Hard #601 Human Traffic of Stadium

▼

Return days with 100+ visitors that appear in a run of three or more consecutive qualifying days.

Tables: Stadium (id, visit_date, people)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A facilities team flags streaks of high-attendance days to justify seasonal staffing or spot event anomalies.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands via Row Number
WITH hi AS ( SELECT id, visit_date, people, id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp FROM Stadium WHERE people >= 100 ) SELECT id, visit_date, people FROM hi WHERE grp IN (SELECT grp FROM hi GROUP BY grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3) ORDER BY visit_date;

Why this is best: The classic gaps-and-islands trick: consecutive ids in the filtered set share (id - rn). HAVING >= 3 selects streaks of 3+.

Performance: One window + one group-by. Linear.

Easy #603 Consecutive Available Seats

▼

Return free seats where an adjacent seat (seat_id ±1) is also free.

Tables: Cinema (seat_id, free)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A ticketing UI offers "two together" as a single click; this query powers the has-a-neighbor filter.

▶ 1 Self-Join on Adjacent IDs
SELECT DISTINCT c1.seat_id FROM Cinema c1 JOIN Cinema c2 ON ABS(c1.seat_id - c2.seat_id) = 1 AND c1.free = 1 AND c2.free = 1 ORDER BY c1.seat_id;

Why this is best: Self-join on "neighbor" condition is the clearest way to test adjacency.

Performance: Fast with an index on seat_id.

Hard #1225 Report Contiguous Dates

▼

Summarize consecutive-day ranges of the same period state (failed/succeeded).

Tables: Failed (fail_date), Succeeded (success_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A SRE team builds an uptime ledger showing contiguous spans of healthy vs unhealthy days for audit reports.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands by State
WITH all_days AS ( SELECT fail_date AS d, 'failed' AS state FROM Failed WHERE fail_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' UNION ALL SELECT success_date, 'succeeded' FROM Succeeded WHERE success_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' ), numbered AS ( SELECT d, state, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY d) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY d) AS grp FROM all_days ) SELECT state AS period_state, MIN(d) AS start_date, MAX(d) AS end_date FROM numbered GROUP BY state, grp ORDER BY start_date;

Why this is best: The difference of two row numbers groups same-state rows that are also contiguous by date.

Performance: Two window passes + one group-by.

▶ 2 Date Minus Row-Number (Postgres-friendly, calendar-consecutive only)
WITH all_days AS ( SELECT 'failed' AS state, fail_date AS d FROM Failed WHERE fail_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' UNION ALL SELECT 'succeeded', success_date FROM Succeeded WHERE success_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' ), numbered AS ( SELECT d, state, d - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY d))::INT AS grp FROM all_days ) SELECT state AS period_state, MIN(d) AS start_date, MAX(d) AS end_date FROM numbered GROUP BY state, grp ORDER BY start_date;

Why this works: consecutive same-state dates produce identical (date - row_number_within_state) values, so the math is more intuitive than the two-row-numbers diff.

Trade-offs vs Rank 1: Postgres-only (DATE - INT math; ::INT cast needed because ROW_NUMBER returns BIGINT). Also requires the date sequence in the data to have NO missing days within an island — see the watch-out below.

Watch out: the two formulations are NOT equivalent when data has missing days

  • rn_overall - rn_per_state groups by data-sequence consecutiveness — "are these the next rows when sorted by date?" It IGNORES calendar gaps where neither table has a row.
  • date - rn_per_state groups by calendar consecutiveness — "are these back-to-back days on the calendar?" If a day is missing from BOTH tables, the math breaks the island.
  • Example: 2024 is a leap year. If the data has Feb 28 = active, no row for Feb 29 (missing from both tables), Mar 1 = active — the date - rn form sees a 2-day gap (Feb 28 → Mar 1 is 2 calendar days because Feb 29 exists) and breaks the island. The rn_overall - rn_per_state form keeps them together because the rows are sequential in the union.
  • Pick by prompt intent: if "continuous" means "every calendar day covered," use date - rn. If "continuous" means "consecutive in the union of source tables, ignoring missing days," use rn_overall - rn_per_state. When in doubt, use rn_overall - rn_per_state — it's the more permissive form and matches most prompts.

Hard Member Workout vs Skip Streaks (UNION + Gaps-and-Islands variant)

▼

Same shape as #1225 in a fitness-app domain: collapse consecutive 'active' (workout) and 'inactive' (skip) days into [period_start, period_end] ranges. Demonstrates the data-sequence vs calendar-consecutive distinction in a 2024 leap-year context.

Tables: completed_workouts (workout_date), skipped_days (skip_date)

Real-World Example

A fitness-tracker app reports each member's continuous workout/skip streaks for engagement scoring. The output drives push-notification logic ("you've skipped 3 days in a row").

▶ 1 Two-Row-Number Difference (handles missing days correctly)
WITH base AS ( SELECT 'active' AS activity_state, workout_date AS activity_date FROM completed_workouts WHERE workout_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31' UNION ALL SELECT 'inactive' AS activity_state, skip_date AS activity_date FROM skipped_days WHERE skip_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31' ), grouping AS ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY activity_date::date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY activity_state ORDER BY activity_date::date) AS grp FROM base ) SELECT activity_state, MIN(activity_date) AS period_start, MAX(activity_date) AS period_end FROM grouping GROUP BY activity_state, grp ORDER BY period_start;

The leap-year trap that makes this anchor different from #1225:

  • 2024 is a leap year. Suppose the data has Feb 28 = active, no row for Feb 29 (missing from both tables), Mar 1 = active, Mar 2 = active.
  • Using date - row_number_per_state: Feb 28 minus N = 2024-02-28 - N. Mar 1 minus (N+1) = 2024-02-29 - N. Different group ids — islands break.
  • Using rn_overall - rn_per_state: rn_overall increments by 1 for each row regardless of calendar gap, so Feb 28, Mar 1, Mar 2 share the same (overall - per-state) difference and stay in one island.
  • Expected output keeps them as one island, so this prompt's "continuous" means data-sequence consecutive, not calendar consecutive.

Trace through 4 sample rows around the leap-year boundary:

activity_date activity_state rn_overall rn_per_state grp (overall - per-state) date - rn_per_state (broken)
2024-02-28activeNKN-K2024-02-28 minus K
2024-03-01activeN+1K+1N-K (same)2024-02-29 minus K (different)
2024-03-02activeN+2K+2N-K (same)2024-02-29 minus K (same as Mar 1)
2024-03-03inactiveN+31N+2 (new group)2024-03-02 minus 1 (new group)

With rn_overall - rn_per_state, Feb 28 / Mar 1 / Mar 2 all share group N-K and collapse into one island (period_start=2024-02-28, period_end=2024-03-02). With the date - rn form, Feb 28 ends up in group "2024-02-28 minus K" while Mar 1 and 2 end up in group "2024-02-29 minus K" — two islands instead of one.

Watch out:

  • Pick the formulation by what "continuous" means in the prompt. If the prompt says "every day in the range" or "no missing calendar days," use date - rn. If the prompt says "consecutive in the data" or doesn't specify, use rn_overall - rn_per_state.
  • Filter to the date range in EACH UNION branch's WHERE. A trailing WHERE on the outer query only filters whatever the WHERE clause is attached to in a UNION ALL.
  • Don't include activity_date in the GROUP BY. If you do, every date becomes its own group and islands never collapse.
  • Don't ORDER BY inside the base CTE. It has no effect on the outer query and can confuse window functions downstream.
  • Both source tables must have rows for ONE state only. If completed_workouts were to also include a status column, you'd skip the UNION ALL entirely and just GROUP BY status from one table.

Hard Collapse Order Status Periods (UNION + per-entity partition)

▼

Same gaps-and-islands shape as #1225, but each entity (order_id) has its own timeline. The window functions must partition by the entity key, not just by status, or runs from different entities collide.

Tables: processing_orders (order_id, process_date), shipped_orders (order_id, ship_date)

Real-World Example

An e-commerce ops team builds an order timeline view: each order shows one row per status period (processing then shipped) with start and end dates, fed into the customer-facing tracking page.

▶ 1 Two-Row-Number Difference, Partitioned by Entity
WITH base AS ( SELECT 'processing' AS status, order_id, process_date AS status_date FROM processing_orders UNION ALL SELECT 'shipped' AS status, order_id, ship_date AS status_date FROM shipped_orders ), date_grouping AS ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY status_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, status ORDER BY status_date) AS grp FROM base ) SELECT order_id, status, MIN(status_date) AS start_date, MAX(status_date) AS end_date FROM date_grouping GROUP BY order_id, status, grp ORDER BY MIN(status_date), order_id;
