What makes this anchor different from #1225 and the workout/skip variant:

  • Each order_id has its OWN timeline. Order 101's shipped run on Jan 4-6 must not be split just because order 103's processing row sits in between in the global date order.
  • BOTH window functions must PARTITION BY order_id — not just the inner one.
  • The inner window adds status to the partition: PARTITION BY order_id, status.
  • The GROUP BY uses three keys: order_id, status, grp. The grp label is local to one (entity, status) pair, so dropping order_id would mash different orders into one row.

Trace through the bug when order_id is missing from the outer window:

status_date order_id status global rn per-status rn grp
2024-01-04101shipped615
2024-01-05103processing7——
2024-01-06101shipped826

Order 101's two shipped rows land on different grp values (5 vs 6) because order 103's row inflated the global rn between them. Result: 101 shipped is split into two output rows instead of one. Adding PARTITION BY order_id to the outer window restarts the global rn at 1 inside each order's timeline, so 101's shipped rows get rn 4 then 5 (no gap), share the same grp, and collapse correctly.

Trace of the fixed version for order 101:

status_date status rn within order_id rn within (order_id, status) grp
2024-01-01processing110
2024-01-02processing220
2024-01-03processing330
2024-01-04shipped413
2024-01-05shipped523
2024-01-06shipped633

All three shipped rows share grp = 3 and collapse into one row: (101, shipped, 2024-01-04, 2024-01-06). The processing rows share grp = 0 and collapse into (101, processing, 2024-01-01, 2024-01-03).

Watch out:

  • Both windows need ORDER BY status_date. Without it on the outer one, the row numbering is undefined and the gaps-and-islands math breaks silently.
  • Both windows need PARTITION BY order_id. Skipping it on the outer one is the bug above.
  • GROUP BY needs all three keys: order_id, status, grp. The grp label only means "same run" within a fixed (entity, status) pair.
  • Use UNION ALL, not UNION. The two source tables can't produce duplicates, so the dedupe sort is wasted work.
  • Monotonic status transitions don't change the shape. Even though "once shipped, stays shipped" guarantees at most two periods per order, the same query handles repeated transitions if the prompt allowed them.

Medium #1285 Find the Start and End Number of Continuous Ranges

▼

Collapse a sorted id list into [start, end] ranges of consecutive integers.

Tables: Logs (log_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

An analytics export compresses a discrete id log into tidy ranges for storage and readability.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands Integer
WITH grouped AS ( SELECT log_id, log_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY log_id) AS grp FROM Logs ) SELECT MIN(log_id) AS start_id, MAX(log_id) AS end_id FROM grouped GROUP BY grp ORDER BY start_id;

Why this is best: Subtracting the row number from the id produces identical grp values for consecutive ids.

Performance: One window + one group-by.

Medium #1454 Active Users

▼

Find users who logged in on five or more consecutive days.

Tables: Accounts (id, name), Logins (id, login_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A growth team defines "highly engaged users" as those with 5+ day streaks and ships this list to the lifecycle email engine.

▶ 1 Distinct Days + Gaps-and-Islands
WITH distinct_logins AS ( SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date FROM Logins ), groups AS ( SELECT id, login_date, DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date) DAY) AS grp FROM distinct_logins ) SELECT DISTINCT g.id, a.name FROM groups g JOIN Accounts a ON a.id = g.id GROUP BY g.id, a.name, g.grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

Why this is best: Subtract a rolling row-number of days from the date to collapse consecutive days into a single grp. 5+ rows per grp is a streak.

Performance: One window + one group-by.

Medium #1613 Find the Missing IDs

▼

Return ids from 1 through MAX(customer_id) that are absent from Customers.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, customer_name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A data-quality audit surfaces ID holes in a legacy sequence table to investigate deletes or import failures.

▶ 1 Recursive Range + Anti-Join
WITH RECURSIVE seq AS ( SELECT 1 AS id UNION ALL SELECT id + 1 FROM seq WHERE id < (SELECT MAX(customer_id) FROM Customers) ) SELECT s.id AS ids FROM seq s LEFT JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = s.id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;

Why this is best: Generate the complete expected range, then anti-join.

Performance: Recursion depth = max id. Use cte_max_recursion_depth if needed.

Medium #1709 Biggest Window Between Visits

▼

For each user, the largest gap in days between visits (or to 2021-01-01).

Tables: UserVisits (user_id, visit_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A lifecycle analyst finds the longest dormancy per user to define "rolling churn" thresholds.

▶ 1 LEAD with End-of-Window Sentinel
SELECT user_id, MAX(DATEDIFF(next_visit, visit_date)) AS biggest_window FROM ( SELECT user_id, visit_date, LEAD(visit_date, 1, DATE '2021-01-01') OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS next_visit FROM UserVisits ) t GROUP BY user_id;

Why this is best: LEAD with a sentinel handles the last visit gracefully as the gap to Jan 1.

Performance: One window + one aggregate.

Medium #1843 Suspicious Bank Accounts

▼

Accounts whose monthly credit total exceeds maximum balance in two or more consecutive months.

Tables: Accounts (account_id, max_income), Transactions (trans_id, account_id, type, amount, day)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

An AML team investigates accounts receiving unusually large deposits across a streak of months — a red flag for money-laundering patterns.

▶ 1 Monthly Credit Aggregate + Streak
WITH monthly AS ( SELECT account_id, DATE_FORMAT(day, '%Y-%m') AS ym, SUM(amount) AS credit FROM Transactions WHERE type = 'Creditor' GROUP BY account_id, DATE_FORMAT(day, '%Y-%m') ), flagged AS ( SELECT m.account_id, m.ym FROM monthly m JOIN Accounts a ON a.account_id = m.account_id WHERE m.credit > a.max_income ) SELECT DISTINCT f1.account_id FROM flagged f1 JOIN flagged f2 ON f2.account_id = f1.account_id AND PERIOD_DIFF(REPLACE(f2.ym,'-',''), REPLACE(f1.ym,'-','')) = 1 ORDER BY f1.account_id;

Why this is best: Aggregate monthly credit, flag over-threshold months, then self-join on consecutive months.

Performance: Two aggregates + self-join.

Hard #1972 First and Last Call On the Same Day

▼

Find users whose first and last call on the same day were with different people.

Tables: Calls (caller_id, recipient_id, call_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A spam investigator surfaces users whose daily first and last contact differed — a common automation/spam signature.

▶ 1 Normalize Direction + First/Last per Day
WITH norm AS ( SELECT caller_id AS u, recipient_id AS other, call_time FROM Calls UNION ALL SELECT recipient_id, caller_id, call_time FROM Calls ), ranked AS ( SELECT u, other, call_time, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u, DATE(call_time) ORDER BY call_time) AS rn_asc, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u, DATE(call_time) ORDER BY call_time DESC) AS rn_desc FROM norm ) SELECT DISTINCT u AS user_id FROM ranked WHERE rn_asc = 1 OR rn_desc = 1 GROUP BY u, DATE(call_time) HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT other) = 2;

Why this is best: Normalize to a (u, other) view, pick the first and last per day, then check if other differs.

Performance: Two window passes + group-by.

Medium #2228 Users With Two Purchases Within Seven Days

▼

Return users whose any two consecutive purchases are within 7 days of each other.

Tables: Purchases (purchase_id, user_id, purchase_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A retention team identifies quick repeat buyers to feed a "you might also like" reorder email.

▶ 1 LAG per User + DATEDIFF Filter
WITH lagged AS ( SELECT user_id, purchase_date, LAG(purchase_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_date) AS prev_date FROM Purchases ) SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM lagged WHERE DATEDIFF(purchase_date, prev_date) <= 7 ORDER BY user_id;

Why this is best: LAG gives the previous purchase per user; a 7-day filter finds the rapid-repeat cohort.

Performance: Single window pass.

Hard #2474 Customers With Strictly Increasing Purchases

▼

Customers whose yearly spend strictly increases each year in the table.

Tables: Orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

Account management identifies accounts that grow year-over-year with no dips — ideal for upsell prioritization.

▶ 1 Yearly Totals + LAG Check
WITH yearly AS ( SELECT customer_id, YEAR(order_date) AS yr, SUM(price) AS total FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id, YEAR(order_date) ), lagged AS ( SELECT customer_id, yr, total, LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_total, LAG(yr) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_yr FROM yearly ) SELECT customer_id FROM lagged GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN prev_total IS NOT NULL AND (total <= prev_total OR yr <> prev_yr + 1) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0 AND COUNT(*) > 1;

Why this is best: LAG per customer surfaces the prior year. A strict increase is "no violation rows and more than one year".

Performance: Two passes. Linear.

Medium #2688 Find Active Users

▼

Users with two purchases within any 7-day window (like 2228 but from a different table schema).

Tables: Users (user_id, purchase_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A marketplace segments frequent buyers for a weekly digest.

▶ 1 LAG with 7-Day Window
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM ( SELECT user_id, purchase_date, LAG(purchase_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_date) AS prev_date FROM Users ) t WHERE DATEDIFF(purchase_date, prev_date) BETWEEN 1 AND 7 ORDER BY user_id;

Why this is best: Same LAG pattern as 2228; the DATEDIFF range filter returns users with rapid sequential buys.

Performance: One window pass.

Hard #2701 Consecutive Transactions with Increasing Amounts

▼

For each customer, find longest runs of strictly increasing consecutive-day transactions.

Tables: Transactions (transaction_id, customer_id, transaction_date, amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A fraud-watch team inspects customers whose transaction amounts climb sharply over consecutive days — a compromised-card signature.

▶ 1 Island Detection on Two Conditions
WITH t AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, amount, LAG(transaction_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS prev_date, LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS prev_amt FROM Transactions ), flags AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, amount, CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(transaction_date, prev_date) = 1 AND amount > prev_amt THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_island FROM t ), grouped AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, SUM(new_island) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS grp FROM flags ) SELECT customer_id, MIN(transaction_date) AS consecutive_start, MAX(transaction_date) AS consecutive_end FROM grouped GROUP BY customer_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;

Why this is best: Flag each day as "new island" when either gap > 1 or amount not increasing, then cumulative SUM creates the grp key.

Performance: Three window passes. Linear.

Rolling or Cumulative Aggregate Over Ordered Rows 10 problems

▼

A single table with a date or sequence column → each row annotated with a rolling or running aggregate.

Signal words: "rolling," "running total," "last N days," "cumulative," "moving average," "most recent before"

Technique: SUM/AVG OVER (ROWS BETWEEN), running SUM with threshold, subquery for last value before date

Reference Techniques used in Time Window

▼

2 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
SUM() OVER / AVG() OVER Computes an aggregate across a window without collapsing rows You need a running or rolling aggregate while keeping every row in the output 
SELECT day, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day
       ) AS running_total
FROM Trans;
ROWS BETWEEN Defines a sliding window frame (e.g., 6 preceding and current row) for a window aggregate You need a rolling average, running total, or cumulative sum over a fixed number of rows 
SELECT day,
       AVG(sales) OVER (
         ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS rolling_7d
FROM Daily;

#1321 Restaurant Growth (Medium)

▼

Restaurant managers analyze weekly revenue trends to smooth daily volatility. A Wednesday may be slow, but the 7-day average captures the true trend and helps predict capacity needs.

📌
Pattern: Rolling Window (ROWS BETWEEN)

Use SUM/AVG OVER with ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 6 PRECEDING for 7-day rolling average. Business: Restaurant revenue forecasting with weekly averages.

Business Context
Restaurant managers analyze weekly revenue trends to smooth daily volatility. A Wednesday may be slow, but the 7-day average captures the true trend and helps predict capacity needs.
▶ Rank 1: Window Frame with ROWS BETWEEN Correct semantics for rolling window
SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS amount, ROUND(AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS average_amount FROM ( SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS amount FROM Customer GROUP BY visited_on ) daily WHERE visited_on >= (SELECT MIN(visited_on) + INTERVAL '6 days' FROM Customer) ORDER BY visited_on;

Performance Analysis: GROUP BY aggregates to daily totals O(n). Window function processes once over sorted data O(n). ROWS BETWEEN frame: each row looks back 7 days max, so frame size is constant O(7). Memory: O(7) for frame buffer, not O(n). Much faster than RANGE which would match all dates in range.

Why Rank 1: ROWS BETWEEN guarantees exactly 7 rows included. RANGE BETWEEN would be wrong if multiple customers visited same day (would sum duplicates).

▶ Rank 2: Self-Join with Date Range Pre-window approach
SELECT d1.visited_on, SUM(d2.daily_amount) AS amount, ROUND(AVG(d2.daily_amount), 2) AS average_amount FROM ( SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS daily_amount FROM Customer GROUP BY visited_on ) d1 JOIN ( SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS daily_amount FROM Customer GROUP BY visited_on ) d2 ON d2.visited_on BETWEEN d1.visited_on - INTERVAL '6 days' AND d1.visited_on WHERE d1.visited_on >= (SELECT MIN(visited_on) + INTERVAL '6 days' FROM Customer) GROUP BY d1.visited_on ORDER BY d1.visited_on;

Performance Analysis: Two GROUP BY scans. Self-JOIN: each day must join with 7 other days = O(n * 7) = O(n). For 365 days: 365 * 7 = 2555 rows joined. Window function: single O(n) pass. Also requires date range predicate evaluation which is slower than fixed row count.

Why Rank 2: More expensive than window function due to explicit join overhead and date range evaluation.

#1204 Last Person to Fit in the Bus (Medium)

▼

Elevators have weight limits. Queue order matters: if heaviest people are first, fewer board before limit. System must know when to stop admitting passengers to avoid overweight trip.

📌
Pattern: Running Total with Capacity Check

Use SUM(weight) OVER(ORDER BY turn) for running cumulative weight. Find last turn where cumulative <= 1000. Business: Capacity planning (elevator limits, batch processing).

Business Context
Elevators have weight limits. Queue order matters: if heaviest people are first, fewer board before limit. System must know when to stop admitting passengers to avoid overweight trip.
▶ Rank 1: Window Running Total + Filter Clean and direct
SELECT person_name FROM ( SELECT person_name, SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY turn) AS cumulative_weight FROM Queue ) t WHERE cumulative_weight <= 1000 ORDER BY cumulative_weight DESC LIMIT 1;

Performance Analysis: Single scan of Queue: O(n). ORDER BY turn for window: O(n log n) but limited by existing turn order (may already be sorted). SUM OVER: O(n) in single pass with accumulator. Filter cumulative <= 1000: O(n). Identify MAX via ORDER BY DESC LIMIT 1: O(n log n) but only on filtered set. Memory: O(n) for sort buffer, O(1) for running sum.

Why Rank 1: Window function is perfect for running totals. Simple logic: "find last row where cumulative <= 1000".

▶ Rank 2: Self-Join with Cumulative Sum Pre-window approach
SELECT q1.person_name FROM Queue q1 WHERE ( SELECT SUM(q2.weight) FROM Queue q2 WHERE q2.turn <= q1.turn ) <= 1000 ORDER BY q1.turn DESC LIMIT 1;

Performance Analysis: Correlated subquery for each row. Outer scan: O(n). Inner SUM per row: for row i, sums first i rows = O(i). Total: O(1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n) = O(n²). For 1000 rows: 500k comparisons. Window function: O(n log n) = 10k comparisons. 50x slower! With index on turn, inner query still O(i).

Why Rank 2: Demonstrates why window functions are critical for running totals. Quadratic complexity is unacceptable for large queues.

#1164 Product Price at a Given Date (Medium)

▼

When a customer reports a historical transaction, e-commerce needs to show what price they were charged. Product had 3 price changes but customer bought on 2019-08-15 when it was $30, not current $50.

📌
Pattern: ROW_NUMBER with Date Filter

Use ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY change_date DESC) to get most recent price before target date. COALESCE to default price. Business: E-commerce price history lookup.

Business Context
When a customer reports a historical transaction, e-commerce needs to show what price they were charged. Product had 3 price changes but customer bought on 2019-08-15 when it was $30, not current $50.
▶ Rank 1: ROW_NUMBER DESC + COALESCE Handles missing products elegantly
SELECT DISTINCT product_id, COALESCE( (SELECT new_price FROM Products p2 WHERE p2.product_id = p1.product_id AND p2.change_date <= '2019-08-16' ORDER BY change_date DESC LIMIT 1), 10 ) AS price FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products ) p1 ORDER BY product_id;

Performance Analysis: Correlated subquery for each distinct product. Outer DISTINCT: O(n). Inner subquery: must find all changes <= target date per product = O(n/products) on average. With index on (product_id, change_date), becomes O(log n) seek + O(1) fetch. Total: O(products * log n). Alternative with window function avoids subquery overhead.

Why Rank 1: Correlated subquery is readable. COALESCE(10) handles products never changing price (default 10).

▶ Rank 2: Window Function + LEFT JOIN Most efficient for full product catalog
WITH latest_prices AS ( SELECT product_id, new_price, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY change_date DESC) AS rn FROM Products WHERE change_date <= '2019-08-16' ) SELECT p.product_id, COALESCE(lp.new_price, 10) AS price FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products) p LEFT JOIN latest_prices lp ON p.product_id = lp.product_id AND lp.rn = 1 ORDER BY p.product_id;

Performance Analysis: Window function: O(n log n) to sort all products by (product_id, change_date). ROW_NUMBER(): O(n) once sorted. Filter change_date <= target: O(n). LEFT JOIN: O(products) seek + O(n) on Products side. Total: O(n log n) dominated by window sort. Much faster than correlated subquery when many products have many price changes.

Why Rank 2: Window function avoids subquery overhead but more code. Better for large product catalogs.

Hard #579 Find Cumulative Salary of an Employee

▼

For each employee, sum the salary in the current month plus the two prior months (treating missing months as 0), then drop the row for each employee’s most recent working month.

Tables: Employee (id, month, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

Finance reports trailing 3-month salary totals for a pro-rata bonus calculation, excluding the latest unfinished month. The trick is handling employees who skipped months: a gap in month numbers must count as $0, not as silently pulling older rows into the window.

Gotcha — ROWS vs RANGE on missing months: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING counts the two previous rows in the sort, which silently skips over missing months (month 7 after a gap at 5 and 6 would pull in months 4 and 3 instead of treating 5 and 6 as 0). Use RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING or pad the table with zero-rows first.

▶ 1 Minimal: RANGE Window Handles Missing Months Automatically
WITH rolled AS ( SELECT id, month, salary, SUM(salary) OVER ( PARTITION BY id ORDER BY month RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS cum_salary, MAX(month) OVER (PARTITION BY id) AS max_month FROM Employee ) SELECT id, month, cum_salary AS Salary FROM rolled WHERE month <> max_month ORDER BY id ASC, month DESC;

Why this is best: RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING treats month as a numeric value range, so missing months contribute 0 to the sum automatically — no padding, no cross join. One CTE handles both the rolling sum and the max-month computation.

Performance: Two window passes over Employee directly, no extra rows generated.

▶ 2 Staircase CTE: Build a Full Grid, Zero-Fill, Then Roll
WITH distinct_months AS ( SELECT generate_series(1, MAX(month))::int AS month FROM Employee ), distinct_employee AS ( SELECT DISTINCT id FROM Employee ), employee_months AS ( SELECT id, month, MAX(month) OVER (PARTITION BY id) AS max_month FROM Employee ), id_month AS ( SELECT e.id, m.month FROM distinct_employee e CROSS JOIN distinct_months m ), base_table AS ( SELECT i.id, i.month, COALESCE(e.salary, 0) AS salary FROM id_month i LEFT JOIN Employee e ON i.id = e.id AND i.month = e.month ), sum_window AS ( SELECT id, month, salary, SUM(salary) OVER ( PARTITION BY id ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS cum_salary FROM base_table ) SELECT sw.id, sw.month, sw.cum_salary AS Salary FROM sum_window sw JOIN employee_months em ON sw.id = em.id AND sw.month = em.month AND sw.month <> em.max_month ORDER BY id ASC, month DESC;

Why this works: Explicitly builds a full (id, month) grid via CROSS JOIN + generate_series, zero-fills missing months with COALESCE, then a ROWS window works correctly because every month is now a real row. The final JOIN to employee_months keeps only the months each employee actually worked, minus the latest.

Why pick this: Longer but every step is independently verifiable — you can inspect each CTE’s output while debugging. Good when you don’t trust RANGE semantics or the engine you’re on doesn’t fully support them.

Performance: 6 CTE passes plus two joins. Noticeably more work than Rank 1 but linear in output size.

Medium #1308 Running Total for Different Genders

▼

Per gender, return the cumulative score over days.

Tables: Scores (player_name, gender, day, score_points)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

An event scoreboard updates a live running total per team (gender) at every event so organizers can display the race.

▶ 1 Ordered Cumulative SUM
SELECT gender, day, SUM(score_points) OVER (PARTITION BY gender ORDER BY day) AS total FROM Scores ORDER BY gender, day;

Why this is best: Window without explicit frame defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which is exactly a running total.

Performance: One window pass.

Medium #2066 Account Balance

▼

For each account, report the running balance after every transaction date.

Tables: Transactions (account_id, day, type, amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A bank exports a daily account-statement feed that shows the walking balance after each transaction.

▶ 1 Signed Running SUM per Account
SELECT account_id, day, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Deposit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY day) AS balance FROM Transactions ORDER BY account_id, day;

Why this is best: Signed SUM window gives running balance without a subquery.

Performance: One window pass.

Hard #2173 Longest Winning Streak

▼

For each player, return the longest consecutive run of wins.

Tables: Matches (player_id, match_day, result)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A sports analytics newsroom reports player "hot streaks" — the longest win run ever for each athlete.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands on Result
WITH runs AS ( SELECT player_id, match_day, result, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY match_day) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id, result ORDER BY match_day) AS grp FROM Matches ) SELECT m.player_id, COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN r.result = 'Win' THEN cnt END), 0) AS longest_streak FROM (SELECT DISTINCT player_id FROM Matches) m LEFT JOIN ( SELECT player_id, result, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM runs GROUP BY player_id, result, grp ) r USING (player_id) GROUP BY m.player_id;

Why this is best: Difference of two row numbers groups consecutive equal-result matches; the max count per Win group is the streak.

Performance: Two window passes + one aggregate.

Medium #2388 Change Null Values in a Table to the Previous Value

▼

Fill NULL coffee values forward with the most recent non-NULL value, preserving order.

Tables: CoffeeShop (id, drink)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A product catalog pipeline cleans sparsely-recorded fields by carrying the last known good value forward — a common ETL fill-forward.

▶ 1 Fill Forward via Windowed Grouping
WITH grp AS ( SELECT id, drink, COUNT(drink) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp_id FROM CoffeeShop ) SELECT id, FIRST_VALUE(drink) OVER (PARTITION BY grp_id ORDER BY id) AS drink FROM grp ORDER BY id;

Why this is best: Counting non-NULLs as a running counter creates a group id that increments every time a new non-NULL appears. FIRST_VALUE within the group fills forward.

Performance: Two window passes.

Medium #2854 Rolling Average Steps

▼

For users with 3+ day-streaks of activity, compute 3-day rolling average of steps.

Tables: Steps (user_id, steps_count, steps_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A fitness app charts a user's 3-day rolling step average, smoothing daily noise for motivation graphs.

▶ 1 Windowed Average with Row Count Filter
SELECT user_id, steps_date, ROUND(AVG(steps_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY steps_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_average FROM Steps QUALIFY COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY steps_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) = 3 ORDER BY user_id, steps_date;

Why this is best: ROWS frame averages three prior days. QUALIFY drops incomplete early windows (Snowflake/Trino style; use a CTE filter in MySQL).

Performance: Two window passes.

Hard #2994 Friday Purchases II

▼

Report every Friday in November 2023 with its total spend, zero if no sales.

Tables: Purchases (user_id, purchase_date, amount_spend)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

Unlike 2993, this report must include Fridays with no sales to show a complete Nov-Fridays timeline.

▶ 1 Calendar CTE + LEFT JOIN
WITH fridays AS ( SELECT '2023-11-03' AS d UNION ALL SELECT '2023-11-10' UNION ALL SELECT '2023-11-17' UNION ALL SELECT '2023-11-24' ) SELECT FLOOR((DAYOFMONTH(d) - 1) / 7) + 1 AS week_of_month, d AS purchase_date, COALESCE(SUM(p.amount_spend), 0) AS total_amount FROM fridays LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON p.purchase_date = d GROUP BY d ORDER BY d;

Why this is best: Anchoring to a calendar CTE guarantees every Friday appears even with no data.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Flatten Symmetric Pairs Then Aggregate 2 problems

▼

A single table with bidirectional relationships (A-B implies B-A) → UNION ALL both directions, then GROUP BY.

Signal words: "friends," "connections," "either side," "requester or accepter," "both directions"

Technique: UNION ALL of both columns + GROUP BY + ORDER BY

Reference Techniques used in Normalize Bidirectional

▼

2 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
UNION ALL Stacks rows from two queries vertically into one result set (keeps duplicates) Two column roles are interchangeable, or you need both directions to appear as one column 
SELECT name FROM Customers
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM Vendors;
LEAST / GREATEST Returns the smaller or larger of two values, normalizing pair order You need to treat (A, B) and (B, A) as the same pair by sorting them into a consistent order 
SELECT LEAST(user1, user2)    AS person1,
       GREATEST(user1, user2) AS person2,
       COUNT(*)               AS calls
FROM Calls
GROUP BY person1, person2;

#602 Friend Requests II: Who Has the Most Friends (Medium)

▼

Find the person with the most friends. Friendship is bidirectional: if user A sent a request to user B and B accepted, they're friends. Count total friends for each person and return the one with the most.

Schema: RequestAccepted(requester_id, accepter_id, accept_date)

Goal: Find the person with the most friends. Friendship is bidirectional: if user A sent a request to user B and B accepted, they're friends. Count total friends for each person and return the one with the most.

Why this matters
Social network analytics: identifying influencers or highly-connected users, ranking by network size, and understanding community structure.
▶ Rank 1: UNION ALL + GROUP BY + ORDER BY LIMIT 1
SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends GROUP BY id ORDER BY num DESC LIMIT 1;

Why rank 1: UNION ALL combines requester and accepter IDs (each person appears in either role, counting both directions). GROUP BY counts total appearances. ORDER BY DESC + LIMIT 1 gets the maximum without window functions or subqueries.

Performance: O(n log n) due to sorting, but LIMIT 1 stops early once the max is found. Simpler than DENSE_RANK and avoids subquery overhead.

▶ Rank 2: UNION ALL + GROUP BY + DENSE_RANK (for ties)
WITH friend_counts AS ( SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends GROUP BY id ) SELECT id, num FROM friend_counts WHERE DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY num DESC) = 1;

Why rank 2: If multiple people have the same (highest) friend count, this returns all of them. Uses window function DENSE_RANK to handle ties. Follow-up from problem statement: "In the real world, multiple people could have the most friends."

Performance: O(n log n) for aggregation and window ranking. More complex than Rank 1 but necessary if ties must be included.

▶ Rank 3: UNION ALL + GROUP BY + Subquery MAX
SELECT id, num FROM ( SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends GROUP BY id ) AS counts WHERE num = ( SELECT MAX(cnt) FROM ( SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends2 GROUP BY id ) AS max_counts );

Why rank 3: Subquery-based: compute friend counts, then filter to max with WHERE. Redundant: scans the same UNION ALL twice (inefficient). Use only if window functions unavailable.

Performance: O(n log n) but with repeated scans. Slower than Rank 1 and 2. Worse maintainability due to nested subqueries.

📌
Bidirectional Friendship Logic
The key insight: UNION ALL (not UNION) combines rows without deduplication. Each person appears twice if they're in both requester and accepter roles. GROUP BY counts all occurrences, reflecting true friend count.
📊
Decision Tree Links
UNION ALL pattern for combining results

Medium #1699 Number of Calls Between Two Persons

▼

Report call count and total duration per unordered pair of (from_id, to_id).

Tables: Calls (from_id, to_id, duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A telco bills symmetric pair usage. A call from A to B and B to A must combine into one pair for reporting.

▶ 1 LEAST/GREATEST Normalization + Aggregate
SELECT LEAST(from_id, to_id) AS person1, GREATEST(from_id, to_id) AS person2, COUNT(*) AS call_count, SUM(duration) AS total_duration FROM Calls GROUP BY person1, person2;

Why this is best: LEAST/GREATEST gives a canonical representation of each unordered pair, collapsing (A,B) and (B,A) into one group.

Performance: One aggregate pass.

Remove Duplicate Rows In Place 2 problems

▼

A single table with duplicate rows → the table with duplicates removed, keeping only the row with the smallest ID.

Signal words: "delete," "remove duplicates," "keep only," "deduplicate"

Technique: DELETE with self-join keeping MIN(id)

Reference Techniques used in Delete Duplicates

▼

2 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
DELETE + CTE Removes rows from the table using a CTE to identify which rows to keep or remove The problem asks you to physically modify the table 
WITH dups AS (
  SELECT id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id
         ) AS rn
  FROM Users
)
DELETE FROM Users
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM dups WHERE rn > 1);
ROW_NUMBER() Assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition You need to identify duplicates for deletion, pick one row per group, or rank with no ties 
SELECT *,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
         PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
       ) AS rn
FROM Emp;

Filter Rows vs Remove Duplicates: If the problem says "find" or "show" unique values, that is Filter Rows using SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY (the table stays unchanged). This recipe is only for when the problem says "delete" or "remove" and the table itself must be modified. The test: if you ran the query twice, would anything change the second time? With SELECT, no. With DELETE, the second run finds nothing to delete because the rows are already gone.

Easy #196 Delete Duplicate Emails

▼

Delete all duplicate emails, keeping only one unique email with the smallest id. Modify the table in-place with a DELETE statement.

Tables: Person (id, email)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern H: Deduplication (DELETE)

Real-World Example

Database maintenance after a merger deduplicates customer records. Duplicate emails represent the same person; keeping the lowest id (earliest record) preserves historical data integrity.

▶ 1 DELETE with Subquery (NOT IN)
DELETE FROM Person WHERE id NOT IN ( SELECT MIN(id) FROM Person GROUP BY email );

Why this is best: Subquery finds MIN(id) per email (keeps one per email). DELETE all rows whose id is NOT in that set. Simple, readable, and works across dialects.

Gotcha (Critical): Some SQL engines (e.g., older MySQL) forbid deleting from a table when the subquery references the same table. If you hit "You can't specify the target table 'Person' in FROM clause", wrap the subquery in another subquery: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT MIN(id) AS id FROM Person GROUP BY email) t)

Performance: O(n log n) for GROUP BY, then hash join for IN check. Generally fast.

▶ 2 DELETE with Self-Join
DELETE FROM p1 USING Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id;

Why this works: Self-join pairs duplicates. Delete rows where id > partner's id (keeps the lower id). USING is PostgreSQL syntax; MySQL uses different syntax (see variant below).

MySQL Variant: DELETE p1 FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id;

Gotcha: Self-join can be slow if table is large. O(n²) worst case for full cross join before filter.

Performance: Hash join on (email) reduces complexity. Still slower than approach #1 for very large tables.

▶ 3 DELETE with ROW_NUMBER Window Function
DELETE FROM Person WHERE id NOT IN ( SELECT id FROM ( SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM Person ) ranked WHERE rn = 1 );

Why this works: ROW_NUMBER ranks rows per email (ordered by id). rn=1 is the lowest id. Keep all rn=1 rows, delete rest.

Caveat: Window functions require nested subqueries. More complex syntax. Marginally clearer intent ("keep first per group") but overkill for this problem.

Performance: Window function scan, then subquery filter, then DELETE. Similar to approach #1 in cost but more overhead.

Medium Remove Duplicate Pending Transactions by ID

▼

Deduplicate a fintech payment queue on a composite key (user_id, merchant_id, amount), keeping only the row with the smallest queue_id (earliest submission).

Tables: transaction_queue (queue_id, user_id, merchant_id, amount, submitted_at, status)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern H: Deduplication (DELETE) (Note: composite-key dedup, not single-column)

Real-World Example

A fintech app's pending payment queue accumulated duplicate transactions after a client-side retry bug submitted the same charge multiple times within seconds. The natural key is (user_id, merchant_id, amount) — same payer, same payee, same amount — and the smallest queue_id is the original submission. Deduplicating before the queue is drained downstream prevents double-charging the customer.

▶ 1 DELETE with Self-Join via USING (PostgreSQL)
DELETE FROM transaction_queue t1 USING transaction_queue t2 WHERE t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id AND t1.user_id = t2.user_id AND t1.merchant_id = t2.merchant_id AND t1.amount = t2.amount;

Why this works: The self-join pairs every row with every other row in the same (user_id, merchant_id, amount) group. The t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id predicate keeps only pairs where t1 is the later submission, so DELETE removes every row that has at least one earlier twin. The smallest queue_id in each group is never on the t1 side of any qualifying pair, so it survives.

Why "smallest queue_id wins": Reverse the inequality (t1.queue_id < t2.queue_id) and you'd keep the largest instead. The direction of the inequality picks the survivor — pick it deliberately based on the prompt ("earliest submission" = smallest queue_id since the column is SERIAL).

MySQL Variant: DELETE t1 FROM transaction_queue t1 JOIN transaction_queue t2 ON t1.user_id = t2.user_id AND t1.merchant_id = t2.merchant_id AND t1.amount = t2.amount AND t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id;

Gotcha: Forgetting any one of the three equality predicates collapses the dedup key. Drop t1.amount = t2.amount and you'd treat a $49.99 charge and a $1,000 charge from the same user-merchant pair as duplicates.

Performance: Self-join is O(n²) worst case, but a hash or merge join on the composite key (user_id, merchant_id, amount) cuts it to roughly O(n). Slower than a single-column dedup but still fine for queue-sized tables.

▶ 2 DELETE with EXISTS (correlated subquery)
DELETE FROM transaction_queue t1 WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM transaction_queue t2 WHERE t1.user_id = t2.user_id AND t1.merchant_id = t2.merchant_id AND t1.amount = t2.amount AND t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id );

Why this works: For every candidate row t1, EXISTS asks "is there any row in the same (user_id, merchant_id, amount) group with a smaller queue_id?" If yes, t1 is a later duplicate and gets deleted. The smallest queue_id in each group has no qualifying t2, so EXISTS is false and that row survives.

When to prefer this over the self-join: EXISTS is more portable (works on every major dialect with the same syntax) and reads more naturally as "delete me if a smaller twin exists." It also short-circuits — once one qualifying t2 is found, the planner stops looking for more, which can be faster than the self-join's full pair enumeration when groups are large.

Gotcha (NULL handling): Equality predicates against NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. If any of user_id, merchant_id, or amount is nullable and contains NULLs, two NULL-bearing rows would NOT match each other and the dedup would silently miss them. The prompt's NOT NULL constraints on these columns are what make this safe — verify before relying on this pattern.

Gotcha (the inequality direction is the entire spec): Same as approach #1 — flip t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id to < and you'd keep the latest, not the earliest. Read the prompt twice before picking the direction.

Performance: Roughly equivalent to approach #1. The planner often rewrites EXISTS as a semi-join, which uses the same hash-join machinery as the self-join but stops on first match per outer row.

Multi-Table Recipes

4 recipe categories covering 103 problems. Two are join-specific (enrich-join, enrich-aggregate, 59 problems), one is reshape (pivot / unpivot / combine, 12 problems), and one (rank-partition, 32 problems) is reachable from both Single Table and Join 2+ in the Decision Tree. After a join, the result is effectively one table — so the nine Single-Table shape recipes also apply to joined data.

Reference Technique Quick Reference: When and Why Each Method Works

▼

A quick lookup for the SQL techniques used across all 4 multi table recipe categories, with explanations of when each method applies.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
Join Techniques
INNER JOIN Returns only rows that have a matching key in both tables You only want results where both tables have data for that key (the default join type) 
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
LEFT JOIN Returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match You want to keep every row from one table even if there is no match in the other (e.g., "include customers with no orders") 
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
CROSS JOIN Produces every possible combination of rows from both tables You need all combinations (e.g., every student paired with every exam) before filtering or aggregating 
SELECT s.name, e.exam_id
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Exams e;
COALESCE Returns the first non NULL value, useful for replacing NULLs introduced by LEFT JOIN After a LEFT JOIN, you want 0 instead of NULL for missing matches 
SELECT c.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS spend
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
Aggregation After Join
GROUP BY + aggregates Collapses joined rows into summary rows per group After joining, you need totals, counts, or averages per group rather than individual rows 
SELECT c.country, SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM Orders o
JOIN Customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
Ranking After Join
DENSE_RANK() / ROW_NUMBER() Assigns a rank to each row within a partition, allowing you to pick the top N You need the highest, lowest, or Nth row within each group after joining tables 
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT e.*, d.name AS dept,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (
           PARTITION BY d.id ORDER BY e.salary DESC
         ) AS rk
  FROM Emp e JOIN Dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
) t
WHERE rk = 1;
PARTITION BY Divides rows into groups for the window function to operate on independently You need to rank or number rows separately within each group (per department, per customer) 
SELECT name, dept,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg
FROM Emp;
Combining Independent Results
UNION / UNION ALL Stacks rows from separate queries vertically. UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps all The output combines results from independent queries that share the same column structure 
SELECT id, 'order'  AS source FROM Orders
UNION ALL
SELECT id, 'refund'        FROM Refunds;
Subqueries A query nested inside another query, used to compute intermediate results Each section of the UNION needs its own independent logic to produce its rows 
SELECT name
FROM Emp
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Emp);

Reference ON Clause Cheat Sheet (what you can put in ON, and ON vs WHERE)

▼

Quick lookup for what the JOIN ON clause accepts, plus a side-by-side example of the LEFT JOIN gotcha that drops rows you wanted to keep.

What the ON clause can hold — any boolean expression:

Pattern Example
Equality between sides a.id = b.id
Single-table filter b.status = 'open'
Range / inequality a.date BETWEEN b.start AND b.end
Null check b.deleted_at IS NULL
OR a.id = b.id OR a.alt_id = b.id
Function call LOWER(a.name) = LOWER(b.name)

The LEFT JOIN gotcha — ON vs WHERE:

A right-side filter in ON only blocks the match. A right-side filter in WHERE blocks survival. Result: WHERE drops the unmatched left rows you wanted to keep.

Filter location What it does Example outcome
ON (right-side filter) Filters which right rows are eligible to attach during the join Unmatched left rows survive with nulls on the right
WHERE (right-side filter) Filters the assembled result after the join finishes Unmatched left rows are thrown out (LEFT JOIN behaves like INNER)
WHERE (left-side filter) Filters the left table before / during the join Either ON or WHERE is fine; placement does not change the result

Open the full walkthrough with sample tables →

Reference JOIN Checklist

▼

Six verification steps to run through before and after every JOIN to avoid silent row multiplication, dropped rows, and NULL mismatches.

  1. Identify the join key(s) — columns that connect the tables
  2. Choose join type: INNER (default), LEFT (keep all from first table), CROSS (all combinations)
  3. Check for duplicates in keys — many-to-many creates row explosion
  4. Handle NULL join keys — NULLs never match in a standard JOIN
  5. After joining: verify row count to ensure no unexpected multiplication
  6. Right-side filters on a LEFT JOIN belong in ON, not WHERE — otherwise the LEFT JOIN behaves like INNER. See the ON vs WHERE walkthrough.

Look Up Columns From a Reference Table 14 problems

▼

A fact table + a dimension table (or one table playing two roles via self-join) → fact rows enriched with looked-up columns.

Signal words: "find the name for," "replace ID with," "look up," "show along with," "regardless of," manager/employee, parent/child, referrer/referee

Technique: LEFT JOIN, INNER JOIN, CROSS JOIN (for all combinations), self-join (alias the same table twice)

Pitfall: ON vs WHERE on a LEFT JOIN

A right-side filter in WHERE drops unmatched left rows and silently turns your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Put right-side filters in ON to keep every left row.

Open the full ON vs WHERE walkthrough →

Reference Techniques used in Enrich Join

▼

5 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
INNER JOIN Returns only rows that have a matching key in both tables You only want results where both tables have data for that key 
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
LEFT JOIN Returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match You want to keep every row from one table even if there is no match in the other 
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
CROSS JOIN Produces every possible combination of rows from both tables You need all combinations before filtering or aggregating 
SELECT s.name, e.exam_id
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Exams e;
Self-join Aliases the same table twice to compare or look up rows within one table The row needs to look up another row in the same table (employee/manager, parent/child, referrer/referee) 
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON m.id = e.managerId;
COALESCE Returns the first non-NULL value from a list of columns or expressions You need a fallback value when a column might be NULL 
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Unknown') AS display_name
FROM Users;

Self-joins live here too. Even when the prompt mentions only one physical table (Employees with managerId, Categories with parent_id, Users with referee_id), if the row needs to look up another row in the same table, it is a join. Alias the table twice (e.g., Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id) and treat each alias as a separate "virtual" table. The join lives in this recipe, not in row-compare (which is reserved for sequential LAG/LEAD neighbors).

#1378 — Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier

Easy
▼

Show the unique ID of each employee. If an employee has no unique ID, show null instead.

Problem: Show the unique ID of each employee. If an employee has no unique ID, show null instead.

Tables: Employees (id, name) and EmployeeUNI (id, unique_id)

Decision Tree Path

This is a LEFT JOIN pattern — all employees appear in output, with matching unique IDs or NULL.

Real-World Example

HR system merging internal employee IDs with SSO (Single Sign-On) identifiers. Not every employee has migrated to SSO yet, so some have NULL.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — LEFT JOIN with SELECT Order
SELECT eu.unique_id, e.name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN EmployeeUNI eu ON e.id = eu.id ORDER BY eu.unique_id;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN ensures all employees appear. Selecting unique_id first shows NULLs naturally for unmatched employees.

Performance: O(n + m) with index on EmployeeUNI.id. Clean, readable, minimal intermediate rows.

▶ 2 Alternative — COALESCE for Explicit NULL Handling
SELECT COALESCE(eu.unique_id, NULL) AS unique_id, e.name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN EmployeeUNI eu ON e.id = eu.id;

Why this works: COALESCE explicitly handles NULL, making the intent clear (though redundant here since LEFT JOIN already produces NULLs).

When to use: If you need fallback values or multiple NULL coalescing logic.

#1068 — Product Sales Analysis I

Easy
▼

Report product_name, year, and price for each sale. Join Sales and Product tables.

Problem: Report product_name, year, and price for each sale. Join Sales and Product tables.

Tables: Sales (sale_id, product_id, year, quantity, price) and Product (product_id, product_name)

Decision Tree Path

This is an INNER JOIN pattern — only sales with matching products are returned. No unmatched rows.

Real-World Example

E-commerce combining transaction log (Sales) with product catalog (Product) to show what was actually purchased with full product details.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — INNER JOIN
SELECT p.product_name, s.year, s.price FROM Sales s INNER JOIN Product p ON s.product_id = p.product_id;

Why this is best: INNER JOIN filters to only matched rows. Since every sale should have a product, this is safe and fast.

Performance: O(n + m) with index on Product.product_id. Minimal result set.

▶ 2 Alternative — Explicit JOIN Keyword
SELECT p.product_name, s.year, s.price FROM Sales s JOIN Product p USING (product_id);

Why this works: USING clause is cleaner when join key has same name in both tables. Shorter than ON.

Caveat: Some teams prefer explicit ON for consistency.

#577 — Employee Bonus

Easy
▼

Report name and bonus for employees with bonus = 1000.

Problem: Report name and bonus for employees with bonus < 1000 OR no bonus. Filter out employees with bonus >= 1000.

Tables: Employee (empId, name, supervisor, salary) and Bonus (empId, bonus)

Decision Tree Path

This is an anti-join variant using LEFT JOIN with NULL detection. Keep unmatched rows (no bonus) and filter matched rows by condition.

Real-World Example

Payroll processing identifying employees due for bonus review: those with small bonuses (< 1000) or missing bonuses entirely.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — LEFT JOIN with NULL-aware WHERE
SELECT e.name, b.bonus FROM Employee e LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId WHERE b.bonus < 1000 OR b.bonus IS NULL;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN preserves all employees. WHERE clause filters: keep those with small bonuses OR NULL (no bonus at all).

Performance: O(n + m). Key insight: b.bonus IS NULL catches unmatched rows, which are displayed as NULL in output.

▶ 2 Alternative — COALESCE for Null-Safe Comparison
SELECT e.name, b.bonus FROM Employee e LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId WHERE COALESCE(b.bonus, 0) < 1000;

Why this works: COALESCE treats NULL as 0, so NULL < 1000 is TRUE. One WHERE condition instead of OR.

Caveat: Less explicit than IS NULL. Could be confusing if 0 has different meaning. Solution 1 is clearer.

#1581 — Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions

Easy
▼

Find customer IDs and count of visits where NO transaction occurred. Filter for NULL transactions.

Problem: Find customer IDs and count of visits where NO transaction occurred. Filter for NULL transactions.

Tables: Visits (visit_id, customer_id) and Transactions (transaction_id, visit_id, amount)

Decision Tree Path

This is a classic anti-join: LEFT JOIN then filter WHERE transaction IS NULL, then GROUP BY and COUNT.

Real-World Example

Retail analytics identifying "window shoppers" — customers who visited but didn't buy. Helps improve conversion tactics.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — LEFT JOIN + IS NULL Filter + GROUP BY
SELECT v.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS count_no_trans FROM Visits v LEFT JOIN Transactions t ON v.visit_id = t.visit_id WHERE t.transaction_id IS NULL GROUP BY v.customer_id;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN keeps all visits. WHERE t.transaction_id IS NULL filters to unmatched visits only. COUNT(*) tallies them per customer.

Performance: O(n + m + k log k) where k = result size. Index on Transactions.visit_id and GROUP BY column speeds execution.

▶ 2 Alternative — NOT EXISTS Subquery
SELECT v.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS count_no_trans FROM Visits v WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Transactions t WHERE t.visit_id = v.visit_id ) GROUP BY v.customer_id;

Why this works: NOT EXISTS explicitly checks no transaction row exists for each visit. Can be faster on large datasets with good indexing.

Caveat: More verbose; correlated subqueries can be slower without proper indexing. LEFT JOIN + NULL is usually clearer.

#1280 — Students and Examinations

Medium
▼

For each student-subject pair, count exam attempts. Ensure ALL student-subject combinations appear, even if 0 exams attended.

Problem: For each student-subject pair, count exam attempts. Ensure ALL student-subject combinations appear, even if 0 exams attended.

Tables: Students (student_id, student_name), Subjects (subject_name), Examinations (student_id, subject_name)

Decision Tree Path

Combined pattern: CROSS JOIN (all student-subject combos) + LEFT JOIN Examinations + GROUP BY + COUNT. Forces complete result set.

Real-World Example

Learning Management System (LMS) grade report: every student appears for every course, showing exam count or 0 if they haven't taken it yet.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — CROSS JOIN + LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY + COUNT
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name, COUNT(e.student_id) AS attended_exams FROM Students s CROSS JOIN Subjects sub LEFT JOIN Examinations e ON s.student_id = e.student_id AND sub.subject_name = e.subject_name GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;

Why this is best: CROSS JOIN creates all student-subject pairs. LEFT JOIN matches exams; unmatched pairs get COUNT = 0. Guarantees complete output.

Performance: O(n * m + e log(n*m)) where n = students, m = subjects, e = exam records. Be careful with large student/subject counts.

▶ 2 Alternative — COALESCE on COUNT for Readability
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name, COALESCE(COUNT(e.student_id), 0) AS attended_exams FROM Students s CROSS JOIN Subjects sub LEFT JOIN Examinations e ON s.student_id = e.student_id AND sub.subject_name = e.subject_name GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;

Why this works: COALESCE explicitly shows 0 instead of NULL. More explicit, though COUNT already returns 0 for no matches.

Caveat: Redundant; COUNT already handles NULLs. Use if team requires explicit zero display or if aggregating multiple metrics.

SELECT e.name AS Employee FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON m.id = e.managerId WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

Return the device each player first logged in from.

SELECT a.player_id, a.device_id FROM Activity a JOIN ( SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id ) f ON f.player_id = a.player_id AND f.first_date = a.event_date;

Recommend pages that user 1's friends like but user 1 has not liked yet.

SELECT DISTINCT l.page_id AS recommended_page FROM Likes l WHERE l.user_id IN ( SELECT user2_id FROM Friendship WHERE user1_id = 1 UNION SELECT user1_id FROM Friendship WHERE user2_id = 1 ) AND l.page_id NOT IN (SELECT page_id FROM Likes WHERE user_id = 1);

Medium #1747 Leetflex Banned Accounts

▼

Detect accounts whose sessions overlap in time but on different IPs.

Tables: LogInfo (account_id, ip_address, login, logout)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

A streaming service bans concurrent-use accounts by spotting sessions overlapping on different IPs — a shared-credentials signature.

▶ 1 Self-Join on Overlap + Different IP
SELECT DISTINCT a.account_id FROM LogInfo a JOIN LogInfo b ON a.account_id = b.account_id AND a.ip_address <> b.ip_address AND a.login <= b.logout AND b.login <= a.logout;

Why this is best: The overlap condition (a.login <= b.logout AND b.login <= a.logout) is the canonical interval intersection; different ip completes the rule.
