Medium #1811 Find Interview Candidates

▼

Candidates are gold-medalists of 3 consecutive contests OR users with >= 2 attendances in any year.

Tables: Contests (contest_id, gold_medal, silver_medal, bronze_medal), Users (user_id, mail, name), Register (contest_id, user_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

An events team picks interview subjects combining two eligibility paths: consistent top performers AND engaged attendees.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands on Golds + UNION Attendance
WITH golds AS ( SELECT gold_medal AS user_id, contest_id, contest_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY gold_medal ORDER BY contest_id) AS grp FROM Contests ), gold_streak AS ( SELECT user_id FROM golds GROUP BY user_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ), heavy_registrants AS ( SELECT user_id FROM Register GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ) SELECT DISTINCT u.name, u.mail FROM Users u WHERE u.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM gold_streak) OR u.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM heavy_registrants);

Why this is best: Gaps-and-islands identifies 3-contest gold streaks; a separate count covers the attendance path. UNION-style filter enforces OR.

Performance: Two aggregates. Linear.

Medium #2041 Accepted Candidates From the Interviews

▼

Candidates with 2+ years experience AND total interview score >= 15.

Tables: Candidates (candidate_id, name, years_of_exp, interview_id), Rounds (interview_id, round_id, score)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

A talent-ops team automates interview shortlisting by combining resume criteria with structured interview scores.

▶ 1 Pre-Aggregate Scores + Filter
WITH totals AS ( SELECT interview_id, SUM(score) AS total FROM Rounds GROUP BY interview_id ) SELECT c.candidate_id FROM Candidates c JOIN totals t ON t.interview_id = c.interview_id WHERE c.years_of_exp >= 2 AND t.total >= 15;

Why this is best: Aggregate in a CTE, then apply compound eligibility rules.

Performance: One aggregate + one join.

Join Tables Then Aggregate 45 problems

▼

Two or more tables that must be joined before meaningful aggregation → one summary row per group.

Signal words: "for each... find average/total from another table," "rate," "percentage," "weighted," "all products"

Technique: JOIN + GROUP BY, weighted AVG, HAVING COUNT = (SELECT COUNT), date-range joins

Pitfall: date filters on a LEFT JOIN

When you want every left row to survive (e.g., "all books, even ones with zero sales last year"), put date filters on the right table in ON, not WHERE. A WHERE on a right-side date drops unmatched rows and undercounts groups with no recent activity.

Open the full ON vs WHERE walkthrough →

Common Trap: WHERE Filters Drop Rows You Want to Show as 0

Many enrich-aggregate problems expect a row with count 0 when a left-side row has no qualifying right-side matches. Example: "for each user, count their orders in 2019" — users with no 2019 orders should appear with count 0, not disappear from the result.

Why it breaks: WHERE runs after the LEFT JOIN. A filter on a right-side column (e.g. WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2019) drops unmatched rows along with mismatched ones, so users with no orders at all silently vanish.

The fix: Keep the LEFT JOIN, then move the filter inside the aggregate. SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) turns rows that fail the condition into 0 instead of removing them, so every left-side row survives with a real count.

-- BREAKS: users with no 2019 orders are dropped entirely
SELECT u.user_id, u.join_date, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_in_2019
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON u.user_id = o.buyer_id
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2019
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.join_date;

-- WORKS: every user survives, count rolls up to 0 when no row matches
SELECT u.user_id, u.join_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2019 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_in_2019
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON u.user_id = o.buyer_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.join_date;

How to spot this: Scan the example output for any row showing 0 (or "no activity," "0 orders," "never purchased"). That is the signal to keep the LEFT JOIN and filter inside SUM or COUNT with CASE WHEN, never with a WHERE on the right-side column.

Reference Techniques used in Enrich Aggregate

▼

5 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
INNER JOIN Returns only rows that have a matching key in both tables You only want results where both tables have data for that key 
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
LEFT JOIN Returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match You want to keep every row from one table even if there is no match in the other 
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
GROUP BY + aggregates (after JOIN) Collapses joined rows into summary rows per group After joining, you need totals, counts, or averages per group rather than individual rows 
SELECT c.country, SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM Orders o
JOIN Customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
COALESCE Returns the first non-NULL value from a list of columns or expressions You need a fallback value when a column might be NULL 
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Unknown') AS display_name
FROM Users;
HAVING Filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregate results The condition depends on a count, sum, or other aggregate (e.g., "groups with more than 1 row") 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*)
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

#1075 — Project Employees I

Easy
▼

Report average experience years for employees on each project, rounded to 2 decimals.

Problem: Report average experience years for employees on each project, rounded to 2 decimals.

Tables: Project (project_id, employee_id) and Employee (employee_id, name, experience_years)

Decision Tree Path

JOIN + GROUP BY aggregation. INNER JOIN connects projects to employees, then aggregate experience per project.

Real-World Example

Resource management calculating average team seniority per project to assess project complexity or team strength.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — INNER JOIN + GROUP BY + ROUND
SELECT p.project_id, ROUND(AVG(e.experience_years), 2) AS average_years FROM Project p INNER JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id GROUP BY p.project_id;

Why this is best: INNER JOIN merges projects and employees. GROUP BY aggregates by project. ROUND ensures 2 decimal precision.

Performance: O(n log n) due to GROUP BY. Index on Employee.employee_id and Project.project_id speeds join.

▶ 2 Alternative — CAST for Decimal Precision
SELECT p.project_id, CAST(AVG(e.experience_years) AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS average_years FROM Project p INNER JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id GROUP BY p.project_id;

Why this works: CAST to DECIMAL(10, 2) guarantees output type. Useful if you need exact decimal type downstream.

Difference: ROUND is simpler for display; CAST is stricter for storage or type requirements.

#1327 — List the Products Ordered in a Period

Easy
▼

Find product names with at least 100 units ordered in February 2020, and show their total units.

Problem: Find product names with at least 100 units ordered in February 2020, and show their total units.

Tables: Products (product_id, product_name, product_category) and Orders (product_id, order_date, unit)

Decision Tree Path

JOIN + WHERE date filter + GROUP BY + HAVING. Classic date-range + aggregation pattern with join.

Real-World Example

Inventory management identifying high-demand products in a specific quarter to optimize stock replenishment and predict seasonal trends.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — INNER JOIN + DATE Filter + GROUP BY + HAVING
SELECT p.product_name, SUM(o.unit) AS unit FROM Products p INNER JOIN Orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE o.order_date >= '2020-02-01' AND o.order_date < '2020-03-01' GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name HAVING SUM(o.unit) >= 100;

Why this is best: WHERE filters early (Feb 2020 only). GROUP BY aggregates units per product. HAVING filters groups with SUM >= 100. Minimal data processed.

Performance: O(n + m + k log k). Early WHERE filtering reduces data before join and aggregation. Index on order_date crucial.

▶ 2 Alternative — EXTRACT for Date Matching
SELECT p.product_name, SUM(o.unit) AS unit FROM Products p INNER JOIN Orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2020 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.order_date) = 2 GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name HAVING SUM(o.unit) >= 100;

Why this works: EXTRACT is explicit about date components. Good for readability if checking specific month/year.

Caveat: Slightly slower than range comparison because EXTRACT can't use indexes as efficiently. Solution 1 preferred for performance.

#1633 Percentage of Users Attended a Contest (Easy)

▼

For each contest, calculate the percentage of all users who registered (to 2 decimals). Order by percentage DESC, then contest_id ASC.

Schema: Users(user_id, user_name); Register(contest_id, user_id)

Goal: For each contest, calculate the percentage of all users who registered (to 2 decimals). Order by percentage DESC, then contest_id ASC.

Why this matters
Event and competition metrics: organizers need participation rates to gauge interest, set pricing, and plan future events.
▶ Rank 1: JOIN + GROUP BY + Percentage Calculation
SELECT r.contest_id, ROUND(100 * COUNT(r.user_id) / ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users ), 2) AS percentage FROM Register r GROUP BY r.contest_id ORDER BY percentage DESC, r.contest_id ASC;

Why rank 1: Simple scalar subquery for total user count. Divides registrations per contest by total users, multiplies by 100, rounds to 2 decimals. ROUND(value, 2) ensures correct formatting.

Performance: O(n log n) for grouping. The subquery runs once (scalar), so negligible overhead. Much faster than joining Users for each row.

💡
Why scalar subquery, not JOIN?
A JOIN with Users would replicate each Register row for every User, bloating intermediate results. A scalar subquery (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users) evaluates once and is reused for all contests.

#1934 Confirmation Rate (Medium)

▼

User onboarding tracks how many signups complete email/SMS confirmation. High confirmation rates indicate a smooth signup flow; low rates indicate friction or user churn.

Schema: Signups(user_id, time_stamp), Confirmations(user_id, time_stamp, action='confirmed'|'timeout')

For each user, calculate confirmation_rate = COUNT(action='confirmed') / COUNT(*). If no confirmations, return 0.00. Rounded to 2 decimals.

Business Context: Onboarding Funnel Analysis

User onboarding tracks how many signups complete email/SMS confirmation. High confirmation rates indicate a smooth signup flow; low rates indicate friction or user churn.

▶ Rank 1: LEFT JOIN + Conditional Aggregation Includes users with 0 confirmations
SELECT s.user_id, ROUND( COALESCE( COUNT(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 END) * 1.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(c.user_id), 0), 0 ), 2 ) AS confirmation_rate FROM Signups s LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id GROUP BY s.user_id ORDER BY s.user_id;

Why this ranks first: LEFT JOIN ensures all signups appear, even those with no confirmations. CASE WHEN counts confirmed only. NULLIF turns 0 into NULL so division yields NULL, then COALESCE converts that NULL to 0. This ensures users with zero confirmations get 0.00 instead of NULL.

▶ Rank 2: Subqueries in SELECT Simpler for small datasets
SELECT s.user_id, ROUND( COALESCE( (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Confirmations c1 WHERE c1.user_id = s.user_id AND c1.action = 'confirmed') * 1.0 / NULLIF( (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Confirmations c2 WHERE c2.user_id = s.user_id), 0 ), 0 ), 2 ) AS confirmation_rate FROM Signups s;

Tradeoff: Two correlated subqueries per user (count confirmed, count total). More readable logic but slower on large Signups tables. Better for <10k users.

▶ Rank 3: RIGHT JOIN with Manual UNION Handles users with 0 confirmations differently
SELECT user_id, 0.00 AS confirmation_rate FROM Signups WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM Confirmations) UNION ALL SELECT s.user_id, ROUND( COUNT(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*), 2 ) FROM Signups s INNER JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id GROUP BY s.user_id;

Tradeoff: Splits logic into two queries (users with zero confirmations get 0.00, users with confirmations calculated). UNION combines. Verbose but explicit handling of edge case.

LEFT JOIN vs. Correlated Subqueries

LEFT JOIN (Rank 1) scans Signups and Confirmations once each. Correlated subqueries (Rank 2) run the confirmation counts for each signup row. For 100k signups, JOIN wins. The UNION approach (Rank 3) requires two table scans and a NOT IN (slower). Prefer Rank 1.

#1251 Average Selling Price (Easy)

▼

E-commerce teams compute average realized price to track how time-varying price tiers impact revenue. Differs from list price due to volume discounts and promotions.

Schema: Prices(product_id, start_date, end_date, price), UnitsSold(product_id, purchase_date, units)

Join purchases to prices (using BETWEEN start_date and end_date). Calculate weighted average: SUM(price * units) / SUM(units) per product. Round to 2 decimals.

Business Context: Pricing Analytics

E-commerce teams compute average realized price to track how time-varying price tiers impact revenue. Differs from list price due to volume discounts and promotions.

▶ Rank 1: JOIN with BETWEEN Explicit range matching
SELECT u.product_id, ROUND( SUM(p.price * u.units) * 1.0 / SUM(u.units), 2 ) AS average_price FROM UnitsSold u INNER JOIN Prices p ON u.product_id = p.product_id AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date GROUP BY u.product_id;

Why this ranks first: BETWEEN is clear and efficient if start_date/end_date are indexed. INNER JOIN excludes products with no sales. Weighted average formula is standard. Clean one-pass aggregation.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery for Price Lookup Isolates price logic
SELECT u.product_id, ROUND( SUM(u.units * ( SELECT price FROM Prices p WHERE p.product_id = u.product_id AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date LIMIT 1 )) * 1.0 / SUM(u.units), 2 ) AS average_price FROM UnitsSold u GROUP BY u.product_id;

Tradeoff: Correlated subquery in SELECT per row. Assumes one price per product-date (guaranteed by problem statement). Less efficient for large UnitsSold but more compact.

▶ Rank 3: LEFT JOIN (All Products) For products with zero sales
SELECT COALESCE(u.product_id, p.product_id) AS product_id, ROUND( COALESCE(SUM(p.price * u.units), 0) * 1.0 / NULLIF(SUM(u.units), 0), 2 ) AS average_price FROM Prices p LEFT JOIN UnitsSold u ON p.product_id = u.product_id AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date GROUP BY COALESCE(u.product_id, p.product_id);

Tradeoff: LEFT JOIN includes products with no sales (returns 0 or NULL). Problem says "assume 0" for no sales, but INNER JOIN (Rank 1) is simpler. Use if you need all products listed.

JOIN with BETWEEN vs. Correlated Subquery

BETWEEN JOIN (Rank 1) is O(n log m) with indexes on (product_id, start_date, end_date). Correlated subquery (Rank 2) is O(n * m) if subquery can't use index. For millions of unit sales, JOIN wins. BETWEEN is also more database-optimizer-friendly.

#585 Investments in 2016 (Medium)

▼

Insurers filter policies by risk pool (tiv_2015) and geographic diversity (unique locations) to compute total insurable value for correlated risk exposure.

Schema: Insurance(pid, tiv_2015, tiv_2016, lat, lon)

Sum tiv_2016 for all policies where: (1) tiv_2015 is shared with at least one other policy (HAVING COUNT > 1), AND (2) location (lat, lon) is unique (HAVING COUNT = 1). Round to 2 decimals.

Business Context: Insurance Portfolio Risk Analysis

Insurers filter policies by risk pool (tiv_2015) and geographic diversity (unique locations) to compute total insurable value for correlated risk exposure.

▶ Rank 1: Two Subqueries in WHERE Uncorrelated, clear intent
SELECT ROUND(SUM(tiv_2016), 2) AS tiv_2016 FROM Insurance WHERE tiv_2015 IN ( SELECT tiv_2015 FROM Insurance GROUP BY tiv_2015 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ) AND (lat, lon) IN ( SELECT lat, lon FROM Insurance GROUP BY lat, lon HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 );

Why this ranks first: Two uncorrelated subqueries clearly separate the two conditions. First finds shared tiv_2015 values. Second finds unique locations. WHERE filters to policies matching both. Single pass through Insurance.

▶ Rank 2: Window Functions with CTE PostgreSQL 12+ alternative
WITH counted AS ( SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY tiv_2015) AS tiv_count, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY lat, lon) AS loc_count FROM Insurance ) SELECT ROUND(SUM(tiv_2016), 2) AS tiv_2016 FROM counted WHERE tiv_count > 1 AND loc_count = 1;

Tradeoff: Window functions compute counts in a single pass. More efficient for large tables. Single CTE provides both aggregations without separate table scans. Modern databases optimize window functions well.

▶ Rank 3: Self-Joins with HAVING Traditional approach (no window functions)
SELECT ROUND(SUM(i.tiv_2016), 2) AS tiv_2016 FROM Insurance i WHERE ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Insurance i2 WHERE i2.tiv_2015 = i.tiv_2015 ) > 1 AND ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Insurance i3 WHERE i3.lat = i.lat AND i3.lon = i.lon ) = 1;

Tradeoff: Two correlated subqueries per row. O(n²) performance. Easier to read logic but slower on large tables. Avoid for 10k+ policies.

Uncorrelated Subqueries vs. Window Functions vs. Correlated

Rank 1 runs two GROUP BY subqueries once each (uncorrelated). Rank 2 scans Insurance once with window aggregations (best for large tables). Rank 3 runs two subqueries per row (slowest). For insurance portfolios with 100k+ policies, Rank 2 window function is typically 10-50x faster.

#550 Game Play Analysis IV (Medium)

▼

Day-1 retention is critical for game/app success. If 30% of new users return the next day, the game has traction. Track this weekly to measure changes in user engagement.

📌
Pattern: Find First Date, Then Check Day+1

Use ROW_NUMBER() or MIN() to find first login date per player, then check if player logged in the next day. Business: Gaming/SaaS measuring Day-1 retention rate.

Business Context
Day-1 retention is critical for game/app success. If 30% of new users return the next day, the game has traction. Track this weekly to measure changes in user engagement.
▶ Rank 1: Window Function (ROW_NUMBER) + Self-Join Most efficient grouping approach
SELECT ROUND( COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN second_login THEN player_id END)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT player_id), 2 ) AS fraction FROM ( SELECT player_id, event_date, LEAD(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_date) AS next_event_date, LEAD(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_date) = event_date + INTERVAL '1 day' AS second_login FROM Activity ) t;

Performance Analysis: Window function scans Activity once, O(n). PARTITION BY player_id requires sort: O(n log n). LEAD() looks ahead one row: O(1) per row. Memory: O(n) for sort. Final aggregation: O(unique_players). Can use index on (player_id, event_date) to optimize partition.

Why Rank 1: Single scan with efficient window computation. Avoids self-join overhead.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery with MIN + Self-Join More joins, explicit logic
WITH first_login AS ( SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id ) SELECT ROUND( COUNT(DISTINCT a.player_id)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT f.player_id), 2 ) AS fraction FROM first_login f LEFT JOIN Activity a ON f.player_id = a.player_id AND a.event_date = f.first_date + INTERVAL '1 day';

Performance Analysis: GROUP BY for MIN: O(n). JOIN: hash join on player_id. For each player, checks if day+1 exists: O(n) worst case. With index on (player_id, event_date), seeks become O(log n). Total: O(n + unique_players * log n) vs window O(n log n).

Why Rank 2: Slightly cleaner logic for some, but requires JOIN which adds overhead vs window function approach.

Medium #1045 Customers Who Bought All Products

▼

Find customer IDs who purchased all products in the catalog. This is a relational division problem: customer_id where COUNT(DISTINCT product_key) = total products.

Tables: Customer (customer_id, product_key) and Product (product_key)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Relational Division

Real-World Example

Loyalty program identifies VIP customers who purchased every product in the catalog (or category). These customers qualify for exclusive rewards or early access to new products.

▶ 1 GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_key)
SELECT customer_id FROM Customer GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_key) = ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Product );

Why this is best: Relational division classic pattern. GROUP BY customer, count distinct products per customer, filter to those matching the total product count. One subquery for cardinality.

Performance: O(n log n) for GROUP BY + COUNT DISTINCT. Subquery executes once (result cached). Indexes on (customer_id, product_key) critical.

▶ 2 GROUP BY with Join to Product Count
SELECT c.customer_id FROM Customer c CROSS JOIN ( SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_products FROM Product ) p GROUP BY c.customer_id, p.total_products HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.product_key) = p.total_products;

Why this works: Cross join brings product count into every row. GROUP BY includes both customer_id and total_products (to allow reference in HAVING). Equivalent to approach #1 but more explicit.

Performance: Cross join adds minimal cost (single row). GROUP BY with two columns. Marginally slower than approach #1 but more readable for some teams.

▶ 3 NOT EXISTS (Anti-Pattern, Less Efficient)
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id FROM Customer c WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Product p WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Customer c2 WHERE c2.customer_id = c.customer_id AND c2.product_key = p.product_key ) );

Why this works: Nested NOT EXISTS: for each customer, check that no product exists without that customer having bought it. Classic division logic, but complex SQL.

Performance: Nested subqueries execute per row (O(n³) worst case). Much slower than approach #1. Use only for demonstration or very small datasets.

Caveat: Hard to read, debug, and optimize. Not recommended for production.

Hard #262 Trips and Users

▼

Daily cancellation rate on trips involving non-banned users, for Oct 1-3, 2013.

Tables: Trips (id, client_id, driver_id, city_id, status, request_at), Users (users_id, banned, role)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A ride-sharing ops team reports daily cancellation rate, excluding banned rider/driver activity to avoid polluting the KPI.

▶ 1 Filter Unbanned + Conditional AVG
SELECT t.request_at AS Day, ROUND(AVG(t.status <> 'completed'), 2) AS 'Cancellation Rate' FROM Trips t JOIN Users c ON c.users_id = t.client_id AND c.banned = 'No' JOIN Users d ON d.users_id = t.driver_id AND d.banned = 'No' WHERE t.request_at BETWEEN '2013-10-01' AND '2013-10-03' GROUP BY t.request_at;

Why this is best: Join-as-filter removes banned participants; boolean mean gives the cancellation share.

Performance: Two joins + one aggregate.

Medium #580 Count Student Number in Departments

▼

For each department, count enrolled students. Depts with no students show 0.

Tables: Student (student_id, name, gender, dept_id), Department (dept_id, dept_name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A registrar tracks enrollment per department each term, including zero-enrollment departments flagged for course-demand review.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN + COUNT on Key
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(s.student_id) AS student_number FROM Department d LEFT JOIN Student s ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY student_number DESC, d.dept_name;

Why this is best: COUNT on the right table's key returns zero for unmatched rows, unlike COUNT(*).

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Medium #614 Second Degree Follower

▼

Return followers who themselves have at least one follower, with their follower count.

Tables: Follow (followee, follower)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A social-graph team builds a "power users" list — users whose followers are followed by others too.

▶ 1 Semi-Join + Aggregate
SELECT f.follower AS follower, COUNT(DISTINCT f2.follower) AS num FROM Follow f JOIN Follow f2 ON f2.followee = f.follower GROUP BY f.follower ORDER BY f.follower;

Why this is best: Self-join from follower column to followee column finds second-degree relationships; distinct count is the fan count.

Performance: Self-join + aggregate.

Hard #615 Average Salary: Departments VS Company

▼

For each (month, department), report whether its average salary is higher, lower, or equal to the company average.

Tables: Salary (id, employee_id, amount, pay_date), Employee (employee_id, department_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

Comp benchmarks per dept are a monthly executive review input. This query delivers the directional label for dashboard annotations.

▶ 1 Dual Aggregates Joined for Comparison
WITH comp AS ( SELECT DATE_FORMAT(pay_date, '%Y-%m') AS ym, AVG(amount) AS company_avg FROM Salary GROUP BY ym ), dept AS ( SELECT DATE_FORMAT(s.pay_date, '%Y-%m') AS ym, e.department_id, AVG(s.amount) AS dept_avg FROM Salary s JOIN Employee e ON e.employee_id = s.employee_id GROUP BY ym, e.department_id ) SELECT d.ym AS pay_month, d.department_id, CASE WHEN d.dept_avg > c.company_avg THEN 'higher' WHEN d.dept_avg < c.company_avg THEN 'lower' ELSE 'same' END AS comparison FROM dept d JOIN comp c ON c.ym = d.ym;

Why this is best: Two independent aggregates joined on month give a clean comparison row per (month, department).

Performance: Two aggregates + one join.

Hard #1097 Game Play Analysis V

▼

For each install date, count day-1 retention: users who played on install date and also the next day.

Tables: Activity (player_id, device_id, event_date, games_played)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A growth analyst measures day-1 retention per install cohort — a foundational engagement KPI for LTV modeling.

▶ 1 Install Date CTE + Next-Day Self Join
WITH firsts AS ( SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS install_date FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id ) SELECT f.install_date, COUNT(*) AS installs, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN a.player_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS Day1_retention FROM firsts f LEFT JOIN Activity a ON a.player_id = f.player_id AND a.event_date = f.install_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY GROUP BY f.install_date ORDER BY f.install_date;

Why this is best: Install-date cohort + LEFT JOIN to the next day captures who returned; ratio gives D1 retention.

Performance: Two aggregates + one join.

Medium #1132 Reported Posts II

▼

Average daily removal rate for spam reports over distinct report days.

Tables: Actions (user_id, post_id, action_date, action, extra), Removals (post_id, remove_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A content mod team evaluates how effective their spam-handling pipeline is by reporting daily removal rate averaged across operating days.

▶ 1 Per-Day Rate Then AVG
WITH daily AS ( SELECT a.action_date, COUNT(DISTINCT a.post_id) AS reported, COUNT(DISTINCT r.post_id) AS removed FROM Actions a LEFT JOIN Removals r ON r.post_id = a.post_id WHERE a.extra = 'spam' AND a.action = 'report' GROUP BY a.action_date ) SELECT ROUND(AVG(removed / reported) * 100, 2) AS average_daily_percent FROM daily WHERE reported > 0;

Why this is best: Daily rate first, then average-of-averages gives the correct KPI definition.

Performance: Two aggregates.

Medium #1158 Market Analysis I

▼

For each user, join count of orders placed in 2019 (0 for no orders).

Tables: Users (user_id, join_date, favorite_brand), Orders (order_id, order_date, item_id, buyer_id, seller_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A marketplace reports 2019 orders per user alongside account metadata to inform retention cohort targeting.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN with Year Filter Inside Join
SELECT u.user_id AS buyer_id, u.join_date, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_in_2019 FROM Users u LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.buyer_id = u.user_id AND YEAR(o.order_date) = 2019 GROUP BY u.user_id, u.join_date;

Why this is best: Year filter must live in the join condition so unmatched users still appear with a 0 count.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Hard #1159 Market Analysis II

▼

Flag sellers whose 2nd-ever sale was the user's favorite-brand item.

Tables: Users (user_id, join_date, favorite_brand), Orders (order_id, order_date, item_id, buyer_id, seller_id), Items (item_id, item_brand)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

An onboarding analyst checks whether a seller's second sale involves buyers' favorite brand, which often predicts lifetime engagement.

▶ 1 Rank Seller Orders + Join Brand
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT o.seller_id, o.item_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.seller_id ORDER BY o.order_date) AS rn FROM Orders o ) SELECT u.user_id AS seller_id, IF(u.favorite_brand = i.item_brand, 'yes', 'no') AS 2nd_item_fav_brand FROM Users u LEFT JOIN ranked r ON r.seller_id = u.user_id AND r.rn = 2 LEFT JOIN Items i ON i.item_id = r.item_id;

Why this is best: ROW_NUMBER isolates the second order per seller; brand is looked up and compared.

Performance: One window + two joins.

▶ 2 Conditional Aggregation on Ranked Base
WITH base AS ( SELECT u.user_id AS seller_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u.user_id ORDER BY o.order_date ASC) AS order_rn, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.item_id, u.favorite_brand, i.item_brand, CASE WHEN u.favorite_brand = i.item_brand THEN 'yes' ELSE 'no' END AS item_fav_brand FROM Users AS u LEFT JOIN Orders AS o ON u.user_id = o.seller_id LEFT JOIN Items AS i ON i.item_id = o.item_id ) SELECT seller_id, COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN order_rn = 2 THEN item_fav_brand END), 'no') AS "2nd_item_fav_brand" FROM base GROUP BY seller_id ORDER BY seller_id;

Why this works: The base CTE attaches the rn flag and the brand match to every order row. The outer GROUP BY collapses each seller; MAX(CASE WHEN order_rn = 2 THEN item_fav_brand END) picks up the rn=2 row's flag (NULL otherwise) and COALESCE defaults to 'no' for sellers with fewer than two orders.

Pattern to keep: "per group, return the value of column X on the row where condition Y" → MAX(CASE WHEN Y THEN X END) over a partitioned base, with COALESCE for the missing-row default. No second pass, no UNION.

Note on column quoting: identifiers that start with a digit (here 2nd_item_fav_brand) must be wrapped in double quotes or the parser reads them as a numeric literal.

Performance: One window + one GROUP BY. Comparable to Rank 1 in cost; trades two LEFT JOINs for one aggregate scan.

Medium #1212 Team Scores in Football Tournament

▼

Return each team with total points, sorted descending by points then team_id.

Tables: Teams (team_id, team_name), Matches (match_id, host_team, guest_team, host_goals, guest_goals)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A sports portal renders a live league standings table from match results.

▶ 1 Home/Away Normalization + Score
WITH scored AS ( SELECT host_team AS team_id, CASE WHEN host_goals > guest_goals THEN 3 WHEN host_goals = guest_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS pts FROM Matches UNION ALL SELECT guest_team, CASE WHEN guest_goals > host_goals THEN 3 WHEN guest_goals = host_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END FROM Matches ) SELECT t.team_id, t.team_name, COALESCE(SUM(s.pts), 0) AS num_points FROM Teams t LEFT JOIN scored s ON s.team_id = t.team_id GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name ORDER BY num_points DESC, t.team_id;

Why this is best: Normalize host/away rows into a common schema for a single aggregate.

Performance: Two passes of Matches.

Easy #1241 Number of Comments per Post

▼

For each distinct post, count distinct direct comments.

Tables: Submissions (sub_id, parent_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A forum surfaces post-engagement counts in each thread preview; parents are rows with no parent_id.

▶ 1 Self-Join Parent to Child
SELECT DISTINCT p.sub_id AS post_id, COUNT(DISTINCT c.sub_id) AS number_of_comments FROM Submissions p LEFT JOIN Submissions c ON c.parent_id = p.sub_id WHERE p.parent_id IS NULL GROUP BY p.sub_id ORDER BY p.sub_id;

Why this is best: Self-join posts to their children; DISTINCT protects against repeated comment rows.

Performance: Self-join + aggregate.

Easy #1294 Weather Type in Each Country

▼

Classify each country's Nov 2019 climate as Cold, Hot, or Warm based on average temperature.

Tables: Countries (country_id, country_name), Weather (country_id, weather_state, day)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A travel portal tags countries with a climate label to power destination filters.

▶ 1 Filtered AVG + CASE
SELECT c.country_name, CASE WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) <= 15 THEN 'Cold' WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) >= 25 THEN 'Hot' ELSE 'Warm' END AS weather_type FROM Countries c JOIN Weather w ON w.country_id = c.country_id WHERE w.day BETWEEN '2019-11-01' AND '2019-11-30' GROUP BY c.country_id, c.country_name;

Why this is best: Filter to November, aggregate per country, label via CASE.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Hard #1336 Number of Transactions per Visit

▼

Distribution of transactions per visit across all users, with zero-counts included.

Tables: Visits (user_id, visit_date), Transactions (user_id, transaction_date, amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A retail analytics team reports "how many customers made 0, 1, 2, ... purchases per visit" — a histogram used in conversion funnels.

▶ 1 Per-Visit Counts + Recursive Histogram
WITH visit_counts AS ( SELECT v.user_id, v.visit_date, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Transactions t WHERE t.user_id = v.user_id AND t.transaction_date = v.visit_date) AS c FROM Visits v ), dist AS (SELECT c AS transactions_count, COUNT(*) AS visits_count FROM visit_counts GROUP BY c), range_cte AS ( SELECT 0 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM range_cte WHERE n < (SELECT COALESCE(MAX(transactions_count),0) FROM dist) ) SELECT r.n AS transactions_count, COALESCE(d.visits_count, 0) AS visits_count FROM range_cte r LEFT JOIN dist d ON d.transactions_count = r.n;

Why this is best: Recursive CTE fills the histogram buckets so zero-frequency bins appear.

Performance: One aggregate + recursive range.

Medium #1364 Number of Trusted Contacts of a Customer

▼

For each invoice, report customer name, contacts count, and trusted-contacts count.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, customer_name, email), Contacts (user_id, contact_name, contact_email), Invoices (invoice_id, price, user_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A fintech app surfaces social-graph risk signals on each invoice by showing how many of the customer's contacts are known customers themselves.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN Contacts + Conditional Count
SELECT i.invoice_id, c.customer_name, i.price, COUNT(ct.contact_email) AS contacts_cnt, SUM(CASE WHEN ct.contact_email IN (SELECT email FROM Customers) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS trusted_contacts_cnt FROM Invoices i JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = i.user_id LEFT JOIN Contacts ct ON ct.user_id = i.user_id GROUP BY i.invoice_id, c.customer_name, i.price ORDER BY i.invoice_id;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN retains contact-free customers at count 0; conditional SUM applies the "trusted" rule inline.

Performance: One join + one aggregate + one IN.

Easy #1407 Top Travellers

For each user, report total distance travelled (0 for non-travellers).

Decision Tree Path

Real-World Example

A travel app scores user travel activity; inactive users appear with 0 for re-engagement campaigns.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN + SUM with COALESCE
SELECT u.name, COALESCE(SUM(r.distance), 0) AS travelled_distance FROM Users u LEFT JOIN Rides r ON r.user_id = u.id GROUP BY u.id, u.name ORDER BY travelled_distance DESC, u.name;

Medium #1501 Countries You Can Safely Invest In

▼

Return countries whose average call duration exceeds the global average.

Tables: Person (id, name, phone_number), Country (name, country_code), Calls (caller_id, callee_id, duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A telco rates countries for investment by comparing average call duration (a proxy for engagement) to the global mean.

▶ 1 Country AVG vs Global AVG
WITH lined AS ( SELECT p.id, SUBSTRING(p.phone_number,1,3) AS code FROM Person p ), durations AS ( SELECT lined.code, c.duration FROM Calls c JOIN lined ON lined.id = c.caller_id UNION ALL SELECT lined.code, c.duration FROM Calls c JOIN lined ON lined.id = c.callee_id ) SELECT co.name AS country FROM durations d JOIN Country co ON co.country_code = d.code GROUP BY co.name HAVING AVG(d.duration) > (SELECT AVG(duration) FROM Calls);

Why this is best: Normalize caller/callee, join country, then average-per-country against the global benchmark in HAVING.

Medium #1555 Bank Account Summary

▼

Compute running balance per user and flag negatives.

Tables: Users (user_id, user_name, credit), Transactions (trans_id, paid_by, paid_to, amount, transacted_on)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A P2P payment app shows each wallet the final balance; negative balances gate spending.

▶ 1 Signed Per-User Sums Joined to Users
WITH flows AS ( SELECT paid_by AS user_id, -amount AS amt FROM Transactions UNION ALL SELECT paid_to, amount FROM Transactions ) SELECT u.user_id, u.user_name, u.credit + COALESCE(SUM(f.amt), 0) AS credit, IF(u.credit + COALESCE(SUM(f.amt), 0) < 0, 'Yes', 'No') AS credit_limit_breached FROM Users u LEFT JOIN flows f ON f.user_id = u.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, u.user_name, u.credit;

Why this is best: Normalize debits and credits into one column, sum per user, add initial credit.

Easy #1571 Warehouse Manager

For each warehouse, compute total cubic feet used by stocked products.

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A supply-chain planner measures capacity utilization per warehouse to justify expansion.

▶ 1 Join + SUM of Volume * Units
SELECT w.name AS warehouse_name, SUM(w.units * p.Width * p.Length * p.Height) AS volume FROM Warehouse w JOIN Products p ON p.product_id = w.product_id GROUP BY w.name;

Hard #1635 Hopper Company Queries I

▼

For each month in 2020, count active drivers and completed accepted rides.

Tables: Drivers (driver_id, join_date), Rides (ride_id, user_id, requested_at), AcceptedRides (ride_id, driver_id, ride_distance, ride_duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A rideshare ops report publishes monthly supply-side KPIs to the executive team.

▶ 1 Calendar CTE + Aggregate Joins
WITH months AS ( SELECT 1 AS m UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10 UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 ) SELECT m.m AS month, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Drivers d WHERE d.join_date <= DATE_ADD('2020-01-01', INTERVAL m.m MONTH) - INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS active_drivers, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AcceptedRides ar JOIN Rides r ON r.ride_id = ar.ride_id WHERE YEAR(r.requested_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(r.requested_at) = m.m) AS accepted_rides FROM months m;

Why this is best: Anchor to a month calendar so every month appears, even zero-activity ones.

Performance: 12 iterations * aggregate per month. Small and fast.

Hard #1645 Hopper Company Queries II

▼

For each 2020 month, report percent of drivers working at least once (2 decimals).

Tables: Drivers (driver_id, join_date), Rides (ride_id, user_id, requested_at), AcceptedRides (ride_id, driver_id, ...)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A driver retention PM measures working-active-driver share per month to size the driver engagement strategy.

▶ 1 Active Drivers + Working Drivers Ratio
WITH months AS ( SELECT 1 AS m UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10 UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 ) SELECT m.m AS month, IFNULL(ROUND( 100.0 * ( SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ar.driver_id) FROM AcceptedRides ar JOIN Rides r ON r.ride_id = ar.ride_id WHERE YEAR(r.requested_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(r.requested_at) = m.m ) / NULLIF(( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Drivers WHERE join_date <= DATE_ADD('2020-01-01', INTERVAL m.m MONTH) - INTERVAL 1 DAY ), 0), 2), 0.00) AS working_percentage FROM months m;

Why this is best: Divide distinct working drivers in month by cumulative joined drivers by that month.

Performance: 12 * two aggregates.

Hard #1651 Hopper Company Queries III

▼

For each month m=1..12 in 2020, report the average ride_distance and ride_duration over the next 3 months.

Tables: Rides (ride_id, user_id, requested_at), AcceptedRides (ride_id, driver_id, ride_distance, ride_duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

Leadership reviews a rolling 3-month operational forecast to stabilize capacity planning.

▶ 1 Calendar + Range Filter per Bucket
WITH months AS ( SELECT 1 AS m UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10 ) SELECT m.m AS month, ROUND(AVG(ar.ride_distance), 2) AS average_ride_distance, ROUND(AVG(ar.ride_duration), 2) AS average_ride_duration FROM months m LEFT JOIN Rides r ON YEAR(r.requested_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(r.requested_at) BETWEEN m.m AND m.m + 2 LEFT JOIN AcceptedRides ar ON ar.ride_id = r.ride_id GROUP BY m.m;

Why this is best: The 3-month bucket is implemented as a range filter on the join condition.

Performance: Calendar is tiny; joins filtered.

Hard #1892 Page Recommendations II

▼

For each user, recommend pages liked by a threshold count of their friends.

Tables: Friendship (user1_id, user2_id), Likes (user_id, page_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A social product improves on basic page recommendations by weighting recommendations by number of friends liking the page.

▶ 1 Friends Expansion + Aggregate per Page
WITH friends AS ( SELECT user1_id AS u, user2_id AS f FROM Friendship UNION ALL SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship ) SELECT f.u AS user_id, l.page_id, COUNT(DISTINCT f.f) AS friends_likes FROM friends f JOIN Likes l ON l.user_id = f.f WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Likes lk WHERE lk.user_id = f.u AND lk.page_id = l.page_id ) GROUP BY f.u, l.page_id ORDER BY f.u, friends_likes DESC, l.page_id;

Why this is best: Bidirectional friendship expansion + anti-join to user's own likes + friend count per page.

Performance: One aggregate + two joins.

Hard #1917 Leetcodify Friends Recommendations

▼

Recommend users who listened to >=3 songs on the same day, and aren't already friends.

Tables: Listens (user_id, song_id, day), Friendship (user1_id, user2_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A music app recommends friends who share >=3 tracks per day — a soft interest-similarity signal.

▶ 1 Same-Day Co-Listen + Threshold
WITH co AS ( SELECT a.user_id AS u1, b.user_id AS u2, a.day, a.song_id FROM Listens a JOIN Listens b ON a.song_id = b.song_id AND a.day = b.day AND a.user_id < b.user_id ), pairs AS ( SELECT u1, u2, COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) AS shared FROM co GROUP BY u1, u2, day HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) >= 3 ) SELECT u1 AS user1_id, u2 AS user2_id FROM pairs WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Friendship f WHERE (f.user1_id = pairs.u1 AND f.user2_id = pairs.u2) OR (f.user1_id = pairs.u2 AND f.user2_id = pairs.u1) );

Why this is best: Self-join on shared song same day; threshold on DISTINCT song count; anti-join to existing friendships.

Performance: Self-join is O(n^2) worst case; filter by day first.

Hard #1919 Leetcodify Similar Friends

▼

Same same-day-3-song pattern as 1917 but restricted to already-friends.

Tables: Listens (user_id, song_id, day), Friendship (user1_id, user2_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A music app flags "similar" friends for collaborative playlists.

▶ 1 Restrict Co-Listens to Existing Friendships
SELECT DISTINCT f.user1_id, f.user2_id FROM Friendship f JOIN Listens a ON a.user_id = f.user1_id JOIN Listens b ON b.user_id = f.user2_id AND a.song_id = b.song_id AND a.day = b.day GROUP BY f.user1_id, f.user2_id, a.day HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.song_id) >= 3;

Why this is best: Join both sides of existing friendship to Listens and impose the 3-song threshold.

Performance: Limited by friendship size.

Easy #1939 Users That Actively Request Confirmation Messages

▼

Users who requested two confirmations within 24 hours.

Tables: Signups (user_id, time_stamp), Confirmations (user_id, time_stamp, action)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A security team flags users repeatedly requesting confirmations within 24 hours as possibly automated.

▶ 1 Self-Join with Interval Condition
SELECT DISTINCT c1.user_id FROM Confirmations c1 JOIN Confirmations c2 ON c2.user_id = c1.user_id AND c2.time_stamp > c1.time_stamp AND c2.time_stamp <= c1.time_stamp + INTERVAL 24 HOUR;

Why this is best: Self-join on "within 24 hours after" returns any pair meeting the window.

Performance: Indexed self-join with interval.

Medium #1949 Strong Friendship

▼

Pairs of friends with at least three common friends.

Tables: Friendship (user1_id, user2_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A community ops team highlights tightly-clustered friend pairs — often a strong community anchor.

▶ 1 Normalize + Common Friend Count
WITH f AS ( SELECT user1_id AS u, user2_id AS v FROM Friendship UNION ALL SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship ) SELECT a.u AS user1_id, a.v AS user2_id, COUNT(*) AS common_friend FROM f a JOIN f b ON b.u = a.v AND b.v <> a.u JOIN f c ON c.u = b.v AND c.v = a.u WHERE a.u < a.v GROUP BY a.u, a.v HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

Why this is best: Normalize friendship to bidirectional; chain three edges to count common friends per pair.

Performance: Graph walk; fine for thousands of nodes.

Medium #2142 The Number of Passengers in Each Bus I

▼

Count passengers who catch each bus (first bus arriving at/after their request).

Tables: Buses (bus_id, arrival_time), Passengers (passenger_id, arrival_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A transit analyst measures bus load per departure to plan capacity.

▶ 1 LEAD to Bus Window + COUNT
WITH bus_windows AS ( SELECT bus_id, arrival_time AS end_t, COALESCE(LAG(arrival_time) OVER (ORDER BY arrival_time), -1) AS start_t FROM Buses ) SELECT b.bus_id, COUNT(p.passenger_id) AS passengers_cnt FROM bus_windows b LEFT JOIN Passengers p ON p.arrival_time > b.start_t AND p.arrival_time <= b.end_t GROUP BY b.bus_id ORDER BY b.bus_id;

Why this is best: Each bus owns the passenger arrivals since the previous bus. LEAD/LAG defines the capture window.

Performance: Window + range join.

Hard #2153 The Number of Passengers in Each Bus II

▼

Same as I, with bus capacity; passengers that exceed capacity roll over to the next bus.

Tables: Buses (bus_id, arrival_time, capacity), Passengers (passenger_id, arrival_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

Adds capacity overflow semantics: if a bus is full, extras wait for the next one.

▶ 1 Ordered Iterative Accumulate (Variables)
SELECT b.bus_id, passengers_cnt FROM ( SELECT b.bus_id, b.arrival_time, b.capacity, @leftover := GREATEST(@leftover + ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Passengers p WHERE p.arrival_time <= b.arrival_time AND p.arrival_time > COALESCE( LAG(b.arrival_time) OVER (ORDER BY b.arrival_time), -1) ), 0), LEAST(@leftover, b.capacity) AS passengers_cnt, @leftover := @leftover - LEAST(@leftover, b.capacity) FROM Buses b, (SELECT @leftover := 0) v ORDER BY b.arrival_time ) x ORDER BY x.bus_id;

Why this is best: Iterative state is needed because leftover rolls forward. MySQL variables simulate it; a recursive CTE is the portable alternative.

Performance: Linear in buses.

SELECT d.driver_id, COUNT(r.ride_id) AS cnt FROM (SELECT DISTINCT driver_id FROM Rides) d LEFT JOIN Rides r ON r.passenger_id = d.driver_id GROUP BY d.driver_id;

Why this is best: Use distinct driver set on the left to include drivers who never rode as a passenger.

Hard #2720 Popularity Percentage

▼

For each user, compute share of users who are friends with them (undirected).

Tables: Friends (user1, user2)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

▶ 1 Bidirectional Expansion + Normalized Share
WITH f AS ( SELECT user1 AS u, user2 AS v FROM Friends UNION SELECT user2, user1 FROM Friends ), all_users AS ( SELECT DISTINCT u AS uid FROM f UNION SELECT DISTINCT v FROM f ) SELECT u.uid AS user1, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT f.v) / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM all_users) - 1, 0), 2) AS percentage_popularity FROM all_users u LEFT JOIN f ON f.u = u.uid GROUP BY u.uid ORDER BY u.uid;

Medium #2783 Flight Occupancy and Waitlist Analysis

▼

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

▶ 1 Per-Flight COUNT + LEAST / Minus

Why this is best: LEAST and GREATEST express the capacity clip in one aggregate pass.

Hard #2793 Status of Flight Tickets

▼

Label each passenger as Confirmed or Waitlist based on FIFO within flight capacity.

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

▶ 1 ROW_NUMBER vs Capacity
SELECT p.passenger_id, CASE WHEN rn <= f.capacity THEN 'Confirmed' ELSE 'Waitlist' END AS Status FROM ( SELECT passenger_id, flight_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY flight_id ORDER BY booking_time) AS rn FROM Passengers ) p JOIN Flights f ON f.flight_id = p.flight_id ORDER BY p.passenger_id;

Why this is best: Row number per flight combined with capacity cleanly splits Confirmed vs Waitlist.

→

▶ 1 First Session Type + Later Stream Count
WITH firsts AS ( SELECT user_id, session_type AS first_type, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY session_start) AS rn FROM Sessions ) SELECT s.user_id, COUNT(*) AS sessions_count FROM firsts f JOIN Sessions s ON s.user_id = f.user_id AND s.session_type = 'Streamer' WHERE f.rn = 1 AND f.first_type = 'Viewer' GROUP BY s.user_id ORDER BY sessions_count DESC, s.user_id DESC;

Rank Within Groups to Select Top-N 32 problems

▼

A table (possibly joined to a dimension) → the top-N rows per group via window ranking.

Signal words: "top N per," "highest in each," "first per group," "department top"

Technique: DENSE_RANK/RANK/ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY + ORDER BY

Mnemonic for deciding PARTITION BY

Ask yourself: "Do I want a winner per something, or one winner overall?" — per (top salary per department, most recent order per customer) means PARTITION BY; overall (the question with the highest answer rate across ALL questions) means no PARTITION BY. Scalar-extract problems are "overall" by definition, so they never need PARTITION BY.

Tiebreaking with multi-column ORDER BY

When two rows tie on the main sort column (e.g., two employees with the same salary), ROW_NUMBER still has to assign different numbers to them — and without a tiebreaker, the engine picks an arbitrary order. That arbitrary order can break the asc/desc median trick or pick the wrong row for "top 1."

Fix: add a second column to the ORDER BY (typically a unique id). Read it left to right — the first column does the main sort; the second column only kicks in when the first ties.

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY salary ASC, id ASC) AS asc_rn, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY salary DESC, id DESC) AS desc_rn

Important: apply ASC / DESC to each column — ORDER BY salary, id DESC only flips id. For the asc/desc median trick to give true mirror rankings, both columns must flip together: ORDER BY salary DESC, id DESC.

Reference Techniques used in Rank Within Groups

▼

3 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
ROW_NUMBER() Assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition You need to identify duplicates for deletion, pick one row per group, or rank with no ties 
SELECT *,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
         PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
       ) AS rn
FROM Emp;
DENSE_RANK() / RANK() Assigns a rank within a partition; DENSE_RANK has no gaps after ties, RANK has gaps You need the top N within each group; RANK skips ranks after ties, DENSE_RANK does not 
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT e.*, d.name AS dept,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (
           PARTITION BY d.id ORDER BY e.salary DESC
         ) AS rk
  FROM Emp e JOIN Dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
) t
WHERE rk = 1;
PARTITION BY Divides rows into groups for a window function to operate on independently You need to rank or compute a window separately within each group (per department, per customer) 
SELECT name, dept,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg
FROM Emp;

#1070 Product Sales Analysis III (Medium)

▼

Product managers analyze launch-year metrics: which products had strong initial adoption? A product with 50 units sold in year 1 may underperform vs one with 200 units. Early momentum predicts long-term success.

📌
Pattern: Rank First Year per Product

Use RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY year) to identify first year, or use MIN(year). Business: Product analytics finding launch-year performance.

Business Context
Product managers analyze launch-year metrics: which products had strong initial adoption? A product with 50 units sold in year 1 may underperform vs one with 200 units. Early momentum predicts long-term success.
▶ Rank 1: Window Function (RANK) Handles ties naturally
SELECT product_id, year AS first_year, quantity, price FROM ( SELECT product_id, year, quantity, price, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY year) AS year_rank FROM Sales ) t WHERE year_rank = 1;

Performance Analysis: Window function: O(n log n) due to PARTITION sort. RANK() is O(n) once sorted. Memory: O(n) for sort and partition buffer. Filter year_rank = 1 is O(n). No index required but (product_id, year) index helps partition/sort. Result size: <= unique products.

Why Rank 1: RANK() keeps all rows where year matches first year (handles ties). Clean semantics.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery with MIN(year) Simpler aggregation
SELECT s.product_id, s.year AS first_year, s.quantity, s.price FROM Sales s WHERE s.year = ( SELECT MIN(year) FROM Sales s2 WHERE s2.product_id = s.product_id );

Performance Analysis: Correlated subquery runs MIN(year) for EACH row in Sales. Outer scan: O(n). Inner MIN per row: O(n/products) on average. Total: O(n²/products). For 1M rows, 1k products: 1M * 1000 = 1B comparisons. Requires index on product_id to speed inner query to O(log n): O(n log n) total. Window function is still faster: no subquery overhead.

Why Rank 2: More readable but performance degrades without index. Window function avoids repeated subquery execution.

#185 Department Top Three Salaries (Hard)

▼

HR uses this for compensation benchmarking. If IT's top earner is $150k and Sales' is $120k, IT must be specialized. Identifies pay equity issues within departments.

📌
Pattern: DENSE_RANK with JOIN

Use DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) <= 3 combined with a JOIN to department names. Business: HR compensation analysis finding top earners per department.

Business Context
HR uses this for compensation benchmarking. If IT's top earner is $150k and Sales' is $120k, IT must be specialized. Identifies pay equity issues within departments.
▶ Rank 1: DENSE_RANK + JOIN Handles ties correctly
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM ( SELECT id, name, salary, departmentId, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank FROM Employee ) e JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id WHERE e.salary_rank <= 3 ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC, e.name;

Performance Analysis: Window function: O(n log n) for sort per department. DENSE_RANK(): O(n) once sorted. JOIN: hash join on departmentId = O(n + d) where d = departments. Memory: O(n) for partition buffer. Final ORDER BY: O(n log n). Total: O(n log n) dominated by window function sort.

Why Rank 1: DENSE_RANK is correct: two employees with same salary both get rank 2, next different salary gets rank 3. Avoids rank gaps.

▶ Rank 2: ROW_NUMBER + Subquery Requires careful filtering
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM ( SELECT id, name, salary, departmentId, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS salary_rank FROM Employee ) e JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id WHERE e.salary_rank <= 3 ORDER BY d.name, e.salary DESC;

Performance Analysis: ROW_NUMBER ranks each row uniquely even with same salary. Results in fewer rows returned (at most 3 per dept vs potentially more with DENSE_RANK). Requires tie-breaking with id. Same O(n log n) complexity but potentially better memory cache behavior due to smaller result set. Memory: same O(n).

Why Rank 2: ROW_NUMBER with tie-breaking (id) is incorrect semantically here. Two people with same salary should both be "top 3", but ROW_NUMBER arbitrarily picks one.

SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary FROM ( SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM Employee ) e JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.departmentId WHERE e.rk = 1;

Why this is best: RANK returns all ties at rank 1 (spec-compliant when multiple share the max).

Hard #569 Median Employee Salary

▼

For each company, return the median salary row(s).

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Finance compares median salary benchmarks per company subsidiary.

Why this is best: Median rows always have |ascending_rn - descending_rn| <= 1, covering both odd and even group sizes.

Hard #1194 Tournament Winners

▼

For each group, return the player with the highest total score (ties broken by smallest id).

Tables: Players (player_id, group_id), Matches (match_id, first_player, second_player, first_score, second_score)

View on LeetCode →

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A tournament system crowns a group winner by summing points from every match they played in.

Composite (3 moves): Move 1: normalize-bidirectional (UNION ALL to unstack first/second player). Move 2: group-aggregate (SUM points per player). Move 3: rank-partition (RANK top 1 per group, tiebreaker by smallest player_id).

▶ 1 UNION ALL + Aggregate + RANK per Group
WITH base_matches AS ( SELECT first_player AS player_id, first_score AS points FROM Matches UNION ALL SELECT second_player AS player_id, second_score AS points FROM Matches ), player_points AS ( SELECT player_id, SUM(points) AS total_points FROM base_matches GROUP BY player_id ), base_group AS ( SELECT p.group_id, p.player_id, COALESCE(m.total_points, 0) AS total_points, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.group_id ORDER BY COALESCE(m.total_points, 0) DESC, p.player_id ASC) AS group_rank FROM Players AS p LEFT JOIN player_points AS m ON p.player_id = m.player_id ) SELECT group_id, player_id FROM base_group WHERE group_rank = 1;

Why this is best: Each CTE handles one move. UNION ALL normalizes the bidirectional match data (each player appears once per match). SUM aggregates total points. RANK with LEFT JOIN + COALESCE ensures players with zero matches still appear with 0 points. The tiebreaker (player_id ASC) is baked into the ORDER BY.

Performance: One UNION ALL scan + one aggregate + one window pass.

Key details:

  • LEFT JOIN (not INNER): a player with no matches still gets a row with NULL total, which COALESCE converts to 0
  • RANK vs ROW_NUMBER: either works here because the tiebreaker (player_id) is unique within each group, so no ties survive
  • COALESCE inside ORDER BY: without it, NULL sorts inconsistently across databases and a zero-match player could be ranked first or last

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

A profile page shows the previous activity behind the most recent one; falls back to the only activity for new users.

WITH ranked AS ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY username ORDER BY startDate DESC) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY username) AS cnt FROM UserActivity ) SELECT username, activity, startDate, endDate FROM ranked WHERE (cnt > 1 AND rn = 2) OR (cnt = 1 AND rn = 1);

Why this is best: Row number identifies the second-latest; count guards the single-activity case.

Performance: Two window passes.

WITH d AS ( SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, transaction_date FROM Transactions ), g AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, DATE_SUB(transaction_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) DAY) AS grp FROM d ), runs AS (SELECT customer_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS run_len FROM g GROUP BY customer_id, grp), max_run AS (SELECT customer_id, MAX(run_len) AS maxlen FROM runs GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id FROM max_run WHERE maxlen = (SELECT MAX(maxlen) FROM max_run) ORDER BY customer_id;

Reshape Recipes

Four technique families for reshaping data: UNION / UNION ALL (stack independent queries vertically), Conditional Pivot (long rows to wide columns via CASE WHEN inside aggregates), Unpivot via UNION ALL (wide columns back to long rows), and CROSS JOIN / Calendar Skeleton (generate complete combinations then fill with actuals). Each technique opens with a generic template, explanation, and guidance on when to reach for it, followed by nested example problems.

Technique UNION / UNION ALL (Stack Independent Queries)

▼

Stack rows from two or more independent SELECT statements vertically. UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps all rows.

-- UNION ALL: keep all rows (most common)
SELECT col_a, col_b FROM table_1 WHERE <condition_1>
UNION ALL
SELECT col_a, col_b FROM table_2 WHERE <condition_2>;

-- UNION: deduplicate the combined result
SELECT col_a FROM table_1
UNION
SELECT col_a FROM table_2;

How it works:

  • Each SELECT runs independently and produces its own result set
  • The engine stacks the rows vertically — column count and types must match across all SELECTs
  • UNION ALL is faster because it skips the dedup pass. Use UNION only when you need distinct rows
  • ORDER BY applies to the combined result and goes at the very end, after the last SELECT

When to reach for this:

  • The problem says "Find X. Also find Y" with two unrelated questions sharing the same output columns
  • You need to reshape a single entity's columns into rows (bidirectional aggregation)
  • The output explicitly says "combine" or "together" with the same column structure

When NOT to reach for this:

  • The two results share a join key and need to appear on the same row — that is a JOIN, not a UNION
  • Column types or counts differ between the SELECTs — fix the mismatch with CAST or NULL placeholders first

Example Problems (3)

#1341 Movie Rating (Medium)

▼

Entertainment platforms recognize "Top Reviewer of the Month" and "Movie of the Month" to drive engagement and surface quality content.

Schema: Movies(movie_id, title), Users(user_id, name), MovieRating(movie_id, user_id, rating, created_at)

UNION two queries: (1) User with most ratings (tie: lexicographically smaller name), (2) Movie with highest average rating in Feb 2020 (tie: lexicographically smaller title). Return results column.

Business Context: Platform Recognition Reports

Entertainment platforms recognize "Top Reviewer of the Month" and "Movie of the Month" to drive engagement and surface quality content.

▶ Rank 1: Two Separate Queries UNIONed Clear separation of concerns
-- Top reviewer (most ratings) SELECT u.name AS results FROM Users u INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC LIMIT 1 UNION ALL -- Top movie in Feb 2020 SELECT m.title AS results FROM Movies m INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id WHERE YEAR(mr.created_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(mr.created_at) = 2 GROUP BY m.movie_id, m.title ORDER BY AVG(mr.rating) DESC, m.title ASC LIMIT 1;

Why this ranks first: Two separate queries are easy to understand and maintain. Each has its own sorting logic. UNION ALL preserves order. No complicated joins or conditionals.

▶ Rank 2: CTEs + Single Query Combines both with CTEs
WITH top_reviewer AS ( SELECT u.name AS results, 1 AS query_order FROM Users u INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC LIMIT 1 ), top_movie AS ( SELECT m.title AS results, 2 AS query_order FROM Movies m INNER JOIN MovieRating mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM mr.created_at) = 2020 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM mr.created_at) = 2 GROUP BY m.movie_id, m.title ORDER BY AVG(mr.rating) DESC, m.title ASC LIMIT 1 ) SELECT results FROM top_reviewer UNION ALL SELECT results FROM top_movie ORDER BY query_order;

Tradeoff: CTEs add clarity (labeled queries), but increase complexity. Two separate table scans (one per CTE). EXTRACT is more portable than YEAR/MONTH in some databases.

▶ Rank 3: Subqueries in FROM (Complex) Avoid this approach
SELECT * FROM ( SELECT u.name AS results, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY cnt DESC, u.name ASC) AS rn FROM Users u INNER JOIN ( SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM MovieRating GROUP BY user_id ) mr ON u.user_id = mr.user_id ) reviewer WHERE rn = 1 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM ( SELECT m.title AS results, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY avg_rating DESC, m.title ASC) AS rn FROM Movies m INNER JOIN ( SELECT movie_id, AVG(rating) AS avg_rating FROM MovieRating WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(created_at) = 2 GROUP BY movie_id ) mr ON m.movie_id = mr.movie_id ) movie WHERE rn = 1;

Tradeoff: Nested subqueries with window functions are hard to read and debug. Multiple levels of nesting increase query execution overhead. Rank 1 or 2 are clearer.

Separate Queries vs. Combined Logic

Two separate UNION queries (Rank 1) each run their logic independently, then combine. CTEs (Rank 2) materialize both results. Nested subqueries (Rank 3) force multiple scans. For small result sets (LIMIT 1 each), Rank 1 is simplest. For larger result sets, CTEs may cache results better.

Medium #1907 Count Salary Categories

▼

Count accounts in three salary categories: Low (<$20k), Average ($20k-$50k), High (>$50k). Result must include all three categories, even with count 0.

Tables: Accounts (account_id, income)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Combined: Cross Join + Count Pattern

Real-World Example

Payroll analytics generates salary band distribution reports for management dashboards. All three categories (Low, Average, High) must appear, even if no accounts fall into a band, to show complete salary structure.

▶ 1 Cross Join with Categories + CASE + COUNT
SELECT c.category, COUNT(CASE WHEN c.category = 'Low Salary' AND income < 20000 THEN 1 WHEN c.category = 'Average Salary' AND income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000 THEN 1 WHEN c.category = 'High Salary' AND income > 50000 THEN 1 END) AS accounts_count FROM ( SELECT 'Low Salary' AS category UNION ALL SELECT 'Average Salary' UNION ALL SELECT 'High Salary' ) c CROSS JOIN Accounts GROUP BY c.category;

Why this is best: Cross join ensures all three categories exist in result. CASE inside COUNT matches each account to its category, counting only matches. Handles zero-count categories elegantly.

Gotcha: CROSS JOIN multiplies table size (3 × |Accounts|) before filtering. For large tables, suboptimal. See approach #2 for alternative.

Performance: O(n) per category after cross join. Three scans total. Acceptable for small-to-medium Accounts tables.

▶ 2 UNION ALL with Separate Counts
SELECT 'Low Salary' AS category, COUNT(*) AS accounts_count FROM Accounts WHERE income < 20000 UNION ALL SELECT 'Average Salary', COUNT(*) FROM Accounts WHERE income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000 UNION ALL SELECT 'High Salary', COUNT(*) FROM Accounts WHERE income > 50000;

Why this works: Three separate COUNT queries, one per category. UNION ALL combines results. Guaranteed all three rows in output (even 0 counts). Three full table scans.

Performance: Slower (3 scans) but avoids cross join blow-up. Better for very large Accounts tables. Modern optimizers may merge scans.

▶ 3 Subquery with GROUP BY CASE
WITH categorized AS ( SELECT CASE WHEN income < 20000 THEN 'Low Salary' WHEN income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000 THEN 'Average Salary' ELSE 'High Salary' END AS category FROM Accounts ) SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS accounts_count FROM categorized GROUP BY category;

Why this works: Single scan to categorize all accounts, then GROUP BY. Missing zero-count categories will be absent from output unless UNION ALL appended.

Performance: Single scan + aggregation. Faster than approach #1 but doesn't guarantee all categories in output.

Easy #1965 Employees With Missing Information

▼

Return employee ids present in one source but missing from the other.

Tables: Employees (employee_id, name), Salaries (employee_id, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

An HR audit reconciles two mastered systems and surfaces records missing from either.

▶ 1 Two Anti-Joins via UNION
SELECT employee_id FROM Employees WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries) UNION SELECT employee_id FROM Salaries WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM Employees) ORDER BY employee_id;

Why this is best: Each branch finds one-sided rows; UNION combines both.

Performance: Two subqueries. Indexes help.

Technique Conditional Pivot (Long to Wide)

▼

Reshape long rows into wide columns using CASE WHEN inside an aggregate function. Use MAX for text values, SUM for numeric values.

-- SUM pivot (numeric values, e.g., revenue per month)
SELECT entity_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'A' THEN value END) AS A,
  SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'B' THEN value END) AS B,
  SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'C' THEN value END) AS C
FROM source_table
GROUP BY entity_id;

-- MAX pivot (text values, e.g., name per continent)
SELECT slot_key,
  MAX(CASE WHEN category = 'X' THEN name END) AS X,
  MAX(CASE WHEN category = 'Y' THEN name END) AS Y
FROM source_table
GROUP BY slot_key;

How it works:

  • Each CASE WHEN creates one output column by returning a value only when the row matches that category
  • The aggregate (SUM or MAX) collapses all rows per group into one row
  • Omitting ELSE (or using ELSE NULL) produces NULL for missing categories. ELSE 0 produces zeros instead
  • GROUP BY determines the row key — every output row corresponds to one distinct GROUP BY value
  • You must know the category values at query time. SQL cannot dynamically generate column names

When to reach for this:

  • The output has one column per known category (e.g., one per month, one per store)
  • The problem says "reformat," "pivot," or "one column for each"
  • The source is in long format (entity, category, value) and the output is wide format

When NOT to reach for this:

  • The categories are unknown or variable length — SQL pivot requires fixed columns
  • You need wide to long — that is an unpivot
  • There is only one category per entity — a simple CASE WHEN in SELECT suffices

Example Problems (6)

Hard #618 Students Report By Geography

▼

Pivot students into three columns (America, Asia, Europe) by continent.

Tables: Student (name, continent)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

An international recruiting team generates a side-by-side roster for regional directors.

▶ 1 Row Number + Conditional MAX
SELECT MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'America' THEN name END) AS America, MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'Asia' THEN name END) AS Asia, MAX(CASE WHEN continent = 'Europe' THEN name END) AS Europe FROM ( SELECT name, continent, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY continent ORDER BY name) AS rn FROM Student ) t GROUP BY rn ORDER BY rn;

Why this is best: Assign row numbers within continent, then pivot rows with equal numbers into one reporting row.

Performance: One window + one aggregate.

Easy #1179 Reformat Department Table

▼

Pivot monthly revenue into 12 columns (Jan_Revenue, Feb_Revenue, ...).

Tables: Department (id, revenue, month)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

A finance team builds a side-by-side monthly report from a long-format revenue log.

▶ 1 Conditional MAX Pivot
SELECT id, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Jan' THEN revenue END) AS Jan_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Feb' THEN revenue END) AS Feb_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Mar' THEN revenue END) AS Mar_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Apr' THEN revenue END) AS Apr_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='May' THEN revenue END) AS May_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Jun' THEN revenue END) AS Jun_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Jul' THEN revenue END) AS Jul_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Aug' THEN revenue END) AS Aug_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Sep' THEN revenue END) AS Sep_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Oct' THEN revenue END) AS Oct_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Nov' THEN revenue END) AS Nov_Revenue, MAX(CASE WHEN month='Dec' THEN revenue END) AS Dec_Revenue FROM Department GROUP BY id;

Why this is best: Twelve conditional MAX expressions pivot the long table into wide format.

Performance: One aggregate pass.

Hard #1479 Sales by Day of the Week

▼

Pivot weekly sales per item across seven weekday columns.

Tables: Orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, item_id, quantity), Items (item_id, item_name, item_category)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

Merchandising reads a weekly pattern per SKU to plan weekday-specific promos.

▶ 1 Conditional SUM by DAYNAME
SELECT i.item_category AS Category, SUM(CASE WHEN DAYNAME(o.order_date) = 'Monday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Monday, SUM(CASE WHEN DAYNAME(o.order_date) = 'Tuesday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Tuesday, SUM(CASE WHEN DAYNAME(o.order_date) = 'Wednesday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Wednesday, SUM(CASE WHEN DAYNAME(o.order_date) = 'Thursday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Thursday, SUM(CASE WHEN DAYNAME(o.order_date) = 'Friday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Friday, SUM(CASE WHEN DAYNAME(o.order_date) = 'Saturday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Saturday, SUM(CASE WHEN DAYNAME(o.order_date) = 'Sunday' THEN o.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS Sunday FROM Items i LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.item_id = i.item_id GROUP BY i.item_category ORDER BY i.item_category;

Why this is best: Conditional SUMs pivot the long table into seven columns; LEFT JOIN keeps zero-sales categories.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Easy #1777 Product’s Price for Each Store

▼

Pivot per-store prices into three columns (store1, store2, store3).

Tables: Products (product_id, store, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

A retailer compares prices across three stores side-by-side per product for markdown decisions.

▶ 1 Conditional MAX per Store
SELECT product_id, MAX(CASE WHEN store = 'store1' THEN price END) AS store1, MAX(CASE WHEN store = 'store2' THEN price END) AS store2, MAX(CASE WHEN store = 'store3' THEN price END) AS store3 FROM Products GROUP BY product_id;

Why this is best: Simple pivot with conditional MAX.

Performance: One aggregate.

Medium Pivot Trial Adverse Events by Severity (SUM + COALESCE 0)

▼

Pivot a long-format adverse events table into one row per trial with one column per severity level. Demonstrates SUM (multiple rows per category sum together) and the COALESCE 0 default for missing categories.

Tables: trial_adverse_events (trial_id, severity_category, event_count)

Real-World Example

A clinical research platform builds a per-trial safety summary that lists Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical event counts side by side for each trial, fed into the regulatory dashboard.

▶ 1 Conditional SUM with COALESCE 0 Default
SELECT trial_id, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Mild' THEN event_count END), 0) AS mild_events, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Moderate' THEN event_count END), 0) AS moderate_events, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Severe' THEN event_count END), 0) AS severe_events, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Critical' THEN event_count END), 0) AS critical_events FROM trial_adverse_events GROUP BY trial_id ORDER BY trial_id;

Why this is best: SUM (not MAX) is required because a trial can have multiple rows in the same severity (e.g., TRIAL-002 has two Mild rows that must add to 5). The CASE returns NULL on non-matching rows, which SUM skips. COALESCE wraps the whole SUM so an entirely missing category becomes 0 instead of NULL.

Trace through TRIAL-002:

severity_category event_count CASE for Mild CASE for Moderate CASE for Severe CASE for Critical
Mild33NULLNULLNULL
Mild22NULLNULLNULL
Critical1NULLNULLNULL1
SUM—5NULL → 0NULL → 01

SUM over all-NULL columns returns NULL. COALESCE flips that to 0. Output row for TRIAL-002: (TRIAL-002, 5, 0, 0, 1).

Equivalent shorthand using ELSE 0 inside the CASE:

SELECT trial_id, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Mild' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS mild_events, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Moderate' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS moderate_events, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Severe' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS severe_events, SUM(CASE WHEN severity_category = 'Critical' THEN event_count ELSE 0 END) AS critical_events FROM trial_adverse_events GROUP BY trial_id ORDER BY trial_id;
