  • Every row in the table gets evaluated — no row-level eligibility filter, so no WHERE.
  • The CASE WHEN handles ALL the logic: high-risk rows flip to TRUE, low-risk rows flip to FALSE, and middle-risk rows keep whatever flag they had.
  • Useful contrast to the tiered-discount anchor above (which DOES use WHERE for eligibility).

Tables:

Column Type Notes
transaction_idSERIALprimary key
merchant_nameVARCHARpassthrough
amountDECIMAL(10,2)passthrough
risk_scoreINT (0–100)drives the rule
fraud_flagBOOLEANcolumn being updated; middle-risk rows keep the existing value

Prompt: Apply these rules to every row in approvals:

  • risk_score ≥ 80: set fraud_flag = TRUE.
  • risk_score < 50: set fraud_flag = FALSE.
  • risk_score in 50–79: keep the existing fraud_flag.
▶ 1 Single UPDATE with CASE WHEN, no WHERE clause
UPDATE approvals SET fraud_flag = CASE WHEN risk_score >= 80 THEN TRUE WHEN risk_score < 50 THEN FALSE ELSE fraud_flag END; SELECT * FROM approvals ORDER BY transaction_id;

Why no WHERE clause:

  • WHERE is a row-level eligibility filter. It belongs there only when some rows should NOT be touched at all.
  • Here, every row has a rule that applies — even middle-risk rows have a "keep what you have" rule, encoded as ELSE fraud_flag. Touching them and writing back the same value is harmless.
  • Adding WHERE risk_score >= 80 OR risk_score < 50 would also work, but it's redundant: the CASE already routes every row to the correct outcome, and the WHERE just adds noise.
  • Heuristic: if every CASE path produces the right answer (including "leave it alone" via ELSE col), drop the WHERE. If some rows should be ignored entirely, keep the WHERE.

Trace through the example data:

id risk_score flag before CASE branch flag after
115FALSE< 50 → FALSEFALSE
285FALSE≥ 80 → TRUETRUE
355TRUEELSE (50–79)TRUE (kept)
448TRUE< 50 → FALSEFALSE
592TRUE≥ 80 → TRUETRUE
665FALSEELSE (50–79)FALSE (kept)
730FALSE< 50 → FALSEFALSE
880FALSE≥ 80 → TRUETRUE

Watch out:

  • Branch order matters: WHEN risk_score >= 80 must come before WHEN risk_score < 50 only if both could match the same row, which they cannot here. So either order works for this problem — but keep the most-restrictive-first habit so it's safe when ranges might overlap.
  • ELSE fraud_flag is the load-bearing piece. It tells Postgres "for any row not matching a WHEN, write back the column's existing value." Drop ELSE and middle-risk rows get NULL.
  • Boundary check: the rule "keep it" applies to 50–79. risk_score = 80 falls in the ≥ 80 bucket (becomes TRUE). risk_score = 50 is NOT < 50, so it falls into ELSE (kept). Reading the prompt's inclusivity carefully avoids off-by-one mistakes.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM approvals ORDER BY transaction_id; so the harness sees output.

Easy Tag Sleep Logs by Goal Achievement (4-tier ladder)

▼
  • Same shape as the fraud-flag anchor — one bare UPDATE, no WHERE, all logic inside CASE WHEN.
  • Four tiers based on actual_hours as a percentage of target_hours, computed inline as target_hours * N.
  • Demonstrates the actual >= target * 1.1 form (cleaner than actual > target + target * 0.1) and adjacent-range bookkeeping.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
log_idINTprimary key
user_idINTpassthrough
log_dateDATEpassthrough
target_hoursDECIMAL(4,2)user's nightly goal
actual_hoursDECIMAL(4,2)measured for that night
achievement_statusVARCHAR(20)column being updated; one of 'exceeded', 'met', 'partial', 'missed' (starts NULL)

Prompt: Set achievement_status on every row based on the ratio actual_hours / target_hours:

  • actual ≥ 110% of target → 'exceeded'
  • 100% ≤ actual < 110% → 'met'
  • 50% ≤ actual < 100% → 'partial'
  • actual < 50% → 'missed'
▶ 1 Single UPDATE with 4-tier CASE WHEN, top-down ordered ranges
UPDATE sleep_logs SET achievement_status = CASE WHEN actual_hours >= target_hours * 1.1 THEN 'exceeded' WHEN actual_hours >= target_hours THEN 'met' WHEN actual_hours >= target_hours * 0.5 THEN 'partial' ELSE 'missed' END; SELECT * FROM sleep_logs ORDER BY log_id;

Why this is concise:

  • Top-down ordering removes the upper bound. CASE evaluates branches in order. The 'exceeded' branch claims rows at 110%+. The 'met' branch then only sees rows below 110%, so actual_hours >= target_hours is enough — no need to also write AND actual_hours < target_hours * 1.1.
  • Factor the percentage: target_hours + target_hours * 0.1 simplifies to target_hours * 1.1. Same value, less reading.
  • The lowest tier becomes ELSE. Anything that didn't match any earlier branch is below 50% by elimination — no need to write the bound again.
  • Net result: 4 tiers expressed in 4 lines, each with a single comparison.

Trace through the example data:

log_id target actual ratio CASE branch status
18.009.001.125≥ 1.1exceeded
27.507.501.000≥ target (not ≥ 1.1)met
38.006.500.812≥ target * 0.5partial
47.003.000.428ELSEmissed
58.508.000.941≥ target * 0.5partial
66.005.500.917≥ target * 0.5partial

Watch out:

  • Branch order is load-bearing. Flip 'met' above 'exceeded' and a 120% row would land in 'met' (since 120% >= 100% matches first). Always order from most-restrictive to least.
  • The prompt says "≥ 110%" for exceeded and "≥ 100%" for met, both inclusive on the lower end. Use >=, not >, or boundary rows (exactly 110% or 100%) land in the wrong tier.
  • Because every row gets a tier (no row should keep its old status), no WHERE is needed and no ELSE achievement_status fallback is required — the four rules cover every possible value.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM sleep_logs ORDER BY log_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Apply Tiered Review Status Updates (multi-column CASE in one SET)

▼
  • Two columns updated in ONE statement, each with its own CASE WHEN expression in the SET clause.
  • Both CASEs must use the SAME branch order so each rule's row state is consistent across columns.
  • One CASE applies the multiplier to priority_score; rule 3 has no multiplier so it falls through to ELSE priority_score.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
review_idINTprimary key
icd_codeVARCHARpassthrough
days_since_submissionINTdrives rules 2 and 3
denial_countINTdrives all three rules
review_statusVARCHARcolumn being updated (rule 1, 2, 3)
priority_scoreDECIMAL(10,2)column being updated (rule 1, 2 only; rule 3 leaves unchanged)

Prompt: Apply three rules to every row in code_reviews in a single UPDATE:

  • Rule 1: denial_count ≥ 3 → status = 'escalated', score = score * 1.5
  • Rule 2: denial_count = 2 AND days_since_submission > 14 → status = 'attention_needed', score = score * 1.25
  • Rule 3: denial_count = 1 AND days_since_submission > 30 → status = 'flagged', score unchanged
  • Anything else: both columns unchanged
▶ 1 Single UPDATE with two CASE expressions sharing the same branch order
UPDATE code_reviews SET review_status = CASE WHEN denial_count >= 3 THEN 'escalated' WHEN denial_count = 2 AND days_since_submission > 14 THEN 'attention_needed' WHEN denial_count = 1 AND days_since_submission > 30 THEN 'flagged' ELSE review_status END, priority_score = CASE WHEN denial_count >= 3 THEN priority_score * 1.5 WHEN denial_count = 2 AND days_since_submission > 14 THEN priority_score * 1.25 ELSE priority_score END; SELECT * FROM code_reviews ORDER BY review_id;

Why this is the single-UPDATE shape:

  • One UPDATE, two CASE expressions. The SET clause accepts a comma-separated list of column = expression pairs. Each expression can be its own CASE WHEN.
  • Same branch order in both CASEs. Rule 1 fires before rule 2 in both. If you flipped them in only one column, the row could end up with status from rule 1 but score from rule 2 — an inconsistent row.
  • Rule 3 omits the score branch. The second CASE has only two WHEN clauses; rule 3 rows fall through to ELSE priority_score and keep their score unchanged. Status still flips to 'flagged' via the first CASE.
  • Rules don't overlap, but ELSE is still required. Without ELSE col, rows that match no WHEN get NULL written. Always close both CASEs with the column name as the fallback.

Trace through the example data:

id denial_count days Matching rule new status new score
1010none (ELSE/ELSE)pending (unchanged)50.00 (unchanged)
2220rule 2attention_needed60 * 1.25 = 75.00
335rule 1escalated40 * 1.5 = 60.00
4135rule 3flagged55.00 (rule 3 has no multiplier)
5240rule 2attention_needed70 * 1.25 = 87.50
6112none (12 not > 30)pending (unchanged)45.00 (unchanged)

Watch out:

  • Sequential UPDATEs also produce the right answer here because the WHERE clauses (denial_count = 3 vs 2 vs 1) are disjoint — no row can match two rules. The prompt's "single UPDATE statement" constraint is what forces the CASE form.
  • If rules could overlap, sequential UPDATEs would chain the changes. Rule 1 firing first changes the row state that rule 2 sees, which is rarely what the prompt intends. CASE evaluates every row against the ORIGINAL state, no chaining.
  • Don't drop ELSE col from either CASE. Even though rules cover the rows the prompt cares about, "anything else" still has to land somewhere — and that somewhere is the row's existing value, not NULL.
  • Match the percentage form to the schema. priority_score * 1.5 is unambiguous; priority_score + priority_score * 0.5 is the same value but harder to read. Prefer the multiplier.
  • No WHERE on the UPDATE. Every row needs to be evaluated; rows that match no rule are protected by the ELSE branches in both CASEs.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM code_reviews ORDER BY review_id; so the harness sees output.

Single-Statement DELETE recipe

▼
  • One bare DELETE FROM target WHERE ... statement followed by a confirming SELECT.
  • The WHERE clause names which rows to remove. Anything not matching the WHERE survives.
  • For "keep one per group" rules (deduplication), filter by primary key against a SELECT MIN(pk) ... GROUP BY ... subquery.
  • For "remove orphans" rules, use NOT IN or NOT EXISTS against the parent table.

Signal words: "remove duplicates," "keep only the smallest/largest id per group," "delete orphaned rows," "prune rows older than ...," "deduplicate," "purge."

Technique: DELETE FROM target WHERE pk NOT IN (SELECT MIN(pk) FROM target GROUP BY group_cols); for deduplication, or DELETE FROM target WHERE fk NOT IN (SELECT pk FROM parent); for orphan removal.

Common DELETE cases:

Case Description Code
Conditional delete Remove rows where one or more columns meet a rule. 
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE col_a < threshold
   AND col_b = 'flag';
Duplicate rows Keep one row per group, delete the rest. The subquery returns the IDs to KEEP. 
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE pk NOT IN (
     SELECT MIN(pk)
       FROM target_table
      GROUP BY group_col_1, group_col_2
 );
Orphan rows Foreign key has no matching parent row anymore. 
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE fk NOT IN (
     SELECT pk FROM parent_table
      WHERE pk IS NOT NULL
 );
Cross table Delete rows where a related row in another table meets a condition. 
DELETE FROM target_table t
 USING other_table o
 WHERE t.fk = o.id
   AND o.status = 'expired';
Time-based pruning Delete rows older than N days. "Older" means smaller date, so use <. 
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE created_at < CURRENT_DATE - 90;
Two-condition (group + row) Group must qualify AND the individual row must qualify. Two separate filters in the WHERE. 
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE group_id IN (
     SELECT group_id
       FROM target_table
      GROUP BY group_id
     HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
 )
   AND row_status = 'pending';
NULL-safe positive WHERE When the keep-set might contain NULL, NOT IN breaks. Write the WHERE for the rows to DELETE, not the inverse. 
-- Avoid: WHERE pk NOT IN (SELECT keep_pk FROM ...)
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE duration < 180
    OR quality_flag IS NULL;

Common pitfalls:

Pitfall How to avoid
Subquery column shape mismatch WHERE (col_a, col_b) NOT IN (SELECT MIN(pk) FROM ... GROUP BY col_a, col_b) errors with "subquery has too few columns." The subquery returns the IDs to keep; filter the outer DELETE by pk, not by the group key tuple.
NOT IN with NULLs If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row and DELETE removes nothing. Either filter NULLs from the subquery or rewrite as NOT EXISTS (which handles NULLs).
Forgetting WHERE entirely DELETE FROM target; with no WHERE wipes the table. Always read your WHERE clause aloud before submitting.
MySQL "can't reference target table in subquery" MySQL forbids DELETE FROM t WHERE id IN (SELECT ... FROM t) directly. Wrap the subquery with another SELECT (WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT MIN(id) ... ) AS sub)) or use a CTE. Postgres has no such restriction.
Missing trailing SELECT Without a final SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY ...; the harness sees no rows and reports failure even when DELETE succeeded.

Skeleton you'll fill in:

-- Deduplication: keep MIN(pk) per group, delete the rest
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE pk NOT IN (
     SELECT MIN(pk)
       FROM target_table
      GROUP BY group_col_1, group_col_2
 );

-- Orphan removal: delete rows whose foreign key has no parent
DELETE FROM target_table
 WHERE fk NOT IN (SELECT pk FROM parent_table WHERE pk IS NOT NULL);

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY pk;

Anchor problems — article view deduplication (DELETE NOT IN with MIN per group, the canonical "keep one per group" pattern).

Easy Remove Duplicate Article Views by User

▼
  • Classic dedupe: keep one row per (article_id, user_id) group — the one with the smallest view_id.
  • Subquery returns the IDs to KEEP; outer DELETE removes everything else.
  • The first instinct — matching (article_id, user_id) NOT IN (...) — trips on a column-shape mismatch. The fix is to filter on the primary key.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
view_idINTprimary key, monotonic; smallest = earliest
article_idINTfirst part of the dedupe key
user_idINTsecond part of the dedupe key
viewed_atTIMESTAMPpassthrough; not used in the rule
session_idVARCHAR(50)passthrough

Prompt: Remove duplicate views — rows that share the same (article_id, user_id) as another row. Keep only the row with the smallest view_id per group.

▶ 1 DELETE WHERE pk NOT IN (SELECT MIN(pk) ... GROUP BY group_cols)
DELETE FROM article_views WHERE view_id NOT IN ( SELECT MIN(view_id) FROM article_views GROUP BY article_id, user_id ); SELECT * FROM article_views ORDER BY view_id;

How to read the WHERE clause: "Delete every row whose view_id is NOT the minimum within its (article_id, user_id) group." The subquery first computes the minimum view_id per group (the rows to KEEP), then the outer DELETE removes everything else.

The mismatch you'll trip on first:

  • Writing WHERE (article_id, user_id) NOT IN (SELECT MIN(view_id) FROM ... GROUP BY article_id, user_id) errors with "subquery has too few columns."
  • The left side has 2 columns (the tuple), the right side returns 1 column (MIN(view_id)). Postgres can't compare a 2-tuple to a scalar.
  • The fix is to think about it differently: the subquery already gives you the IDs of rows to KEEP. Filter the outer DELETE by view_id, not by the tuple.

Trace through the example data:

view_id article user group MIN of group verdict
11015(101, 5)1keep
21015(101, 5)1delete (2 ≠ 1)
31015(101, 5)1delete (3 ≠ 1)
41025(102, 5)4keep
51017(101, 7)5keep
61017(101, 7)5delete (6 ≠ 5)
71038(103, 8)7keep
81038(103, 8)7delete (8 ≠ 7)

Final state: 4 rows survive (1, 4, 5, 7). Four duplicates (2, 3, 6, 8) get deleted.

Watch out:

  • Subquery shape rule: WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM ...) compares one column to one column. WHERE (x1, x2) NOT IN (SELECT y FROM ...) needs a 2-column subquery (SELECT y1, y2 FROM ...). For dedup, use single-column on both sides — the primary key.
  • NOT IN with NULLs is silent. If view_id can be NULL (it can't here because it's a primary key), one NULL in the subquery makes NOT IN evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row and DELETE keeps everything. Use NOT EXISTS when the column is nullable.
  • MIN vs MAX: the prompt says "smallest view_id," so use MIN. For "keep most recent," swap to MAX. The structure stays the same.
  • MySQL caveat: MySQL forbids reading from the same table you're deleting in a subquery. Wrap with another SELECT layer (WHERE view_id IN (SELECT view_id FROM (SELECT MIN(view_id) ...) AS sub)) or use a CTE. Postgres has no such restriction.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM article_views ORDER BY view_id; so the harness sees the surviving rows.

Medium Remove Obsolete Milestone Records After Final Delivery

▼
  • Two-condition DELETE: a row is removed only if its shipment qualifies AND the row itself isn't exempt.
  • Distinct from the dedup pattern — here the qualification rule is on the SHIPMENT (does it have a delivered milestone?), not on the milestone row.
  • The first instinct — "keep MAX(milestone_id) of the delivered ones" — over-deletes shipments that have NO delivered milestone yet, because none of their IDs land in the keep-set.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
milestone_idSERIALprimary key
shipment_idINTgroups milestones by shipment
milestone_statusVARCHAR(50)'picked_up' | 'in_transit' | 'out_for_delivery' | 'delivered'
milestone_timestampTIMESTAMPpassthrough
location_codeVARCHAR(20)passthrough

Prompt: Delete obsolete milestone records.

  • A shipment is "completed" once it has a 'delivered' milestone.
  • For completed shipments, all earlier milestones become obsolete — delete them.
  • Keep the 'delivered' milestone itself (it's the survivor).
  • Shipments that have NO delivered milestone yet are still in flight — do NOT touch any of their rows.
▶ 1 Two-condition WHERE: shipment-level eligibility AND row-level exemption
DELETE FROM shipment_milestones WHERE shipment_id IN ( SELECT shipment_id FROM shipment_milestones WHERE milestone_status = 'delivered' ) AND milestone_status <> 'delivered'; SELECT * FROM shipment_milestones ORDER BY shipment_id, milestone_timestamp;

How to read the WHERE clause:

  • Subquery (shipment-level eligibility): "list every shipment_id that has at least one delivered milestone." This is the set of completed shipments.
  • First AND-clause: the row's shipment must be in that set. Anything else is an in-flight shipment and gets skipped entirely.
  • Second AND-clause: within those completed shipments, only delete the milestones that are NOT the delivered one.
  • Net effect: delete rows belonging to a completed shipment, but spare the delivered milestone itself.

Trace through the example data:

milestone_id shipment_id status shipment in keep-set? status = delivered? verdict
1100picked_upyes (100 has delivered)nodelete
2100in_transityesnodelete
3100out_for_deliveryyesnodelete
4100deliveredyesYES (exempt)keep
5200picked_upno (in-flight)—keep
6200in_transitno—keep
7300picked_upyes (300 has delivered)nodelete
8300deliveredyesYES (exempt)keep

Survivors: 4 (delivered for ship 100), 5 and 6 (ship 200 still in flight), 8 (delivered for ship 300). Four rows deleted.

Watch out:

  • Group-eligibility vs row-eligibility. When a rule reads "for groups satisfying X, delete rows satisfying Y," the WHERE has TWO conditions: one finds the eligible groups (subquery), one filters within them. Mixing them into a single NOT IN MAX shortcut works for dedup but breaks here.
  • The exemption uses milestone_status <> 'delivered' rather than milestone_id NOT IN (delivered ids). Both work, but the string compare is easier to read and avoids a second subquery.
  • NOT IN with NULLs caveat applies to the subquery. If shipment_id could be NULL on some rows (it can't here, NOT NULL constraint), you'd need NOT EXISTS instead.
  • The trailing SELECT orders by shipment_id, milestone_timestamp to match the prompt; matching the harness's expected sort key is part of correctness.

Easy Remove Incomplete Sleep Sessions (positive WHERE vs NOT IN + NULL handling)

▼
  • Two-condition DELETE where one rule fires on a numeric threshold and the other on NULL.
  • Demonstrates why writing the WHERE as a positive delete (rows-to-act-on) beats inverting through NOT IN.
  • Walks through how NULL behaves in a WHERE clause: NULL comparisons evaluate to NULL, and WHERE only fires on TRUE.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
session_idINTprimary key
user_idINTpassthrough
session_dateDATEpassthrough
duration_minutesINTnumeric threshold column; can be NULL
quality_scoreINT 1-10NULL-trigger column

Prompt: Remove sleep sessions where duration_minutes < 180 OR quality_score IS NULL. Write a single DELETE statement, then a confirming SELECT * FROM sleep_sessions ORDER BY session_id;.

▶ 1 Positive DELETE (writes WHERE for rows to delete, not rows to keep)
DELETE FROM sleep_sessions WHERE duration_minutes < 180 OR quality_score IS NULL; SELECT * FROM sleep_sessions ORDER BY session_id;

How NULL behaves in a WHERE clause (the rule that drives this whole problem):

  • SQL has three possible answers to a comparison: TRUE, FALSE, and NULL.
  • NULL means "unknown." Any comparison involving NULL gives NULL: NULL < 180 is NULL, NULL = 7 is NULL, even NULL = NULL is NULL.
  • The only operator that gives a real TRUE/FALSE answer for NULL is IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL).
  • WHERE only fires on TRUE. Both FALSE and NULL are treated the same: the row stays untouched.
  • So in a DELETE, a NULL-valued comparison means the row is NOT deleted — even though the comparison didn't strictly say "false."

Why "write the WHERE for rows to delete" wins over "invert through NOT IN": three sample rows show how each approach behaves. Session 14 (duration=120, quality=7) and session 16 (duration=200, quality=NULL) should be DELETED. Session 18 (duration=NULL, quality=7) should be KEPT.

Approach 1: Positive DELETE — WHERE duration < 180 OR quality IS NULL

session_id duration quality first check first result second check second result combined OR DELETE fires? action correct?
141207120 < 180TRUE7 IS NULLFALSETRUEYESDELETEDYES
16200NULL200 < 180FALSENULL IS NULLTRUETRUEYESDELETEDYES
18NULL7NULL < 180NULL7 IS NULLFALSENULLNOKEPTYES

Approach 2: NOT IN with AND keep set — keep set = quality IS NOT NULL AND duration >= 180

session_id duration quality first check first result second check second result combined AND in keep set? NOT IN deletes? action correct?
1412077 IS NOT NULLTRUE120 >= 180FALSEFALSENOYESDELETEDYES
16200NULLNULL IS NOT NULLFALSE200 >= 180TRUEFALSENOYESDELETEDYES
18NULL77 IS NOT NULLTRUENULL >= 180NULLNULLNOYESDELETEDNO

Approach 3: NOT IN with OR keep set — keep set = quality IS NOT NULL OR duration >= 180

session_id duration quality first check first result second check second result combined OR in keep set? NOT IN deletes? action correct?
1412077 IS NOT NULLTRUE120 >= 180FALSETRUEYESNOKEPTNO
16200NULLNULL IS NOT NULLFALSE200 >= 180TRUETRUEYESNOKEPTNO
18NULL77 IS NOT NULLTRUENULL >= 180NULLTRUEYESNOKEPTYES

The takeaway: Approach 1 has YES all the way down. Approach 2 fails on session 18 (the NULL-duration row). Approach 3 fails on sessions 14 and 16 (the regular delete rows). Neither AND nor OR in the inverted keep set covers every case — only the positive DELETE handles NULLs cleanly without you having to think about how three-valued logic propagates through inversion.

Watch out:

  • Rule of thumb: express WHERE clauses as the condition for the rows you want to ACT on, not as the inverse of the rows you want to keep. It's almost always shorter and almost always handles NULLs correctly.
  • If you really need the inverted form, coalesce NULLs to a sentinel that passes the threshold: WHERE quality_score IS NOT NULL AND COALESCE(duration_minutes, 999) >= 180. The COALESCE(NULL, 999) turns NULL into 999, which passes >= 180, so the NULL-duration row stays in the keep set. Awkward but correct.
  • Tuple comparison with NULL is also broken. (col1, col2) <> (NULL, NULL) evaluates to NULL because any equality with NULL is NULL. Always use col1 IS NOT NULL AND col2 IS NOT NULL when you want to filter for both columns being populated.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM sleep_sessions ORDER BY session_id; so the harness sees the post-delete snapshot.

Single-Statement INSERT recipe

▼
  • One bare INSERT INTO target (cols) SELECT ... statement followed by a confirming SELECT.
  • Transformations (computed columns, literals, type changes) live in the inner SELECT's column list.
  • Source-row eligibility lives in the inner SELECT's WHERE clause.
  • Use this to seed or archive rows from one table into another, applying transformations along the way.

Signal words: "archive applications into ...," "copy qualifying rows to ...," "seed the target table from ...," "insert all rows where ...," "do not duplicate existing rows."

Technique: INSERT INTO target_table (col1, col2, ...) SELECT expr1, expr2, ... FROM source WHERE cond AND key NOT IN (SELECT key FROM target_table); followed by SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY ...;.

Common pitfalls:

Pitfall How to avoid
Duplicate-key conflict If the target's primary key already exists, plain INSERT errors out with "duplicate key value violates unique constraint." Filter the source with WHERE key NOT IN (SELECT key FROM target) or use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING if the dialect supports it.
Column count or order mismatch The inner SELECT's column list must line up positionally with the INSERT INTO target (...) column list. Always name the target columns explicitly — never rely on table column order, which can change.
Computed column on the wrong side Calculations like approval_date - submission_date happen inside the SELECT, not as a target column expression. Add an alias (AS days_to_approval) so the column maps cleanly to the target.
NOT IN with NULLs If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row and excludes everything. Filter NULLs out (WHERE key IS NOT NULL) or use NOT EXISTS, which handles NULLs cleanly.
Missing trailing SELECT Without a final SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY ...; the harness sees no rows and reports failure even when the INSERT worked.

Skeleton you'll fill in:

INSERT INTO target_table (col_a, col_b, computed_col, literal_col)
SELECT s.col_a,
       s.col_b,
       expr_using_source_columns AS computed_col,
       'literal value'           AS literal_col
  FROM source_table AS s
 WHERE eligibility_predicate
   AND s.key NOT IN (SELECT key FROM target_table WHERE key IS NOT NULL);

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY key;

Anchor problems — archive approved loan applications (INSERT ... SELECT with computed columns, literals, and an anti-join against existing target rows).

Medium Archive Approved Loan Applications into History

▼
  • One bare INSERT INTO ... SELECT statement copies qualifying rows from loan_applications into application_history.
  • Three transformations: computed days_to_approval, literal 'funded', and the run-time archive_date.
  • NOT IN anti-join against application_history keeps already-archived rows from being inserted twice.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
loan_applications
(source)		application_idINTprimary key, used for anti-join
applicant_nameVARCHARpassthrough
submission_dateDATEpassthrough; subtracted from approval_date
approval_dateDATEsubtracted from submission_date for days_to_approval
funded_dateDATEeligibility filter; NOT NULL means funded
loan_amountDECIMAL(10,2)passthrough
statusVARCHAReligibility filter; must equal 'approved'
application_history
(target)		application_idINTprimary key
applicant_nameVARCHARcopied from source
submission_dateDATEcopied from source
approval_dateDATEcopied from source
funded_dateDATEcopied from source
loan_amountDECIMAL(10,2)copied from source
days_to_approvalINTcomputed: approval_date - submission_date
archive_dateDATEruntime: CURRENT_DATE
archive_reasonVARCHAR(50)literal: 'funded'

Prompt: Insert qualifying rows from loan_applications into application_history:

  • Eligibility: status = 'approved' AND funded_date IS NOT NULL.
  • Skip rows whose application_id already exists in application_history.
  • Compute days_to_approval = approval_date - submission_date.
  • Set archive_date to the current date.
  • Set archive_reason to the literal 'funded'.
▶ 1 INSERT INTO ... SELECT with computed columns, literals, and a NOT IN anti-join
INSERT INTO application_history ( application_id, applicant_name, submission_date, approval_date, funded_date, loan_amount, days_to_approval, archive_date, archive_reason ) SELECT la.application_id, la.applicant_name, la.submission_date, la.approval_date, la.funded_date, la.loan_amount, la.approval_date - la.submission_date AS days_to_approval, CURRENT_DATE AS archive_date, 'funded' AS archive_reason FROM loan_applications AS la WHERE la.status = 'approved' AND la.funded_date IS NOT NULL AND la.application_id NOT IN ( SELECT application_id FROM application_history ); SELECT * FROM application_history ORDER BY application_id;

How the four pieces map to the prompt:

  • Eligibility filter — WHERE status = 'approved' AND funded_date IS NOT NULL drops rows that aren't ready to archive.
  • Anti-join — application_id NOT IN (SELECT application_id FROM application_history) protects against duplicate-key conflicts when the script runs more than once.
  • Computed column — la.approval_date - la.submission_date AS days_to_approval calculates inline. The alias matches the target column name.
  • Literal and runtime values — 'funded' is a hardcoded string, CURRENT_DATE is evaluated at INSERT time. Both get aliases so the column list lines up.

Trace through the example data:

app_id status funded_date already in history? inserted?
101approved2024-01-15noyes
102approved2024-01-20YESno (anti-join skips)
103approvedNULLnono (not funded)
104pendingNULLnono (not approved)
105approved2024-01-28noyes

Two rows inserted (101, 105). Row 102 is skipped by the anti-join. Final state: 3 rows in application_history — the original 102 plus the two new ones.

Watch out:

  • NOT IN with NULLs is the silent killer. If application_history.application_id ever contains NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row and the INSERT inserts nothing. Either guard with WHERE application_id IS NOT NULL in the subquery, or rewrite as NOT EXISTS: AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM application_history h WHERE h.application_id = la.application_id).
  • Column lists line up by position, not by name. The order of expressions in the SELECT must match the order of columns in INSERT INTO target (...). Aliases inside SELECT are documentation; they do not steer the mapping.
  • CURRENT_DATE evaluates at INSERT time, so re-running the script tomorrow would write a different archive_date. That's usually the desired behavior for an archive timestamp.
  • approval_date - submission_date in Postgres returns an INTEGER number of days. If either operand is TIMESTAMP, you'd get an INTERVAL instead and have to extract days; sticking to DATE columns keeps the math simple.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM application_history ORDER BY application_id; so the harness sees the post-insert state.

Window Function Edges topic

▼
  • Window function distinctions that flip the answer.
  • ROWS vs RANGE — controls whether the frame counts physical rows or value ranges; affects rolling windows over missing values.
  • RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER — differ on how ties and gaps are handled.
  • Window functions evaluate at the SELECT step, so they cannot be referenced in WHERE or HAVING — wrap in a CTE or subquery.

Reference Window Function Edges

▼

The two window-function distinctions that flip answers: ROWS vs RANGE, and RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER.

ROWS BETWEEN vs RANGE BETWEEN

What it does
ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE counts by ORDER BY value. They diverge when ORDER BY values repeat or have gaps.
When to reach for it
Time-series with missing dates: use RANGE for "last 7 days" so missing days still count. Use ROWS for "last 7 records" regardless of date.
SUM(amt) OVER (
  ORDER BY d
  RANGE BETWEEN
    INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING
    AND CURRENT ROW
)

RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER

What it does
RANK skips numbers after ties (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2); ROW_NUMBER never ties (1, 2, 3) and the tiebreak depends on ORDER BY.
When to reach for it
"Nth distinct" use DENSE_RANK; "exactly one winner per group" use ROW_NUMBER with a tiebreak; "Olympic-style ranking" use RANK.
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
  PARTITION BY dept
  ORDER BY salary DESC
)
